uni-ba-pol-international-relations.title: International Relations
uni-ba-pol-international-relations.description: Theories of international relations, power and security concepts, the Cold War and after, the UN and global governance, globalisation and India's foreign policy. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Political Science programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Theories of International Relations
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Global Politics / IR core)
courses.summary: Origins of IR as a discipline and the great debates; classical realism and neo-realism; liberalism, neo-liberal institutionalism and democratic peace; Marxist and critical theories; constructivism, feminism and the English School.
outcomes: Trace the emergence of IR and its 'great debates'
Explain Morgenthau's six principles and Waltz's structural realism
Explain liberal institutionalism, interdependence and democratic peace
Explain Marxist, constructivist and feminist approaches

scenes.text: After the carnage of World War I, a Welsh university founded the first chair in International Politics.
Scholars hoped law and the League of Nations would end war.
Twenty years later, a new war forced a rethink.

steps.title: Birth of the discipline
steps.body: The Woodrow Wilson Chair at Aberystwyth (1919) is usually taken as IR's founding. Early 'idealists' (Wilson's Fourteen Points, Norman Angell's The Great Illusion, 1910) believed war could be abolished through collective security, international law and public opinion.

steps.title: First debate: idealism vs realism
steps.body: E.H. Carr (The Twenty Years' Crisis, 1939) attacked 'utopianism' for ignoring power. Hans Morgenthau (Politics Among Nations, 1948) built classical realism. This debate (1930s–40s) left realism dominant.

steps.title: Second, third and fourth debates
steps.body: Second (1950s–60s): traditionalists (Hedley Bull) vs behaviouralists (Morton Kaplan, J. David Singer) on method. Third (1970s–80s): 'inter-paradigm debate' among realism, liberalism/pluralism and structuralism/Marxism; also neo-neo debate. Fourth (late 1980s on): rationalists vs reflectivists (Robert Keohane's 1988 framing) — positivism vs post-positivism (critical theory, constructivism, post-structuralism, feminism).

steps.title: Worked example: sorting arguments
steps.body: 'The League failed because states pursued power, not law' — realist critique (Carr). 'Quantify alliance patterns from 1815–1945 to predict war' — behavioural (Singer's Correlates of War project, begun 1963). 'Sovereignty is a social construct' — reflectivist/constructivist.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Carr was a critic of idealism but also warned against pure realism — he argued sound thought needs both utopia and reality.

quiz.q: The Twenty Years' Crisis was written by
quiz.why: Carr's 1939 book critiqued inter-war idealism.

quiz.q: The first IR chair was established at
quiz.why: The Woodrow Wilson Chair at Aberystwyth was founded in 1919.

quiz.q: The second great debate concerned
quiz.why: It pitted historical-philosophical approaches against behavioural science.

scenes.text: In 416 BCE Athens demanded that tiny Melos surrender.
'The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must,' said the Athenians (Thucydides).
Realists see this logic recurring through history.

steps.title: Classical realism
steps.body: Roots: Thucydides, Machiavelli, Hobbes. Morgenthau's six principles: (1) politics is governed by objective laws rooted in human nature; (2) interest defined in terms of power; (3) interest is a universal concept whose content varies; (4) universal moral principles cannot be applied to states' actions in the abstract; (5) no nation's moral aspirations equal universal moral law; (6) autonomy of the political sphere. Other figures: Reinhold Niebuhr, George Kennan.

steps.title: Neo-realism (structural realism)
steps.body: Kenneth Waltz (Theory of International Politics, 1979): explanation from the structure of the system, not human nature. Structure = (1) ordering principle — anarchy; (2) function of units — alike (states as 'like units'); (3) distribution of capabilities — polarity. Bipolarity is more stable than multipolarity. States are security maximisers (defensive realism).

steps.title: Offensive realism and security dilemma
steps.body: John Mearsheimer (The Tragedy of Great Power Politics, 2001): states seek to maximise relative power and regional hegemony. Security dilemma (John Herz, 1950; Robert Jervis): measures one state takes for security reduce others' security, triggering arms races.

steps.title: Worked example: security dilemma
steps.body: State A raises its defence budget from $50 bn to $60 bn for 'defence'. State B sees a 20% rise ((60 − 50)/50) and responds with +20% of its own, from $40 bn to $48 bn. A interprets B's move as hostile and raises again. Neither is safer; both are poorer — the spiral model.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Classical realism blames human nature; neo-realism blames anarchic structure. Don't call Waltz a human-nature realist.

quiz.q: For Waltz, bipolarity is
quiz.why: Two great powers can monitor and balance each other with fewer miscalculations.

quiz.q: A state's budget rises from 80 to 100. Percentage increase
Politics Among Nations was first published in
quiz.why: Morgenthau's textbook appeared in 1948.

quiz.q: Offensive realists believe states maximise
quiz.why: Mearsheimer argues the best guarantee of survival is to be the strongest.

story.title: Why don't France and Germany fight anymore?

scenes.text: They fought three wars between 1870 and 1945.
Then they pooled coal and steel (1951) and built the European Union.
Liberals credit interdependence, institutions and democracy.

steps.title: Liberal roots
steps.body: Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795): republican constitutions, a federation of free states, cosmopolitan right. Adam Smith and Richard Cobden: free trade promotes peace. Wilsonian idealism: self-determination, collective security.

steps.title: Interdependence and institutions
steps.body: Keohane and Nye (Power and Interdependence, 1977): 'complex interdependence' — multiple channels, no hierarchy of issues, military force less useful. Neo-liberal institutionalism (Keohane, After Hegemony, 1984): even in anarchy, institutions reduce transaction costs, provide information and lengthen the 'shadow of the future', enabling cooperation. Absolute gains matter more than relative gains. Functionalism (David Mitrany) and neo-functionalism (Ernst Haas, spillover) explain European integration.

steps.title: Democratic peace
steps.body: Michael Doyle (1983) revived Kant: liberal democracies rarely, if ever, fight wars with each other (though they fight non-democracies). Explanations: institutional constraints and shared norms.

steps.title: Worked example: prisoner's dilemma
steps.body: Two states choose Cooperate (C) or Defect (D). Payoffs (A, B): CC = (3, 3), CD = (0, 5), DC = (5, 0), DD = (1, 1). In a one-shot game, D is dominant for both (5 > 3 and 1 > 0), giving (1, 1). Repeated play with institutions that monitor compliance makes tit-for-tat viable, yielding (3, 3) — Axelrod's Evolution of Cooperation (1984).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Neo-liberals accept anarchy and state-centrism; they differ from neo-realists on whether cooperation is achievable and on relative vs absolute gains.

items.text: Democracies do not fight each other

quiz.q: 'Complex interdependence' is from
quiz.why: Their 1977 book introduced the concept.

quiz.q: In the payoff matrix CC (3,3), CD (0,5), DC (5,0), DD (1,1), the one-shot equilibrium is
quiz.why: Defecting is better for each whatever the other does, so both defect.

quiz.q: Perpetual Peace was written by
quiz.why: Kant published it in 1795.

lessons.title: Marxism, constructivism, feminism and the English School

scenes.text: The USA feels less threatened by 500 British nuclear weapons than by 5 North Korean ones.
Material power alone can't explain this.
Alexander Wendt: what matters is shared ideas — friend or enemy.

steps.title: Marxist and critical theories
steps.body: Lenin's theory of imperialism; dependency and world-systems (Wallerstein); Gramscian IR (Robert Cox: 'Theory is always for someone and for some purpose', 1981) distinguishes problem-solving and critical theory; hegemony as consent-based world order.

steps.title: Constructivism
steps.body: Alexander Wendt ('Anarchy is What States Make of It', 1992; Social Theory of International Politics, 1999): anarchy has no fixed logic — Hobbesian (enemy), Lockean (rival), Kantian (friend) cultures. Identities and interests are socially constructed through interaction; norms matter (Martha Finnemore, Kathryn Sikkink — norm life cycle). Nicholas Onuf coined 'constructivism' in IR (1989).

steps.title: Feminism
steps.body: J. Ann Tickner (Gender in International Relations, 1992) reformulated Morgenthau's principles from a feminist perspective; Cynthia Enloe (Bananas, Beaches and Bases, 1989): 'the personal is international'. Focus on gendered security, women in conflict (UNSC Resolution 1325, 2000).

steps.title: The English School
steps.body: Hedley Bull (The Anarchical Society, 1977), Martin Wight: states form an 'international society' bound by common rules and institutions (diplomacy, international law, balance of power, war, great-power management) even without world government. Pluralist vs solidarist strands.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Constructivism is not an idealist hope that ideas are nice; it holds that ideas constitute interests, which can produce conflict as well as cooperation.

activity.prompt: Match the text to the theory
pairs: Anarchy is What States Make of It
Theory is always for someone and for some purpose

quiz.q: Wendt's three cultures of anarchy are
quiz.why: They correspond to relations of enmity, rivalry and friendship.

quiz.q: UNSC Resolution 1325 concerns
quiz.why: Adopted in 2000, it calls for women's participation in peace processes.

quiz.q: Hedley Bull belongs to
quiz.why: Bull's international-society approach is central to the English School.

options: War is economically irrational in an interdependent world
questions.why: Angell claimed economic interdependence made conquest unprofitable.

options: Interest defined in terms of power
questions.why: His second principle states it directly.

questions.q: Waltz's structure has three parts; which is NOT one?
questions.why: Waltz explicitly moved explanation away from human nature to system structure.

questions.q: Defensive realism holds that states maximise
questions.why: Waltz's defensive realism sees states seeking enough power to be secure.

questions.q: After Hegemony (1984) is by
questions.why: Keohane explained how regimes persist after US hegemony declines.

questions.q: Neo-functional 'spillover' is from
questions.why: Haas argued integration in one sector spreads to others.

questions.q: Democratic peace thesis was revived by
questions.why: Doyle's 1983 articles on Kant and liberal legacies revived it.

questions.q: A state's defence budget goes 40 → 48 → 60. Total percentage rise

questions.why: Nicholas Onuf introduced it in World of Our Making (1989).

questions.why: She rewrote Morgenthau's six principles from a feminist view.

questions.why: Keohane's 1988 ISA presidential address set up this divide.

questions.why: Robert Cox drew it in his 1981 article.

questions.q: In a repeated prisoner's dilemma, cooperation becomes possible mainly because
options: The shadow of the future makes reciprocity pay
questions.why: Future interactions let states punish defection and reward cooperation.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Power, National Interest and Security
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Global Politics / IR core)
courses.summary: National power and its elements, hard/soft/smart power, national interest, balance of power, collective security, deterrence and arms control, and non-traditional and human security.
outcomes: List elements of national power and distinguish hard, soft and smart power
Explain national interest and instruments of foreign policy
Compare balance of power and collective security
Explain nuclear deterrence, arms control and human security

scenes.text: Over 170 countries mark International Yoga Day, which India proposed at the UN in 2014.
India also builds aircraft carriers like INS Vikrant.
Power comes from attraction as well as coercion.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Power in IR is the ability of a state to influence others' behaviour to achieve its goals. Morgenthau: 'man's control over the minds and actions of other men'. Power is relative, situational and dynamic.

steps.title: Elements of national power (Morgenthau)
steps.body: Tangible: geography, natural resources, industrial capacity, military preparedness, population. Intangible: national character, national morale, quality of diplomacy, quality of government. Ray Cline's formula: Pp = (C + E + M) × (S + W), where C = critical mass (population + territory), E = economic capability, M = military capability, S = strategic purpose, W = will to pursue national strategy.

steps.title: Worked example: Cline's formula
steps.body: Country X: C = 80, E = 120, M = 100 (each out of a scale), S = 0.6, W = 0.7. Pp = (80 + 120 + 100) × (0.6 + 0.7) = 300 × 1.3 = 390. Country Y: C = 100, E = 150, M = 120, S = 0.4, W = 0.4 → 370 × 0.8 = 296. X has less material power but more perceived power because of stronger strategy and will.

steps.title: Hard, soft and smart power
steps.body: Joseph Nye (Bound to Lead, 1990; Soft Power, 2004): hard power — coercion through military and economic means (sticks and carrots); soft power — attraction through culture, political values and foreign policies seen as legitimate. Smart power — combining both. Indian soft power: Bollywood, yoga, diaspora, democracy, vaccine diplomacy (Vaccine Maitri, 2021).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Economic sanctions and aid are hard power (carrots/sticks), not soft power. Cline's formula multiplies material power by strategy and will — weak will can shrink large capabilities.

quiz.q: Using Cline's formula with C+E+M = 200 and S+W = 1.5, perceived power is
Soft power was coined by
quiz.why: Joseph Nye introduced it in 1990.

quiz.q: Which is an intangible element of power?
quiz.why: Morale is a psychological factor that cannot be directly measured.

lessons.title: National interest and instruments of foreign policy

scenes.text: After 2022, India kept buying discounted Russian oil despite Western pressure.
Its minister said India buys where it gets the best deal for its people.
A clear statement of national interest.

steps.title: National interest
steps.body: The goals a state pursues in external relations. Morgenthau: the minimum national interest is survival — protecting physical, political and cultural identity. Classifications (Thomas Robinson): primary (survival), secondary, permanent, variable, general, specific. Critics: vague, can justify anything; constructivists: interests are shaped by identity.

steps.title: Instruments
steps.body: Diplomacy (negotiation, persuasion — Morgenthau's 'four tasks': determine objectives, assess others' objectives, assess compatibility, use suitable means); propaganda/public diplomacy; economic instruments (aid, trade, sanctions); alliances; military force and coercive diplomacy (Thomas Schelling: compellence vs deterrence).

steps.title: Worked example: deterrence vs compellence
steps.body: Deterrence: 'If you invade, we will retaliate' — aims to prevent an action. Compellence: 'Withdraw your troops or we will strike' — aims to make the other start or stop an action. Schelling argued compellence is harder because the target must visibly comply.

steps.title: Strategic autonomy
steps.body: India frames its national interest through 'strategic autonomy' — keeping options open with multiple partners (Quad with the USA, Japan and Australia; BRICS and SCO with Russia and China).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Diplomacy is not just friendliness; it is the management of relations by negotiation, including hard bargaining.

activity.prompt: Match the instrument to the example

quiz.q: Morgenthau's minimum national interest is
quiz.why: He saw survival of identity as the irreducible core.

quiz.q: Compellence aims to
quiz.why: Schelling defined it as making an adversary do or undo something.

quiz.q: 'Strategic autonomy' refers to India's
quiz.why: It means keeping freedom of action by engaging multiple powers.

lessons.title: Balance of power and collective security

scenes.text: After Napoleon, the great powers met at Vienna in 1815.
They aimed at equilibrium so no one could dominate.
Europe avoided a general war for almost a century.

steps.title: Balance of power
steps.body: A situation or policy in which power is distributed so that no state can dominate others. Methods: alliances and counter-alliances, armaments, compensation (territorial), divide and rule, buffer states, intervention, 'holder of the balance' (Britain in 19th-century Europe). Waltz: balancing is the system's tendency; Stephen Walt: states balance against threats (power, proximity, offensive capability, intentions), not just power. Alternative: bandwagoning.

steps.title: Collective security
steps.body: 'All for one and one for all': an attack on any member is an attack on all, met by collective response. Embodied in the League Covenant (Art. 16) and UN Charter Chapter VII (Arts 39–51). Conditions: agreement on aggressor, willingness to act even against friends, overwhelming preponderance. Failures: Manchuria (1931), Abyssinia (1935). UN: Korea (1950, during Soviet boycott), Gulf War (1991, Resolution 678).

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body: Balance of power is decentralised and directed against a specific power; collective security is universal and directed against any aggressor. Collective defence (NATO's Article 5) is an alliance of some states against an outside threat — not collective security.

steps.title: Worked example: classify
steps.body: NATO responding to 9/11 by invoking Article 5 (2001) — collective defence. UNSC authorising force to expel Iraq from Kuwait (1990–91) — collective security. Britain switching sides to check the strongest continental power — balance of power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: NATO is not a collective security organisation in the strict sense; it is collective defence. Article 51 of the UN Charter preserves individual and collective self-defence.

activity.prompt: Balance of power, collective security, or collective defence?

quiz.q: Walt's 'balance of threat' adds which factor to power?
quiz.why: Walt argued perceived aggressive intentions shape alliances.

quiz.q: UN collective security is in Chapter
quiz.why: Chapter VII covers threats to peace and enforcement.

quiz.q: The League failed to stop Italy's invasion of
quiz.why: Sanctions on Italy in 1935–36 were weak and ineffective.

lessons.title: Nuclear deterrence, arms control and human security

scenes.text: October 1962: Soviet missiles in Cuba bring the world close to nuclear war.
Afterwards a Washington–Moscow hotline is set up (1963).
Deterrence and arms control become pillars of Cold War stability.

steps.title: Deterrence
steps.body: Deterrence works if threats are capable, credible and communicated. Mutual Assured Destruction (MAD): each side retains a second-strike capability, so first use is suicidal. Bernard Brodie (1946): the chief purpose of the military is now to avert wars. India's nuclear doctrine (2003): credible minimum deterrence, No First Use, retaliation to be 'massive', civilian political control via the Nuclear Command Authority.

steps.title: Arms control and disarmament
steps.body: Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963); NPT (signed 1968, in force 1970; India did not sign as it divides nuclear 'haves' and 'have-nots'); SALT I (1972); INF Treaty (1987, ended 2019); START (1991), New START (2010); CTBT (1996, not in force); Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2017, in force 2021). Regimes: MTCR (India joined 2016), Wassenaar (2017), Australia Group (2018); NSG (India not a member; 2008 NSG waiver for civil nuclear cooperation).

steps.title: Non-traditional and human security
steps.body: UNDP Human Development Report 1994 defined human security as 'freedom from fear and freedom from want', with seven dimensions: economic, food, health, environmental, personal, community, political. Copenhagen School (Barry Buzan, Ole Wæver): securitisation — an issue becomes a security issue when framed as an existential threat and accepted by an audience. Non-traditional threats: terrorism, climate change, pandemics, cyber attacks.

steps.title: Worked example: securitisation
steps.body: A government declares migration an 'existential threat to national identity' and passes emergency measures; if the public accepts, migration is securitised — moved from normal politics to emergency politics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: India is not a member of the NSG; it joined the MTCR, Wassenaar and Australia Group. The NPT came into force in 1970, not 1968.

quiz.why: The 1994 HDR framed it as freedom from fear and freedom from want.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Cold War, Post-Cold War Order and Global Governance
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Global Politics / IR core)
courses.summary: Origins, phases and end of the Cold War; Non-Alignment; post-Cold War unipolarity and multipolarity debates; the United Nations and its reform; globalisation, Bretton Woods institutions and regional organisations.
outcomes: Explain origins and phases of the Cold War and its end
Explain the Non-Aligned Movement
Describe UN organs, the Security Council veto and reform debates
Explain globalisation, the IMF/World Bank/WTO and regionalism

scenes.text: In March 1946 Churchill said an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe.
In 1961 the Berlin Wall made it concrete.
In November 1989 Berliners chipped it down.

steps.title: Origins
steps.body: Ideological rivalry (liberal capitalism vs Soviet communism), wartime disagreements (Yalta, Potsdam 1945), Soviet control of Eastern Europe, US atomic monopoly (until 1949). Interpretations: orthodox (Soviet expansionism), revisionist (US economic expansion — William Appleman Williams), post-revisionist (mutual misperception — John Lewis Gaddis).

steps.title: Key doctrines and events
steps.body: Kennan's Long Telegram (1946) and 'X' article (1947) → containment. Truman Doctrine (March 1947), Marshall Plan (1947–51), Berlin blockade (1948–49), NATO (1949), Warsaw Pact (1955), Korean War (1950–53), Cuban Missile Crisis (1962), Vietnam War, détente (1970s — SALT I, Helsinki Final Act 1975), Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979) → 'second Cold War' under Reagan.

steps.title: End of the Cold War
steps.body: Gorbachev (from 1985): glasnost (openness), perestroika (restructuring), 'new thinking' and abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine (the 'Sinatra Doctrine'). Fall of the Berlin Wall (9 November 1989), German reunification (3 October 1990), dissolution of the USSR (26 December 1991) into 15 republics. Explanations: Soviet economic stagnation, arms-race burden, ideas and leadership (constructivists), US pressure (realists).

steps.title: Worked example: phasing
steps.body: Phase 1 (1945–53) emergence; Phase 2 (1953–62) confrontation and crises; Phase 3 (1962–79) détente; Phase 4 (1979–85) new Cold War; Phase 5 (1985–91) end. Using phases structures a 15-mark answer clearly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The USSR dissolved in December 1991, not 1989. Containment is Kennan's concept; the Truman Doctrine applied it to Greece and Turkey.

quiz.q: The 'Long Telegram' was sent by
quiz.why: George Kennan sent it from Moscow in February 1946.

quiz.q: Perestroika means
quiz.why: Gorbachev's perestroika aimed to restructure the Soviet economy.

quiz.q: The USSR split into how many republics?
quiz.why: Fifteen union republics became independent states.

lessons.title: Non-Alignment and the post-Cold War order

scenes.text: Nehru refused to join either the US or Soviet bloc.
With Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah he helped found the Non-Aligned Movement.
After 1991 the question became: what world order replaces bipolarity?

steps.title: Non-Alignment
steps.body: Not neutrality or isolation but independent judgement on each issue. Founders: Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia), Nkrumah (Ghana). First summit Belgrade 1961 (25 members). Criteria from Cairo preparatory meeting (1961): independent policy, support for liberation movements, no membership of military alliances or bilateral pacts with great powers in the context of their conflicts, no foreign bases. Later agenda: New International Economic Order (1974), disarmament, anti-apartheid. NAM today has 120 members.

steps.title: Post-Cold War debates
steps.body: Fukuyama ('The End of History?', 1989): liberal democracy as the end-point of ideological evolution. Huntington (Clash of Civilizations, 1993/1996): future conflicts along civilisational fault lines. Charles Krauthammer's 'unipolar moment' (1990). Later: rise of China, Russia's resurgence, 'multipolarity' and 'multi-alignment'; BRICS (2009; expanded 2024).

steps.title: Worked example: is NAM relevant?
steps.body: For: platform for 120 developing states; voice on climate equity, debt, UN reform; India's strategic autonomy echoes it. Against: bipolarity is gone; members are divided; India's own multi-alignment (Quad + SCO) goes beyond classical NAM. Balanced conclusion: relevance as principle (autonomy) more than as institution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Non-alignment ≠ neutrality: India took positions (e.g. on Suez 1956, decolonisation) rather than abstaining from world politics.

quiz.why: Belgrade hosted it in September 1961.

quiz.why: It meant freedom to decide on merits without bloc discipline.

scenes.text: Thirteen of fifteen Security Council members vote yes.
One permanent member votes no.
The resolution fails — the veto in action.

steps.title: Founding and purposes
steps.body: UN Charter signed at San Francisco on 26 June 1945; in force 24 October 1945 (UN Day). Purposes (Art. 1): international peace and security, friendly relations, cooperation on economic/social/humanitarian problems, a centre for harmonising actions. Members: 193.

steps.title: Six principal organs
steps.body: General Assembly (all members, one vote each; important questions need two-thirds). Security Council (15: 5 permanent — USA, UK, France, Russia, China — and 10 non-permanent for two-year terms; substantive decisions need 9 votes including no negative vote of a P5 — Art. 27(3)). ECOSOC (54 members). Trusteeship Council (suspended 1994 after Palau). International Court of Justice (15 judges, The Hague). Secretariat (Secretary-General appointed by GA on SC recommendation).

steps.title: Worked example: Security Council vote
steps.body: Vote: 10 yes, 3 no (all non-permanent), 2 abstentions (one P5). Passes: ≥ 9 yes and no P5 negative vote (abstention isn't a veto by practice since 1946). Vote: 12 yes, 1 no (a P5), 2 abstain → fails because of the veto. Vote: 8 yes, 0 no, 7 abstain → fails, fewer than 9 yes.

steps.title: Reform
steps.body: Demands: expand permanent and non-permanent seats; G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) seek permanent seats; Africa's Ezulwini Consensus (2005) seeks two permanent seats with veto; Uniting for Consensus group (Italy, Pakistan, etc.) opposes new permanent seats. Amendment requires two-thirds of GA and ratification by two-thirds of members including all P5 (Art. 108). India has served eight non-permanent terms (latest 2021–22).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Abstention by a P5 is not a veto. The GA's resolutions are generally recommendations; only SC decisions under Chapter VII bind members.

statements.s: A resolution with 9 yes, 0 no and 6 abstentions passes.
statements.why: It has nine affirmative votes and no permanent-member veto.

statements.s: A P5 abstention counts as a veto.
statements.why: Established practice treats abstention as not blocking.

statements.s: The ICJ has 15 judges.
statements.why: The Statute of the ICJ provides for 15 judges elected for nine years.

statements.s: ECOSOC has 15 members.
statements.why: ECOSOC has 54 members after amendments in 1965 and 1973.

quiz.q: SC vote: 11 yes, 2 no (one is the UK), 2 abstain. Result
quiz.why: A negative vote by a permanent member defeats a substantive resolution.

quiz.q: UN Day is
quiz.why: The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945.

quiz.q: G4 includes
quiz.why: The four jointly seek permanent seats.

lessons.title: Globalisation, global economic institutions and regionalism

scenes.text: A smartphone is designed in one country, its chips made in another, assembled in a third.
It ships worldwide under rules set by global institutions.
Globalisation connects economies — and politics.

steps.title: Globalisation
steps.body: Intensification of worldwide social relations linking distant localities (Anthony Giddens). Dimensions: economic (trade, finance, production networks), political (global governance), cultural (media, migration), technological. Debates: hyperglobalists (Kenichi Ohmae, 'borderless world'), sceptics (Hirst and Thompson), transformationalists (David Held). Critics: inequality, loss of policy space (Joseph Stiglitz, Globalization and Its Discontents, 2002).

steps.title: Bretton Woods institutions and WTO
steps.body: Bretton Woods Conference (July 1944) created the IMF (balance-of-payments support; quota-based voting) and the IBRD/World Bank (development lending). GATT (1947) → WTO (1 January 1995, Marrakesh Agreement) with dispute settlement; Doha Round (2001) stalled; Appellate Body non-functional since December 2019 because of blocked appointments. New institutions: New Development Bank (BRICS, 2015), AIIB (2016).

steps.title: Regionalism
steps.body: EU (Maastricht 1992; euro 1999/2002), ASEAN (1967; India's Act East policy), SAARC (1985, Dhaka; stalled since the 2016 Islamabad summit was cancelled), BIMSTEC (1997), African Union (2002), SCO (2001; India and Pakistan joined 2017). Old vs new regionalism (open, multi-dimensional).

steps.title: Worked example: weighted voting
steps.body: In a fund, Country A has quota share 16.5% and decisions on major issues need 85% of votes. A can block alone because 100 − 16.5 = 83.5% < 85%. This is why the US share (about 16.5% in the IMF) gives it an effective veto on major decisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The WTO replaced GATT as an organisation in 1995, but GATT rules continue within the WTO. SAARC was founded in Dhaka, not Kathmandu (the Secretariat is in Kathmandu).

courses.title: Unit 4 · India's Foreign Policy
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Global Politics / IR core; India's Foreign Policy)
courses.summary: Determinants and evolution of India's foreign policy from Nehru to the present; relations with neighbours (Pakistan, China, South Asia); relations with major powers (USA, Russia); nuclear policy and India in multilateral forums.
outcomes: Explain the determinants and phases of India's foreign policy
Analyse India–Pakistan and India–China relations
Explain Neighbourhood First and Act East policies
Analyse India's relations with the USA and Russia and its multilateral diplomacy

scenes.text: In September 1946 Nehru announced India would keep away from power blocs.
In 1991, facing a balance-of-payments crisis, India liberalised and looked East.
Today it speaks of multi-alignment and being a 'Vishwabandhu'.

steps.title: Determinants
steps.body: Geography (subcontinental size, Himalayan frontier, Indian Ocean centrality); history (colonial experience, national movement values); economy (development needs, energy imports — India imports over 80% of its crude oil); domestic politics and federal inputs; leadership; international system (bipolar → unipolar → multipolar). Constitutional basis: Article 51 (promotion of international peace).

steps.title: Phases
steps.body: 1947–62: Nehruvian non-alignment, Panchsheel (1954). 1962–71: realism after China war; 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty and Bangladesh war. 1971–91: regional pre-eminence (Indira Doctrine), Pokhran I (1974). 1991–98: liberalisation, Look East policy (Narasimha Rao), Gujral Doctrine (1996: non-reciprocal concessions to smaller neighbours). 1998–2014: Pokhran II, strategic partnership with the USA, civil nuclear deal (2008). 2014–: Neighbourhood First, Act East (upgraded 2014), Quad revival (2017), 'multi-alignment', G20 presidency (2023).

steps.title: Panchsheel
steps.body: Five principles in the India–China agreement on Tibet (29 April 1954): mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty; mutual non-aggression; mutual non-interference in internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; peaceful coexistence.

steps.title: Worked example: Gujral Doctrine
steps.body: Five principles: with neighbours like Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka, India does not ask for reciprocity but gives in good faith; no South Asian country should allow its territory to be used against another; no interference in internal affairs; respect for territorial integrity; peaceful bilateral settlement of disputes. Example: the 1996 Ganga Waters Treaty with Bangladesh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Look East (1991) and Act East (2014) are distinct labels. Panchsheel was signed with China, not at Bandung (though Bandung's ten principles drew on it).

quiz.q: Panchsheel was signed in
quiz.why: It was part of the April 1954 India–China agreement.

quiz.q: Non-reciprocity with smaller neighbours is a principle of the
quiz.why: I.K. Gujral proposed it in 1996.

quiz.q: Article 51 of the Constitution concerns
options: Promotion of international peace and security
quiz.why: It is a Directive Principle on international peace.

scenes.text: In June 2020 Indian and Chinese troops clashed in Galwan Valley.
Two decades earlier India fought Pakistan on the heights of Kargil.
Managing both frontiers defines India's security policy.

steps.title: India–Pakistan
steps.body: Wars: 1947–48 (Kashmir), 1965, 1971 (Bangladesh liberation; Simla Agreement 1972 — bilateralism, LoC), Kargil 1999. Indus Waters Treaty (1960, World Bank-brokered: eastern rivers Ravi, Beas, Sutlej to India; western Indus, Jhelum, Chenab mainly to Pakistan) — held 'in abeyance' by India in April 2025 after the Pahalgam attack. Lahore Declaration (1999), Composite Dialogue (2004–08), 26/11 Mumbai attacks (2008), Uri (2016) and surgical strikes, Pulwama–Balakot (2019), abrogation of Article 370's special status (August 2019), Operation Sindoor (May 2025).

steps.title: India–China
steps.body: Recognition of PRC (1950), Panchsheel (1954), Dalai Lama's asylum (1959), war (1962). Rajiv Gandhi's visit (1988) → normalisation; 1993 and 1996 border peace agreements; Special Representatives mechanism (2003). Disputes: Aksai Chin (western sector), Arunachal Pradesh (eastern; McMahon Line from 1914 Simla Convention). Frictions: Doklam (2017), Galwan (2020), China–Pakistan Economic Corridor through PoK, trade deficit (around US$85–100 billion annually in recent years). October 2024 patrolling arrangement at Depsang and Demchok.

steps.title: Worked example: trade deficit
steps.body: If India's imports from China are US$118 billion and exports US$17 billion in a year, the deficit = 118 − 17 = US$101 billion, and the import-to-export ratio ≈ 118/17 ≈ 6.9. Such imbalances motivate policies like PLI schemes and scrutiny of Chinese FDI (Press Note 3, 2020).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Simla Agreement (1972) is India–Pakistan; the Simla Convention (1914) produced the McMahon Line. Don't confuse them.

scenes.text: In May 2014, SAARC leaders attended the new Indian PM's swearing-in.
It signalled 'Neighbourhood First'.
Eastward, India deepened ties with ASEAN and the Indo-Pacific.

steps.title: Neighbourhood First
steps.body: Priorities: connectivity, trade, development partnerships, people-to-people links. Achievements: Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh (ratified 2015, 100th Constitutional Amendment — exchange of 111 Indian and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves); BBIN motor vehicles agreement (2015); hydro projects with Bhutan and Nepal; assistance to Sri Lanka in its 2022 economic crisis (about US$4 billion). Challenges: China's presence (Hambantota port lease 2017), Nepal map dispute (2020), 'India Out' campaign in Maldives.

steps.title: Act East and Indo-Pacific
steps.body: From Look East (1991, economic) to Act East (2014, economic + strategic + cultural). ASEAN–India FTA in goods (2009/2010); Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with ASEAN (2022). Projects: India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway; Kaladan Multi-Modal project. SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region, 2015); Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (2019); Quad (India, USA, Japan, Australia; leaders' summits from 2021). India withdrew from RCEP negotiations in November 2019.

steps.title: Worked example: enclave exchange
steps.body: Under the 2015 LBA, 111 Indian enclaves went to Bangladesh and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves went to India: total 162 enclaves. Residents could choose nationality; about 14,000 people in former Bangladeshi enclaves became Indian citizens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The LBA was implemented by the 100th Amendment (2015), not the 101st (GST). India did not join RCEP.

quiz.why: The Constitution (100th Amendment) Act, 2015 gave effect to it.

quiz.q: SAGAR stands for
options: Security and Growth for All in the Region
quiz.why: It is India's 2015 maritime vision for the Indian Ocean.

quiz.q: India withdrew from RCEP in
quiz.why: India stepped back in November 2019 over trade-deficit and market-access concerns.

lessons.title: Major powers, nuclear policy and multilateralism

scenes.text: After Pokhran II (1998) the USA imposed sanctions on India.
Ten years later the two signed a civil nuclear agreement.
Meanwhile India kept its old partnership with Russia.

steps.title: India–USA
steps.body: Cold War estrangement (US tilt to Pakistan, 1971 USS Enterprise episode). Clinton visit (2000); Next Steps in Strategic Partnership (2004); 123 Agreement (2008) after NSG waiver; 'Major Defence Partner' (2016); foundational agreements — LEMOA (2016), COMCASA (2018), BECA (2020); iCET (2023). Tensions: tariffs, Russia ties, visa issues.

steps.title: India–Russia
steps.body: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (August 1971); Indo-Russian Treaty of Friendship (1993); Declaration on Strategic Partnership (2000), 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership' (2010). Defence: S-400, BrahMos joint venture, Kudankulam nuclear plant. Since 2022 India's oil imports from Russia rose sharply; India abstained on most UN votes condemning the invasion of Ukraine, calling for dialogue.

steps.title: Nuclear policy
steps.body: Nehru's opposition to tests; Pokhran I (18 May 1974, 'peaceful nuclear explosion'); refusal of NPT (1968) and CTBT (1996) as discriminatory; Pokhran II (11 and 13 May 1998, Operation Shakti); doctrine 2003 (NFU, credible minimum deterrence); civil nuclear cooperation after 2008.

steps.title: Multilateralism
steps.body: UN peacekeeping (India among the largest cumulative troop contributors, over 2.75 lakh personnel since 1950); UNSC reform (G4); G20 presidency 2023 — New Delhi Declaration, African Union admitted as permanent member; International Solar Alliance (2015, with France); BRICS, SCO, Quad; climate stance on 'common but differentiated responsibilities'; Panchamrit targets at COP26 (2021): net zero by 2070.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pokhran I was 1974 and Pokhran II 1998. The 123 Agreement is named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act of 1954.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Revision, practicals & exam
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Global Politics / IR core)
courses.summary: Theory map and timeline sheet, a crisis-simulation lab applying theories, a UN Security Council voting lab, and previous-year-style questions with a final exam.
outcomes: Recall the theories, thinkers and dates of IR
Apply realist, liberal and constructivist lenses to a crisis
Compute Security Council outcomes correctly
Write structured IR answers

story.title: The whole course on one page

scenes.text: Four theory families, five Cold War phases, one Indian story.
Link each to a thinker and a date.
Revision becomes recall, not rereading.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: Realism: Thucydides, Morgenthau (1948), Waltz (1979), Mearsheimer (2001). Liberalism: Kant (1795), Keohane & Nye (1977), Keohane (1984), Doyle (1983). Marxist/critical: Lenin (1916), Wallerstein (1974), Cox (1981). Constructivism: Onuf (1989), Wendt (1992, 1999). Feminism: Enloe (1989), Tickner (1992). English School: Bull (1977).

steps.title: Global timeline
steps.body: 1919 League · 1944 Bretton Woods · 1945 UN · 1947 Truman Doctrine · 1949 NATO · 1955 Warsaw Pact & Bandung · 1961 NAM Belgrade · 1962 Cuba · 1968 NPT · 1975 Helsinki · 1989 Wall falls · 1991 USSR ends · 1995 WTO · 2001 9/11 & SCO · 2009 BRICS · 2022 Ukraine war.

steps.title: India timeline
steps.body: 1954 Panchsheel · 1962 China war · 1965 war & 1966 Tashkent · 1971 Indo-Soviet treaty & Bangladesh · 1972 Simla · 1974 Pokhran I · 1985 SAARC · 1991 Look East · 1996 Gujral Doctrine · 1998 Pokhran II · 1999 Kargil & Lahore · 2008 123 Agreement · 2014 Act East · 2015 LBA & ISA · 2017 SCO membership & Quad revival · 2020 Galwan · 2023 G20 presidency.

steps.title: How to use the map
steps.body: For any theory question, name the founding text with its year, state the core assumption (about anarchy, actors and cooperation), and give one event the theory explains well and one it explains poorly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bandung (1955) is not the first NAM summit (Belgrade 1961). The NPT opened for signature in 1968 but entered into force in 1970.

lessons.title: Lab: Crisis simulation through three lenses

scenes.text: Imagine two navies face off in a contested strait vital for trade.
Each mobilises; markets panic.
How would each theory explain and resolve it?

steps.title: Realist reading
steps.body: Cause: shifting balance of power and security dilemma. Prescription: credible deterrence, alliances, avoid appearing weak; seek a balance rather than total victory. Prediction: the weaker side bandwagons or balances with outside powers.

steps.title: Liberal reading
steps.body: Cause: weak institutions and incomplete information. Prescription: use regional forums (e.g. ASEAN Regional Forum), confidence-building measures, hotlines, economic interdependence as restraint, arbitration under UNCLOS (as in the 2016 South China Sea award).

steps.title: Constructivist reading
steps.body: Cause: identities framed as rivals; nationalist narratives. Prescription: change discourse, build shared norms, track-II dialogue, symbolic gestures that shift a Hobbesian culture toward a Lockean one.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Write a 12-line answer to: 'Which theory best explains the 2020 Galwan crisis?' Use at least two theories and one counter-argument.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not just label theories — show how each identifies a different cause and a different remedy.

scenes.text: Fifteen hands; five of them hold a veto.
Nine yeses and no P5 'no' — that's the rule.
Practise until it is automatic.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: Procedural matters: any 9 votes. Substantive matters: 9 affirmative votes including the concurring votes of the permanent members — read in practice as 'no negative vote by a P5'; abstention or absence does not block. A party to a dispute must abstain on Chapter VI decisions (Art. 27(3)).

steps.title: Case A
steps.body: Yes 9 (including 3 P5), No 2 (non-permanent), Abstain 4 (including 2 P5). → Passes.

steps.title: Case B
steps.body: Yes 14, No 1 (Russia). → Fails (veto).

steps.title: Case C
steps.body: Yes 8, No 0, Abstain 7. → Fails (only 8 yes).

steps.title: Case D (procedural)
steps.body: Yes 9, No 6 (including 2 P5) on adopting the agenda. → Passes, because procedural votes have no veto.

statements.s: 10 yes, 5 abstain (all P5) on a substantive matter passes.
statements.why: Nine or more yes and no P5 negative vote.

statements.s: 13 yes, 2 no (France and one elected member) passes.
statements.why: France's negative vote is a veto.

statements.s: 9 yes, 6 no (including China) on a procedural matter passes.
statements.why: The veto does not apply to procedural matters.

statements.s: 8 yes, 7 abstain on a substantive matter passes.
statements.why: At least nine affirmative votes are needed.

quiz.why: Abstention by a permanent member does not block adoption.

quiz.why: Procedural matters need any nine votes and the veto does not apply.

uni-ba-pol-political-theory.title: Political Theory
uni-ba-pol-political-theory.description: Concepts and approaches of political theory: state, sovereignty, liberty, equality, justice, rights, democracy and citizenship. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Political Science programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature and Approaches of Political Theory
courses.summary: What political theory is, why it matters, and the main approaches used to study politics: normative, historical, empirical, behavioural, post-behavioural, Marxist and feminist.
outcomes: Define politics and political theory and distinguish theory, philosophy and science
Explain the normative and empirical traditions
Describe the behavioural revolution and Easton's post-behavioural Credo
Evaluate Marxist and feminist critiques of mainstream theory
Discuss the 'decline of political theory' debate

lessons.title: What is politics and political theory?

scenes.text: Hostel students argue about who should run the mess committee and how fees should be shared.
Some want elections, some want rotation, some want the warden to decide. Each proposal rests on an idea of fairness and authority.
Asking 'who should decide, and why?' is already political theory.

steps.title: Meaning of politics
steps.body: Politics has been defined in several ways: Aristotle saw it as the activity of the polis aimed at the good life; Harold Lasswell defined it as 'who gets what, when, how'; David Easton as the 'authoritative allocation of values for a society'. A broad modern view treats politics as the process by which groups make collective decisions and manage conflict over power and resources.

steps.title: Meaning of political theory
steps.body: Political theory is the systematic reflection on political life: it describes and explains political phenomena and also evaluates them against ideals such as liberty, equality and justice. Andrew Hacker distinguished theory as combining a 'dispassionate search for principles of good state and society' with 'disinterested search for knowledge of political and social reality'. Theory therefore has an explanatory side and a normative (prescriptive) side.

steps.title: Theory, philosophy, science, ideology
steps.body: Political philosophy is the most abstract, asking what ought to be (e.g. what is justice?). Political science seeks testable generalisations about how political actors actually behave. Political ideology is a more action-oriented set of ideas meant to mobilise (liberalism, socialism). Political theory overlaps all three and is often used as an umbrella term.

steps.title: Worked example: classifying statements
steps.body: (1) 'Turnout in urban constituencies is lower than in rural ones' — empirical claim, testable with data. (2) 'Every adult should have an equal vote' — normative claim, defended by argument. (3) 'Workers of the world, unite!' — ideological slogan aimed at action. Exam answers score well when they show this distinction with examples.

steps.title: Relevance in India
steps.body: Debates on reservations, uniform civil code or freedom of speech online are theory in action: they ask what equality, secularism or liberty require. The Preamble's ideals — justice, liberty, equality, fraternity — are normative concepts studied in this course.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not say political theory is 'only about the state' — modern theory also studies power in society, family and markets. Do not confuse Lasswell's definition (power/distribution) with Easton's (authoritative allocation).

activity.prompt: Match the thinker to the definition of politics
pairs: Activity of the polis directed at the good life
Striving to share or influence the distribution of power

quiz.q: 'Who gets what, when, how' is the definition given by
quiz.why: Lasswell's 1936 book bore this title and defined politics as the distribution of valued things through power.

quiz.q: A statement about what ought to be is called
quiz.why: Normative claims prescribe ideals and are defended by argument rather than measurement.

quiz.q: Easton defined politics as the
quiz.why: Easton saw the political system as allocating values authoritatively for a whole society.

quiz.q: Which is most action-oriented?
quiz.why: Ideologies are designed to mobilise people for political action, unlike detached analysis.

story.title: Reading Plato in a Delhi library

scenes.text: A student wonders why a 2,400-year-old book is still on her syllabus.
Plato asked what a just city looks like — a question no survey can settle.
She realises old texts give permanent questions and a vocabulary to argue about them.

steps.title: Normative approach
steps.body: The normative (philosophical) approach asks what the good, just or legitimate political order should be. It works through conceptual analysis and reasoned argument. Classical examples: Plato's Republic, Aristotle's Politics, Rousseau's Social Contract; modern revival: John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971).

steps.title: Historical approach
steps.body: The historical approach studies political ideas in their historical context: who wrote, against whom, for what audience. The 'Cambridge School' (Quentin Skinner, J.G.A. Pocock) argued that texts must be read as speech-acts within their linguistic context, against the idea of 'timeless' meanings.

steps.title: Strengths and limits
steps.body: Strengths: they clarify values, offer standards for criticism and keep alive great debates. Limits: normative claims cannot be tested empirically, can be utopian, and classic texts may reflect the prejudices of their era (e.g. Aristotle on slavery).

steps.title: Worked example: normative argument
steps.body: Question: Should voting be compulsory? Normative answer structure: (1) state the value (equal participation / legitimacy); (2) argument for (higher turnout makes outcomes more representative); (3) objection (liberty includes the freedom not to vote); (4) evaluate and conclude. This four-step structure suits 15-mark answers.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: When asked 'Is political theory dead?', mention that Rawls's 1971 work is usually seen as reviving normative theory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The historical approach is not just narrating events; it is about interpreting ideas in context.

activity.prompt: Sort each work or idea into its approach

items.text: Rawls asks which principles free and equal persons would choose
Skinner reads Machiavelli against Renaissance humanist conventions
Plato designs the ideal just city
Pocock traces republican language from Florence to America
Asking whether inequality can ever be just

quiz.q: The Cambridge School is associated with
quiz.why: Skinner, with Pocock, championed contextual reading of political texts.

quiz.q: Rawls's A Theory of Justice was published in
quiz.why: Its 1971 publication is widely credited with reviving normative theory.

quiz.q: A key limit of the normative approach is that
options: Its claims cannot be verified empirically
quiz.why: Normative claims rest on argument about values and cannot be settled by observation alone.

scenes.text: In 1950s America researchers surveyed voters to explain how they actually chose.
Politics, they said, should be a science like economics or psychology.
By 1969, amid the Vietnam War, critics asked: what use is precise data if it ignores urgent social crises?

steps.title: The behavioural revolution
steps.body: Behaviouralism (dominant c. 1945–1965, especially in the USA) shifted focus from institutions and legal texts to the observable behaviour of individuals and groups. Key names: Charles Merriam and the Chicago School (forerunners), David Easton, Robert Dahl, Heinz Eulau.

steps.title: Easton's eight intellectual foundations
steps.body: Easton listed: (1) regularities, (2) verification, (3) techniques, (4) quantification, (5) values (kept separate from facts), (6) systematisation, (7) pure science, (8) integration with other social sciences.

steps.title: Post-behaviouralism
steps.body: In his 1969 APSA presidential address Easton himself announced a 'post-behavioural revolution'. Its Credo of Relevance stressed: substance before technique; social change rather than preservation; facing the real crises of mankind; values are central; intellectuals have a responsibility; knowing means acting; politicisation of the profession. Slogans: 'relevance' and 'action'.

steps.title: Worked example: designing a behavioural study
steps.body: Question: Does education affect voting in a Bihar constituency? Steps: hypothesis (more schooling → higher turnout); define variables (years of schooling; voted or not); random sample of, say, 600 voters; survey; compare turnout across education groups; test whether the difference is statistically significant. This illustrates verification and quantification.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Post-behaviouralism did not reject scientific methods; it demanded that they serve relevant problems. And it was Easton, a leading behaviouralist, who announced it.

steps.title: Critique
steps.body: Critics (e.g. Leo Strauss) argued behaviouralism's fact–value separation hid a conservative bias in favour of the status quo.

statements.s: Quantification is one of Easton's eight foundations of behaviouralism.
statements.why: Easton listed measurement and quantification as central tenets.

statements.s: Post-behaviouralism rejected all use of scientific techniques.
statements.why: It kept techniques but put substance and relevance before them.

statements.s: Easton announced post-behaviouralism in 1969.
statements.why: He did so in his APSA presidential address that year.

statements.s: Behaviouralists focused mainly on constitutional texts.
statements.why: They moved away from legal-institutional study to observable behaviour.

quiz.q: 'Credo of Relevance' belongs to
quiz.why: Easton framed post-behaviouralism's demands as a Credo of Relevance.

quiz.q: Which is NOT among Easton's behavioural foundations?
quiz.why: Revolution is not a methodological tenet; the eight are regularities, verification, techniques, quantification, values, systematisation, pure science and integration.

quiz.q: Behaviouralism treated facts and values as
quiz.why: Behaviouralists held that ethical evaluation and empirical explanation should be kept distinct.

lessons.title: Marxist and feminist approaches; decline debate

scenes.text: A factory worker sees laws protecting the owner's property first.
His wife works ten hours at home unpaid; no theory of 'public life' counts it.
Marxists and feminists ask what mainstream theory leaves out.

steps.title: Marxist approach
steps.body: Marxism explains politics through the economic base: relations of production shape the superstructure (state, law, ideology). The state is seen as an instrument of the dominant class (Communist Manifesto: 'executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie'). Method: historical materialism and class analysis. Later Marxists (Gramsci) added hegemony — rule by consent through culture.

steps.title: Feminist approach
steps.body: Feminism challenges the public/private divide: 'the personal is political' (Carol Hanisch's 1969 essay title, popularised by second-wave feminism). It examines patriarchy, gendered citizenship and unpaid care. Strands: liberal (equal rights — Mary Wollstonecraft, J.S. Mill), radical (patriarchy as root — Kate Millett), socialist/Marxist feminism, and later intersectional feminism (Kimberlé Crenshaw).

steps.title: The decline of political theory debate
steps.body: In the 1950s scholars claimed theory had declined: Peter Laslett (1956) wrote 'for the moment anyway, political philosophy is dead'; David Easton blamed historicism; Alfred Cobban blamed the lack of engagement with real problems. Defenders such as Isaiah Berlin argued political theory survives as long as people disagree about ends. Rawls (1971) and Nozick (1974) are cited as its resurgence.

steps.title: Worked example: three readings of one law
steps.body: A minimum-wage law: liberal reading — protects individual welfare within a market; Marxist reading — a concession that stabilises capitalism without ending exploitation; feminist reading — asks whether domestic workers (mostly women) are covered at all.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not attribute 'the personal is political' to Marx. Do not say Laslett ended theory permanently — he said it was dead 'for the moment'.

courses.title: Unit 2 · State, Sovereignty, Power and Authority
courses.summary: Elements and theories of the state, Austin's monistic sovereignty and its pluralist critique, and the concepts of power, authority and legitimacy (Weber).
outcomes: List the elements of the state and distinguish state, government, nation and society
Compare liberal, Marxist and Gandhian views of the state
Explain Austin's theory of sovereignty and the pluralist critique
Distinguish power, authority and legitimacy and apply Weber's three types

lessons.title: Meaning and elements of the state

story.title: Is a cricket club a state?

scenes.text: A club has members, rules and officers. Can it jail anyone who breaks its rules?
Only the state can legally compel everyone in a territory.
That difference — sovereign, compulsory authority over a territory — defines the state.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Max Weber: the state is a human community that (successfully) claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. Garner: a community of persons, more or less numerous, permanently occupying a definite territory, independent of external control, with an organised government to which the inhabitants render habitual obedience.

steps.title: Four elements
steps.body: (1) Population, (2) Territory (land, territorial waters, airspace), (3) Government — the agency through which the state's will is expressed, (4) Sovereignty — supreme internal authority and external independence. The Montevideo Convention (1933) adds 'capacity to enter into relations with other states' as a criterion of statehood in international law.

steps.title: State vs government, nation, society
steps.body: Government is the changing machinery; the state is permanent. A nation is a community bound by sentiment (culture, history); a state is a legal-political entity — some nations lack a state (Kurds) and some states contain many nations. Society includes all associations; the state is one association, distinguished by compulsory membership and coercive power.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: When a government falls after a no-confidence vote, does India cease to be a state? No — population, territory and sovereignty remain; only the government (one element) is reconstituted. This shows government ≠ state.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not list 'recognition by the UN' as an essential element; recognition is debated (declaratory vs constitutive theory) and not one of the classical four.

activity.prompt: Which belongs to the State and which to Government?

quiz.q: Monopoly of legitimate physical force defines the state for
quiz.why: Weber's 'Politics as a Vocation' (1919) gives this famous definition.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four classical elements?
quiz.why: Parties operate within states but are not constitutive elements of statehood.

quiz.q: The Kurds are often cited as an example of a
quiz.why: Kurds share national identity but are spread across several states without their own.

lessons.title: Theories of the state: liberal, Marxist, Gandhian

story.title: Three views of the police station

scenes.text: A liberal sees the police protecting everyone's rights.
A Marxist sees them protecting property of the dominant class.
Gandhi sees organised violence and hopes villages can govern themselves without it.

steps.title: Liberal theory
steps.body: Classical liberals (Locke, Adam Smith) favour a limited state protecting life, liberty and property — the 'night-watchman' state. Welfare liberals (T.H. Green, Keynes, Hobhouse) accept a positive state that removes hindrances to good life through education, health and social security. Neo-liberals (Hayek, Nozick) return to a minimal state.

steps.title: Marxist theory
steps.body: The state arises when society splits into antagonistic classes (Engels, Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State). It is an instrument of class domination; after a proletarian revolution and a transitional dictatorship of the proletariat, the state will 'wither away'. Later debates: Miliband (instrumentalist) vs Poulantzas (structuralist, relative autonomy of the state).

steps.title: Gandhian view
steps.body: Gandhi called the state 'violence in a concentrated and organised form' because it rests on coercion. His ideal was 'enlightened anarchy' of self-regulating individuals; practically, a decentralised polity of self-sufficient village republics (gram swaraj) with minimal state, trusteeship of property and non-violence.

steps.title: Worked example: MGNREGA
steps.body: Liberal-welfare: guaranteed work enables real freedom. Marxist: it legitimises capitalism and reproduces labour cheaply. Gandhian: valued if it builds village self-reliance through gram sabha planning (the Act gives gram sabhas a role in selecting works).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Withering away of the state' is Engels' phrase (Anti-Dühring), not Lenin's invention; Lenin elaborated it in The State and Revolution.

activity.prompt: Match the idea to the theory

quiz.q: Gandhi described the state as
options: Violence in a concentrated and organised form
quiz.why: Because the state relies on coercion, Gandhi viewed it as organised violence.

quiz.q: The book 'Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State' is by
quiz.why: Engels published it in 1884, tracing the state to class division.

quiz.q: Welfare liberalism differs from classical liberalism by
options: Accepting an active state role in social provision
quiz.why: Welfare liberals argue the state must enable freedom by providing education, health and security.

scenes.text: Hobbes and Austin say every state needs one supreme, unlimited authority.
Pluralists point out churches, trade unions and universities have their own legitimate spheres.
Today, global institutions raise new questions about absolute sovereignty.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Sovereignty (from Latin superanus, 'supreme') is the supreme power of the state over citizens and subjects, unrestrained by law (Bodin, Six Books of the Commonwealth, 1576). Internal sovereignty = supremacy within; external = independence from outside control. Characteristics in the classical view: absoluteness, permanence, universality, inalienability, indivisibility, exclusiveness.

steps.title: Austin's monistic theory
steps.body: John Austin (Lectures on Jurisprudence, 1832): 'If a determinate human superior, not in a habit of obedience to a like superior, receive habitual obedience from the bulk of a given society, that determinate superior is sovereign in that society.' Law is the command of the sovereign backed by sanction. Features: sovereign is determinate, receives habitual obedience, is indivisible and unlimited.

steps.title: Pluralist critique
steps.body: Pluralists (Harold Laski, Ernest Barker, Léon Duguit, J.N. Figgis, Maitland) argued society is federal: associations are as natural as the state and hold their own authority, so sovereignty is divided. Laski: 'It would be of lasting benefit to political science if the whole concept of sovereignty were surrendered.' Further critiques: Maine showed customary law (e.g. Ranjit Singh obeyed custom) is not commanded; in federations sovereignty is shared.

steps.title: Popular sovereignty
steps.body: Rousseau located sovereignty in the people's general will; modern constitutions echo this — the Indian Preamble opens 'We, the people of India … give to ourselves this Constitution'.

steps.title: Worked example: applying Austin to India
steps.body: Who is Austin's 'determinate superior' in India? Parliament is limited by the Constitution and judicial review (basic structure doctrine, Kesavananda Bharati 1973), and power is divided between Union and states. So Austin's indivisible, unlimited sovereign is hard to locate — a classic 15-mark critique.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not say pluralists wanted to abolish the state; they wanted the state to be first among associations, coordinating rather than dominating.

statements.s: Austin held that sovereignty is divisible.
statements.why: For Austin the sovereign is determinate and indivisible.

statements.s: Jean Bodin wrote on sovereignty in 1576.
statements.why: His Six Books of the Commonwealth appeared in 1576.

statements.s: Laski was a pluralist critic of absolute sovereignty.
statements.why: In his early works Laski argued authority is federal and divided among associations.

statements.s: Henry Maine supported Austin by showing all law is a command.
statements.why: Maine cited Ranjit Singh's rule, where custom rather than command governed, to criticise Austin.

quiz.q: 'Law is the command of the sovereign' is the view of
quiz.why: Austin's analytical jurisprudence defines law as a sovereign's command backed by sanction.

quiz.q: Popular sovereignty is closely linked to
quiz.why: Rousseau placed sovereignty in the general will of the people, which cannot be transferred.

quiz.q: Pluralists see society as
quiz.why: They held authority is spread among many associations, making society federal.

quiz.q: Which Indian case limits Parliament's amending power?
quiz.why: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held Parliament cannot amend the Constitution's basic structure.

story.title: Why do we stop at a red light at 2 a.m.?

scenes.text: No police are around, yet most drivers stop.
They accept the rule as rightful — that is authority, not just power.
When people stop accepting rules as rightful, governments face a legitimacy crisis.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: Power is the capacity to make others act as one wishes. Robert Dahl: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do. Steven Lukes's three dimensions (1974): (1) decision-making (visible conflict), (2) non-decision-making / agenda-setting (Bachrach and Baratz), (3) shaping preferences so conflict never arises (ideological power).

steps.title: Authority
steps.body: Authority is power accepted as rightful — 'legitimate power'. Weber's three ideal types: Traditional (based on custom and inherited status, e.g. a hereditary chief); Charismatic (based on extraordinary personal qualities, e.g. a revolutionary leader); Legal-rational (based on rules and office, e.g. a district collector acting under law).

steps.title: Legitimacy
steps.body: Legitimacy is the belief that a regime has the right to rule. Sources: consent and elections, constitutional procedures, performance (development, order), tradition and ideology. Jürgen Habermas (Legitimation Crisis, 1973) argued late-capitalist states face crises when they cannot meet expectations they have raised.

steps.title: Worked example: classifying authority
steps.body: (a) A Supreme Court judge's order — legal-rational. (b) Gandhi's call for the Salt March followed by millions — charismatic. (c) A village elder settling disputes because his family always has — traditional. Weber noted real cases mix types, and charisma tends to be 'routinised' into legal or traditional authority after the leader's death.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Power without legitimacy is coercion, not authority. Lukes's third dimension is about invisible power over preferences, not open conflict.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Liberty, Equality and Justice
courses.summary: Negative and positive liberty (Mill, Berlin), formal and substantive equality, Rawls's justice as fairness and its libertarian, communitarian and other critiques.
outcomes: Explain Mill's harm principle and Berlin's two concepts of liberty
Distinguish equality of opportunity, outcome and treatment; explain affirmative action
State Rawls's original position and two principles of justice
Compare Nozick's entitlement theory and communitarian critiques

scenes.text: A neighbour plays music at full volume at 1 a.m., claiming 'my freedom'.
Others can't sleep. Where does one person's liberty end?
Mill's harm principle gives a test: liberty may be limited to prevent harm to others.

steps.title: Mill's On Liberty (1859)
steps.body: Harm principle: 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.' Mill distinguished self-regarding actions (free) from other-regarding actions (may be regulated). He defended freedom of thought and discussion: a silenced opinion may be true; even a false one keeps truth from becoming 'dead dogma'. He also warned against the 'tyranny of the majority' in social opinion.

steps.title: Berlin's Two Concepts of Liberty (1958)
steps.body: Negative liberty: 'freedom from' — the area within which a person can act unobstructed by others (Hobbes, Locke, Mill). Positive liberty: 'freedom to' — being one's own master, self-realisation (Rousseau, Hegel, T.H. Green). Berlin warned that positive liberty can be abused when rulers claim to know people's 'true' selves and force them to be free.

steps.title: Other views
steps.body: T.H. Green: liberty is 'a positive power or capacity of doing or enjoying something worth doing'. Marxists: formal liberty is empty without economic freedom. Republicans (Philip Pettit, Quentin Skinner): liberty as non-domination — not being subject to another's arbitrary will even if they don't interfere.

steps.title: Indian Constitution
steps.body: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, but Article 19(2) allows 'reasonable restrictions' on grounds such as sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence — a practical version of limiting liberty to prevent harm.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Is a helmet law compatible with Mill? Strictly, riding without a helmet is largely self-regarding, so Mill would resist paternalism; but defenders argue public costs (ambulances, hospital care) make it other-regarding. Good answers present both sides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Berlin did not reject positive liberty as meaningless; he warned of its political abuse. Mill's harm principle concerns harm to others, not offence or dislike.

items.text: Free schooling so I can realise my potential
Self-mastery and acting on my rational will
Hobbes: liberty is absence of external impediments

quiz.q: The harm principle is from
quiz.why: Mill set out the harm principle in On Liberty (1859).

quiz.q: 'Freedom to' corresponds to
quiz.why: Positive liberty concerns the capacity to be self-directed and pursue one's goals.

quiz.q: Liberty as non-domination is associated with
quiz.why: Philip Pettit's republicanism defines freedom as not being under arbitrary power.

story.title: The same race, different starting lines

scenes.text: Two runners race 100 m. One starts at 0 m, the other 30 m behind due to earlier injury.
Same rules for both — but is the race fair?
Substantive equality asks us to look at starting points, not just rules.

steps.title: Dimensions of equality
steps.body: Natural vs social inequality (Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality distinguished natural from conventional inequality). Legal equality: equality before law and equal protection. Political equality: one person, one vote. Social equality: absence of caste/status hierarchy. Economic equality: reducing disparities of income and wealth.

steps.title: Opportunity, outcome, treatment
steps.body: Formal equality of opportunity: careers open to talents, no legal bars. Fair (substantive) equality of opportunity: equal chances for those with equal talent and effort, regardless of background — requires education, health access. Equality of outcome: reducing differences in results. Laski: equality means absence of special privileges and adequate opportunities for all.

steps.title: Affirmative action in India
steps.body: Article 14 (equality before law), 15 (no discrimination; 15(4) special provisions for backward classes, SCs, STs), 16 (equal opportunity in public employment; 16(4) reservation), 17 (abolition of untouchability). Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld OBC reservation, introduced the creamy-layer exclusion and normally capped total reservations at 50%. The 103rd Amendment (2019) added 10% EWS reservation, upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).

steps.title: Worked example: computing a reserved share
steps.body: A recruitment has 200 posts. Central quotas: SC 15%, ST 7.5%, OBC 27%, EWS 10%. SC = 0.15 × 200 = 30; ST = 0.075 × 200 = 15; OBC = 0.27 × 200 = 54; EWS = 0.10 × 200 = 20. Reserved total = 119; open = 81. Note the Indra Sawhney 50% ceiling applies to SC/ST/OBC (49.5% here), while EWS was held to be a separate class.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equality does not mean identical treatment of all; Indian courts accept 'reasonable classification' with an intelligible differentia having a rational nexus to the object of the law.

pairs: Equality before law and equal protection
Reservation in public posts for backward classes

quiz.q: With 300 posts and 27% OBC quota, OBC posts are
Fair equality of opportunity requires
options: Equal chances regardless of social background
quiz.why: It goes beyond formal openness to ensure background does not determine prospects.

quiz.q: Rousseau distinguished natural inequality from
quiz.why: He argued most inequality is created by society and convention, not nature.

quiz.q: 'Reasonable classification' is a test used under Article
quiz.why: Courts read Article 14 as permitting classification with intelligible differentia and rational nexus.

scenes.text: If the person who cuts the cake picks last, they'll cut equal pieces.
Rawls asks us to choose society's rules without knowing our own position.
Behind this 'veil of ignorance', what principles would we choose?

steps.title: The original position
steps.body: In A Theory of Justice (1971), John Rawls imagines free, equal, rational persons choosing principles behind a 'veil of ignorance' — they do not know their class, talents, sex, race or conception of the good. Because no one can tailor rules to their advantage, the choice is fair; hence 'justice as fairness'. Rawls argues they would use the 'maximin' rule: maximise the minimum position.

steps.title: Two principles
steps.body: First (equal liberty): each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with a similar scheme for all. Second: social and economic inequalities are to be arranged so that they are (a) to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle) and (b) attached to offices and positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity. Lexical priority: first principle over second; 2(b) over 2(a).

steps.title: Worked example: applying the difference principle
steps.body: Three possible societies (incomes of the poorest, middle, richest group, in ₹ thousand/month): A = 10, 20, 30; B = 15, 40, 120; C = 12, 25, 35. Maximin picks the arrangement with the highest minimum: A's minimum is 10, B's is 15, C's is 12. So Rawls's difference principle favours B — even though it is the most unequal — because the worst-off are best off there. This shows Rawls is not a strict egalitarian.

steps.title: Primary goods
steps.body: The parties seek primary goods every rational person wants: rights and liberties, opportunities, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect. Later, Political Liberalism (1993) recast justice as a 'political' conception based on an overlapping consensus among reasonable comprehensive doctrines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The difference principle does not demand equal incomes; it permits inequality that improves the position of the least advantaged. Liberty cannot be traded for economic gain because of lexical priority.

quiz.why: They know general facts but not particular facts about themselves.

quiz.why: Rawls developed it in Political Liberalism (1993) to explain stability amid pluralism.

lessons.title: Critics of Rawls: Nozick, communitarians, Sen

scenes.text: Fans happily pay 25 cents each to watch a star player; he becomes rich.
Every transfer was voluntary. Is the result unjust?
Nozick says no — and so challenges Rawls.

steps.title: Nozick's entitlement theory
steps.body: Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974): a distribution is just if it arises through (1) justice in acquisition, (2) justice in transfer, and (3) rectification of past injustice. Justice is historical, not 'patterned' (like 'to each according to need'). The Wilt Chamberlain example claims liberty upsets patterns; taxation of earnings is 'on a par with forced labour'. He defends a minimal state.

steps.title: Communitarian critique
steps.body: Michael Sandel (Liberalism and the Limits of Justice, 1982) attacked Rawls's 'unencumbered self' — persons are constituted by community attachments. Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue), Charles Taylor and Michael Walzer (Spheres of Justice: different goods have different distributive principles — 'complex equality') argued justice is rooted in shared meanings of a community.

steps.title: Amartya Sen and others
steps.body: Sen (The Idea of Justice, 2009) criticised 'transcendental institutionalism' (searching for a perfectly just society) and proposed comparative, realisation-focused justice, using the capability approach — what people are actually able to do and be. His example of three children and a flute illustrates rival claims (need, entitlement from making it, ability to use it). Feminists (Susan Okin) asked whether justice reaches inside the family.

steps.title: Worked example: three children and a flute
steps.body: Anne can play the flute; Bob is poorest and has no toys; Carla made it. Utilitarian focus on pleasure favours Anne, economic egalitarian favours Bob, libertarian favours Carla. Sen's point: there can be plural, impartial reasons, so we should compare options rather than seek one perfect theory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Nozick is a libertarian, not a conservative traditionalist; Walzer's 'complex equality' is not equality of income.
