courses.title: Unit 4 · Rights, Democracy and Citizenship
courses.summary: Theories of rights and human rights, models of democracy (procedural, elitist, pluralist, participatory, deliberative), and theories of citizenship from Marshall to multiculturalism.
outcomes: Compare natural, legal, historical and social-welfare theories of rights
Distinguish procedural and substantive democracy and explain elite and pluralist theories
Explain participatory and deliberative democracy
Describe T.H. Marshall's three stages of citizenship and multicultural citizenship

lessons.title: Theories of rights and human rights

scenes.text: In 1948 the world adopted a Universal Declaration of Human Rights after the horrors of war.
Do rights exist because laws grant them, or do laws exist to protect rights we already have?
Different theories answer differently.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: A right is a justified claim recognised by society and enforced by the state. Laski: 'Rights are those conditions of social life without which no man can seek, in general, to be himself at his best.' Hohfeld analysed rights into claims, liberties, powers and immunities.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: Natural rights (Locke): life, liberty and property are pre-political; government exists to protect them. Legal theory (Bentham, Austin): rights are created by law — Bentham called natural rights 'nonsense upon stilts'. Historical theory (Burke): rights grow from long-standing customs. Social-welfare theory (Bentham's utility, Laski): rights are conditions for social good. Marxist: bourgeois rights protect property; real rights require economic emancipation.

steps.title: Human rights and generations
steps.body: UDHR adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. Karel Vasak's three generations: first — civil and political (ICCPR 1966); second — economic, social and cultural (ICESCR 1966); third — solidarity rights (development, environment, peace). Debate: universalism vs cultural relativism (e.g. 'Asian values' argument).

steps.title: India
steps.body: Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable via Article 32, which Ambedkar called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Directive Principles (Part IV) resemble second-generation rights; courts have read many into Article 21 (e.g. right to livelihood, Olga Tellis 1985; privacy, Puttaswamy 2017).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Nonsense upon stilts' is Bentham, not Burke. UDHR is a declaration, not itself a binding treaty; the 1966 covenants are treaties.

activity.prompt: Match the theory to its thinker

quiz.q: UDHR was adopted on
quiz.why: The UN General Assembly adopted it on 10 December 1948, now Human Rights Day.

quiz.q: The right to privacy was recognised as fundamental in
quiz.why: A nine-judge bench in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy held privacy intrinsic to Article 21.

quiz.q: Economic, social and cultural rights are
quiz.why: Vasak classified them as second-generation rights tied to equality.

lessons.title: Democracy: procedural, elitist and pluralist theories

scenes.text: A country holds regular elections but the same families win every time.
Business groups and unions lobby fiercely between elections.
Is it rule by the people, by elites, or by competing groups?

steps.title: Meaning and classical theory
steps.body: Democracy: rule by the demos (people). Lincoln: 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'. Classical theory (Rousseau, Bentham, J.S. Mill) assumed rational, informed citizens pursuing a common good through participation.

steps.title: Schumpeter's procedural democracy
steps.body: Joseph Schumpeter (Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy, 1942): democracy is 'that institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote'. Citizens choose leaders; they do not rule. This is the competitive-elitist or procedural model.

steps.title: Elite theory
steps.body: Classical elitists: Vilfredo Pareto (circulation of elites — 'lions' and 'foxes'), Gaetano Mosca (ruling class vs ruled), Robert Michels ('iron law of oligarchy' — 'who says organisation, says oligarchy'). C. Wright Mills (The Power Elite, 1956): corporate, military and political leaders in the USA form an interlocking elite.

steps.title: Pluralism and polyarchy
steps.body: Robert Dahl (Who Governs?, 1961; Polyarchy, 1971): power is dispersed among competing groups; no single elite dominates every issue. Polyarchy has two dimensions — public contestation and inclusiveness (participation) — and requires institutions such as free elections, freedom of expression, alternative information and associational autonomy. Neo-pluralists (later Dahl, Lindblom) admitted business holds a 'privileged position'.

steps.title: Worked example: which theory fits?
steps.body: Observation: in a state, 60% of MLAs are relatives of former legislators. Elitist reading: a political class reproduces itself (Mosca). Pluralist reply: check if different groups (farmers, unions, caste associations) win on different issues. Procedural view: as long as elections are competitive, the system is democratic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The 'iron law of oligarchy' is Michels, not Mosca. Polyarchy is Dahl's term for real-world democracies, not an ideal democracy.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the theorist

quiz.why: He saw democracy as an institutional method of competition for votes.

quiz.why: Polyarchy combines high public contestation with broad participation.

scenes.text: Under a banyan tree, villagers debate whether to spend funds on a road or a school wall.
Arguments change minds; a landless woman's point about water wins support.
Democracy here is talking and deciding together, not just voting every five years.

steps.title: Participatory democracy
steps.body: Carole Pateman (Participation and Democratic Theory, 1970) and C.B. Macpherson argued participation in workplaces and local bodies educates citizens and deepens democracy. Examples: Porto Alegre participatory budgeting (Brazil, from 1989), Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996), India's gram sabhas under the 73rd Amendment (1992).

steps.title: Deliberative democracy
steps.body: Legitimacy comes from public reasoning among free and equal citizens, not just aggregating preferences. Jürgen Habermas: ideal speech situation and the public sphere; decisions should be justified by the 'unforced force of the better argument'. Joshua Cohen and Rawls's 'public reason' are related. Tools: citizens' assemblies (e.g. Ireland's 2016–18 assembly on the Eighth Amendment), deliberative polls (James Fishkin).

steps.title: Aggregative vs deliberative
steps.body: Aggregative: preferences are fixed; voting counts them. Deliberative: preferences can change through reasoned exchange. Critics: deliberation favours the articulate and educated (Iris Marion Young urged including testimony and storytelling); it is slow and hard to scale.

steps.title: Worked example: counting vs deliberating
steps.body: A 30-member ward committee first votes: road 18, school wall 12 — road wins by aggregation. After a deliberation session where a teacher explains safety risks, a new vote gives road 13, school wall 17. The deliberative model treats the second outcome as more legitimate because preferences were formed through reasons.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Participatory democracy is not the same as direct democracy of ancient Athens; it supplements representative institutions.

quiz.q: 'Participation and Democratic Theory' (1970) is by
quiz.why: Carole Pateman argued participation has educative effects on citizens.

quiz.q: The 'unforced force of the better argument' is Habermas's
quiz.why: Habermas holds legitimate decisions follow from reason-giving free of coercion.

quiz.q: Participatory budgeting began famously in
quiz.why: Porto Alegre in Brazil introduced participatory budgeting in 1989.

scenes.text: A Malayali nurse in the Gulf works for years but cannot become a citizen there.
Back home she has voting rights, pension schemes and a sense of belonging.
What exactly does citizenship give — and to whom?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Citizenship is full membership of a political community, carrying rights and duties. Aristotle: a citizen is one who shares in deliberative and judicial office. Liberal citizenship stresses rights; republican citizenship stresses civic virtue and participation.

steps.title: T.H. Marshall
steps.body: In Citizenship and Social Class (1950), Marshall traced English citizenship in three stages: civil rights (18th century — liberty of person, speech, property, justice), political rights (19th century — franchise), social rights (20th century — welfare, education, a share in social heritage). Social citizenship moderates class inequality. Critics: the sequence is Anglocentric and gender-blind.

steps.title: Multicultural and global citizenship
steps.body: Will Kymlicka (Multicultural Citizenship, 1995): group-differentiated rights — self-government rights for national minorities, polyethnic rights for immigrant groups, special representation rights. Iris Marion Young: 'differentiated citizenship'. Cosmopolitan and global citizenship debates arise with migration and refugees.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Articles 5–11 of the Constitution deal with citizenship; the Citizenship Act, 1955 provides acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. India does not allow dual citizenship but has the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) scheme. Fundamental Duties are in Article 51A (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Marshall's order is civil → political → social, not political first. OCI is not citizenship and does not confer voting rights.

scenes.text: Ravi has one evening and fifty pages of notes.

steps.title: Unit 1 triples
steps.body: Lasswell — Politics: Who Gets What, When, How (1936). Easton — The Political System (1953); post-behavioural Credo (1969). Laslett — 'political philosophy is dead' (1956). Skinner — contextualism. Gramsci — hegemony. Hanisch — 'the personal is political'.

steps.title: Unit 2 triples
steps.body: Weber — monopoly of legitimate force; traditional/charismatic/legal-rational authority. Bodin — Six Books (1576). Austin — sovereign as determinate superior (1832). Laski — pluralism. Engels — Origin of the Family (1884). Lukes — three dimensions of power (1974). Gandhi — gram swaraj.

steps.title: Unit 3 triples
steps.body: Mill — On Liberty (1859), harm principle. Berlin — Two Concepts of Liberty (1958). Rawls — A Theory of Justice (1971): veil of ignorance, two principles, maximin. Nozick — Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974). Sandel (1982). Walzer — Spheres of Justice (1983). Sen — The Idea of Justice (2009).

steps.title: Unit 4 triples
steps.body: Schumpeter — Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942). Michels — iron law of oligarchy (1911). Dahl — Who Governs? (1961), Polyarchy (1971). Pateman (1970). Habermas — deliberation. Marshall — Citizenship and Social Class (1950). Kymlicka — Multicultural Citizenship (1995).

steps.body: For any question, open with a definition, name two thinkers with books, give an Indian example, present a critique, and conclude with your own reasoned view.

lessons.title: Ideologies map: liberalism, socialism, nationalism, secularism

scenes.text: The same budget can be read as freedom, exploitation, national pride or religious neutrality.
Ideologies are maps that select what matters.
Knowing the maps helps you place every thinker.

steps.title: Liberalism
steps.body: Core: individual, liberty, rights, limited government, rule of law, consent. Phases: classical (Locke, Smith), welfare/new liberalism (Green, Hobhouse, Keynes), neo-liberalism (Hayek, Friedman, Nozick).

steps.title: Socialism
steps.body: Core: equality, community, social ownership or regulation of means of production. Variants: utopian (Owen, Saint-Simon), scientific/Marxist, Fabian (gradual, parliamentary — Webbs), democratic socialism, Indian variants (Nehru, Lohia, J.P. Narayan). The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'socialist' and 'secular' to the Preamble.

steps.title: Nationalism
steps.body: A nation is an 'imagined community' (Benedict Anderson, 1983). Ernest Gellner linked nationalism to industrialisation. Civic vs ethnic nationalism. Indian debates: Tagore's critique of aggressive nationalism; Gandhi and Nehru's composite nationalism.

steps.title: Secularism
steps.body: Western (esp. French laïcité): strict separation of church and state. Indian secularism (Rajeev Bhargava's 'principled distance'): the state keeps distance from all religions but may intervene for equality (e.g. temple-entry laws, abolishing untouchability), and Articles 25–30 protect religious freedom and minority rights. S.R. Bommai (1994) held secularism part of the basic structure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Indian secularism is not 'anti-religion'; it is equal respect plus principled intervention. Fabianism is gradualist, not revolutionary.

steps.title: The template
steps.body: Introduction (definition + context, 3–4 lines) → Main arguments of the thinker (3–4 paragraphs with technical terms) → Indian application or example → Critique (2–3 named critics) → Conclusion (balanced evaluation). Aim for about 900–1,100 words in 40 minutes.

steps.title: Worked example: 'Critically examine Rawls's theory of justice'
steps.body: Intro: Rawls revived normative theory in 1971; justice is the first virtue of social institutions. Body: original position, veil of ignorance, maximin, two principles, lexical priority, primary goods. Application: reservations and DPSP as difference-principle reasoning. Critique: Nozick (entitlement), Sandel (unencumbered self), Sen (capabilities), Okin (family). Conclusion: despite critiques, Rawls frames contemporary debate.

lessons.title: Plato: justice and the ideal state

scenes.text: In 399 BCE Athens condemned Socrates to drink hemlock.
His pupil Plato concluded democracy let the ignorant rule.
In the Republic he designed a city ruled by wisdom.

steps.title: Context and method
steps.body: Plato (c. 427–347 BCE) wrote dialogues; the Republic asks 'What is justice?' He rejected Cephalus (telling truth and paying debts), Polemarchus (helping friends, harming enemies), Thrasymachus ('justice is the interest of the stronger') and Glaucon (justice as a social contract of the weak).

steps.title: Theory of justice
steps.body: Soul has three parts — reason, spirit, appetite; the state has three classes — rulers (guardians), auxiliaries (soldiers), producers. Corresponding virtues: wisdom, courage, temperance. Justice is the harmony in which each class/part performs its own function without interfering — 'one man, one work'. It is the principle of specialisation and functional excellence.

steps.title: Education
steps.body: State-controlled, compulsory education to produce guardians. Stage 1 (to 18): music and gymnastics; 18–20: military training; 20–30: mathematics and sciences; 30–35: dialectic; 35–50: practical administration; at 50 the best become philosopher-kings. Women could be guardians — Plato admitted equal capacity in kind.

steps.title: Worked example: applying Plato
steps.body: A talented farmer's son who excels in reasoning: in Plato's system he is promoted to the guardian class (the 'noble lie' of metals — gold, silver, bronze/iron — allows mobility by merit). A guardian's child with no aptitude is demoted. This shows the Republic is a meritocracy, not strict heredity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thrasymachus, not Plato, said justice is the interest of the stronger. Plato's justice is not legal equality but functional harmony.

activity.prompt: Match the soul part to its class and virtue
pairs: Justice is the interest of the stronger

quiz.q: For Plato justice means
quiz.why: Justice is harmony when each class performs its proper role.

quiz.q: Philosopher-kings begin to rule at about age
quiz.why: After 15 years of practical service from 35, the best rule at 50.

quiz.q: The 'noble lie' concerns
quiz.why: It tells citizens they are made of gold, silver or bronze to justify class roles.

lessons.title: Plato: philosopher-king, communism and later works

scenes.text: Plato imagines a ship where sailors quarrel to steer, none knowing navigation.
Only the true navigator — the philosopher — should command.
Rule belongs to knowledge, not numbers.

steps.title: Philosopher-king
steps.body: 'Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy … cities will never have rest from their evils.' Philosopher-kings know the Form of the Good; their rule is absolute and above law. Critics: Karl Popper (The Open Society and Its Enemies, 1945) called Plato an enemy of the open society and a forerunner of totalitarianism.

steps.title: Communism of property and wives
steps.body: Applies only to guardians and auxiliaries, not producers. Purpose: remove private interest and family attachment so rulers serve the common good. Guardians live in common barracks, have no private property, and mating is regulated by the state; children are raised in common. Aristotle criticised it: 'what is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it'.

steps.title: Statesman and Laws
steps.body: In the Statesman and especially the Laws (his last work), Plato accepted a 'second-best' state governed by law, a mixed constitution combining monarchy and democracy, private property and family, and a Nocturnal Council.

steps.title: Worked example: Platonic vs Marxian communism
steps.body: Plato: for rulers only, spiritual/political purpose, aristocratic, no class abolition. Marx: for all, economic purpose, produced by class struggle and aimed at a classless, stateless society. A 10-mark answer can use this four-point contrast.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Plato's communism did not apply to producers. The Laws, not the Republic, introduces rule of law as second-best.

items.text: Applies only to the ruling classes
Purpose: freeing rulers from private interest
Includes abolition of family for guardians
Economic basis — ownership of means of production

quiz.q: Popper's critique of Plato is in
options: The Open Society and Its Enemies
quiz.why: Popper's 1945 book attacked Plato as a forerunner of closed societies.

quiz.q: Plato's last work is
quiz.why: The Laws presents a second-best state ruled by law.

quiz.q: Plato's communism applied to
quiz.why: It was meant to keep rulers free from economic and family interests.

scenes.text: Aristotle and his students collected 158 Greek constitutions.
He compared them like a biologist compares species.
He is often called the father of political science.

steps.title: The state as natural
steps.body: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), Politics: 'Man is by nature a political animal.' The state evolves from family → village → polis; it 'comes into existence for the sake of life, and continues for the sake of the good life'. Teleology: the polis is the end (telos) of human association and is prior to the individual, as the whole is prior to the part. One who can live outside it is 'either a beast or a god'.

steps.title: Classification of constitutions
steps.body: Criteria: number of rulers (one, few, many) and end (common good vs selfish interest). Good forms: monarchy, aristocracy, polity. Perverted forms: tyranny, oligarchy, democracy. Polity — a mixture of oligarchy and democracy resting on a large middle class — is the best practicable state.

steps.title: Worked example: classify
steps.body: Rule by the wealthy few for their own benefit → oligarchy. Rule by many poor for their own benefit → democracy (perverted, in Aristotle's sense). Rule by many, with a strong middle class, for the common good → polity.

steps.title: Cycle and the middle class
steps.body: Aristotle observed constitutions change over time; the 'golden mean' and middle-class predominance give stability since the middle class neither covets others' property nor is coveted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: For Aristotle 'democracy' is the perverted rule of the many poor; his good form of rule by many is 'polity'.

quiz.why: Aristotle wrote this in Book I of the Politics.

quiz.q: Aristotle's best practicable state is
quiz.why: Polity mixes oligarchic and democratic elements around a middle class.

lessons.title: Aristotle: revolution, slavery, citizenship and property

scenes.text: Greek cities saw frequent stasis — civil strife.
Aristotle diagnosed causes like a physician.
And prescribed remedies for each constitution.

steps.title: Revolution (Book V)
steps.body: General cause: a feeling of inequality — the many want equality, the few want superiority. Particular causes: desire for gain and honour, insolence, fear, contempt, disproportionate increase of one part, election intrigues, carelessness, neglect of small changes, dissimilarity of elements. Remedies: obedience to law, avoiding small infringements, preventing excessive power in one person, political education, fairness to all classes, and keeping the middle class strong.

steps.title: Slavery
steps.body: Aristotle defended 'natural slavery': some lack full deliberative capacity and benefit from being ruled. He distinguished natural from legal (war captive) slavery and doubted the justice of the latter. This is the most criticised part of his thought.

steps.title: Citizenship and property
steps.body: A citizen is one who shares in the administration of justice and in holding office (deliberative and judicial). Excludes women, slaves, foreigners, artisans (in the best state). Property: private ownership with common use; criticised Plato's communism; wealth acquisition by natural means (household) is fine, but usury is unnatural.

steps.title: Worked example: Plato vs Aristotle
steps.body: Method: Plato deductive/idealist; Aristotle inductive/empirical. Property: Plato communism for rulers; Aristotle private property. Family: Plato abolished for guardians; Aristotle natural institution. Law: Plato above law (Republic); Aristotle sovereignty of law. Best state: Plato's ideal; Aristotle's polity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Aristotle's citizen is defined by participation in office, not merely by residence or birth.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Machiavelli and the Social Contract Thinkers
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Western Political Thought core)
courses.summary: Machiavelli's separation of politics from ethics; the social contract theories of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau — human nature, state of nature, contract, sovereignty and the general will.
outcomes: Explain Machiavelli's realism, virtù and fortuna
Explain Hobbes's state of nature and absolute sovereign
Explain Locke's natural rights, limited government and right of resistance
Explain Rousseau's general will and compare the three contractualists

scenes.text: In 1513, dismissed and tortured, Niccolò Machiavelli wrote by candlelight on his farm.
He dedicated The Prince to the Medici, hoping for a job.
The book made 'Machiavellian' a byword for cunning.

steps.title: Context
steps.body: Machiavelli (1469–1527), Florentine diplomat; works: The Prince (written 1513, published 1532), Discourses on Livy (republicanism), The Art of War. Context: Renaissance, divided Italy invaded by France and Spain; his goal was a unified, strong Italy.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body: Separation of politics from ethics and religion: the prince should 'learn how not to be good' when necessary; judged by results ('in the actions of men … one looks to the end'). Human nature: 'ungrateful, fickle, liars and deceivers, shunners of danger, greedy for gain'. Better to be feared than loved, if one cannot be both — but avoid being hated. The prince must be both fox (to recognise traps) and lion (to frighten wolves). Virtù (energy, skill, boldness) vs fortuna (chance) — fortune controls half our actions. Rely on citizen militia, not mercenaries. Double standard of morality: one for rulers, one for citizens.

steps.title: Republican Machiavelli
steps.body: In the Discourses he prefers republics with mixed government, civic virtue and conflict between nobles and people as source of liberty (Rome). Quentin Skinner and J.G.A. Pocock stress this republican side.

steps.title: Worked example: evaluating Machiavelli
steps.body: Was he immoral? Arguments for: endorses deceit and cruelty. Against: he was amoral in politics, describing what rulers must do for state survival; he condemned unnecessary cruelty (Agathocles) and wrote for a specific crisis. Isaiah Berlin: Machiavelli showed there are two incompatible moralities — Christian and pagan-civic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Machiavelli is called the 'father of modern political thought' because he separated politics from theology — not because he invented absolutism.

statements.s: Machiavelli advised rulers to rely on mercenary armies.
statements.why: He considered mercenaries useless and dangerous and urged citizen militias.

statements.s: The Prince was published posthumously in 1532.
statements.why: It was written in 1513 and printed after his death.

statements.s: Machiavelli said it is better to be feared than loved if one cannot be both.
statements.why: He thought fear is more reliable than love, though hatred must be avoided.

statements.s: Fortuna, for Machiavelli, controls all human actions.
statements.why: He said fortune governs about half, leaving the rest to virtù.

quiz.q: The fox and lion metaphor means a ruler needs
quiz.why: The fox detects traps and the lion frightens wolves.

quiz.q: Machiavelli's republican work is
quiz.why: The Discourses analyse Roman republican liberty.

quiz.q: Machiavelli's main aim was
quiz.why: He ends The Prince with an exhortation to free Italy from barbarians.

story.title: Born with fear as a twin

scenes.text: Hobbes said his mother gave birth to twins in 1588 — himself and fear — as the Spanish Armada approached.
He lived through the English Civil War.
Leviathan (1651) argued only an absolute sovereign can prevent chaos.

steps.title: Human nature
steps.body: Materialist, mechanistic psychology: humans are driven by appetites and aversions; 'a perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceaseth only in death'. Humans are roughly equal in ability, which breeds competition, diffidence (fear) and glory — the three causes of quarrel.

steps.title: State of nature
steps.body: A war 'of every man against every man', with 'no arts, no letters, no society; and which is worst of all, continual fear and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. No justice or property — 'where there is no common power, there is no law'. Laws of nature (dictates of reason): seek peace; lay down the right to all things if others do; keep covenants.

steps.title: Contract and sovereign
steps.body: Each person agrees with every other to transfer all rights (except self-preservation) to a third party — the sovereign — who is not party to the contract and so cannot breach it. Sovereign is absolute, indivisible, inalienable, the source of law and property, controls the church and opinion. Subjects keep only the right to self-preservation: they may resist if the sovereign threatens their life. Best form: monarchy. 'Covenants, without the sword, are but words.'

steps.title: Worked example: is Hobbes a liberal?
steps.body: Absolutist features: unlimited sovereign, no right of rebellion. Liberal-individualist features (Macpherson's 'possessive individualism', Oakeshott): starts from equal individuals, authority based on consent, state exists for individuals' security, 'silence of the law' leaves liberty. Conclusion: absolutist conclusion from individualist premises.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Hobbesian sovereign is not a party to the contract. Hobbes did not claim the state of nature was a real historical stage everywhere — it is a thought experiment (though he cited civil war and American 'savages').

items: Humans are equal and driven by desire and fear
State of nature becomes a war of all against all
Reason discovers laws of nature that seek peace
Individuals covenant with each other to transfer rights
An absolute sovereign is created to enforce covenants

quiz.q: 'Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' describes
quiz.why: This is Hobbes's famous description in Leviathan, chapter 13.

quiz.q: Hobbes's three causes of quarrel are
quiz.why: Leviathan names these as the principal causes of conflict.

quiz.q: Hobbes's subjects retain the right to
quiz.why: No one can transfer the right to defend one's own life.

scenes.text: In 1688 England replaced James II with William and Mary without bloodshed.
Locke's Two Treatises (1689) justified government by consent.
Echoes reached the American Declaration of Independence.

steps.title: State of nature
steps.body: Second Treatise (1689): a state of 'perfect freedom' and 'equality', governed by the law of nature (reason) — 'no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions'. Not a state of war, but 'inconveniences': no established law, no impartial judge, no power to enforce judgments.

steps.title: Property
steps.body: Natural right to 'life, liberty and estate' — collectively 'property'. Labour theory: mixing one's labour with nature makes it one's own, subject to provisos — leave 'enough and as good' for others and no spoilage. Money allows unequal accumulation without spoilage.

steps.title: Contract and government
steps.body: Two stages often read in Locke: social contract forming civil society, then trust to government. Government's purpose: preserve property. Limited government: legislative supreme but bound by natural law; separation of legislative and executive (and 'federative' power for foreign affairs); majority rule; consent — express (citizens) and tacit (residence). Right of revolution when government breaches trust. Letter Concerning Toleration (1689): religious toleration (excluding atheists and Catholics).

steps.title: Worked example: Hobbes vs Locke
steps.body: State of nature: war vs peace with inconveniences. Rights surrendered: all (except life) vs only the right to enforce natural law. Sovereign: absolute vs limited and fiduciary. Resistance: only for self-preservation vs right to revolution. Legacy: absolutism vs liberal constitutionalism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Locke's 'property' in the broad sense includes life and liberty. C.B. Macpherson read Locke as justifying capitalist accumulation.

items.text: State of nature is a state of war
Covenants without the sword are but words

quiz.q: Locke's 'property' includes
quiz.why: He used property broadly for life, liberty and possessions.

quiz.q: Tacit consent is given by
options: Living in and enjoying the protection of a country
quiz.why: Locke held residence and use of property imply consent.

quiz.q: Locke's 'federative' power concerns
quiz.why: It is power over war, peace and alliances.

scenes.text: In 1749 Rousseau read an essay contest question on whether the arts had improved morals.
He had a sudden 'illumination': civilisation had corrupted humanity.
'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'

steps.title: State of nature and corruption
steps.body: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755): natural man is solitary, peaceful, self-sufficient, guided by self-love (amour de soi) and pity — the 'noble savage' (a phrase associated with him though not his own). Private property began inequality: 'The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying This is mine … was the real founder of civil society.' Amour-propre (vanity, comparison) corrupts.

steps.title: The social contract
steps.body: The Social Contract (1762): 'Each of us puts his person and all his power in common under the supreme direction of the general will, and, in our corporate capacity, we receive each member as an indivisible part of the whole.' Each gives himself to all, and so to no one in particular. Sovereignty lies with the people, is inalienable, indivisible and cannot be represented — the English are free only during elections.

steps.title: General will
steps.body: General will (volonté générale) aims at the common good; distinct from the will of all (sum of private wills). It is always right but the people may be deceived. Whoever refuses to obey it 'shall be compelled to do so by the whole body … he will be forced to be free'. Government is an agent, not sovereign. Civil religion, a Legislator to frame laws. Critics: Talmon ('totalitarian democracy'), Berlin (positive liberty abused); defenders: democratic and participatory theorists.

steps.title: Worked example: will of all vs general will
steps.body: A town votes on a park. Private wills: A wants a car park near his shop, B a cricket ground, C a quiet garden. The will of all is the tally of these interests. The general will asks: which option serves every citizen as a citizen? Rousseau says when private differences cancel out ('the pluses and minuses'), the remainder of the differences is the general will.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: General will ≠ majority will ≠ will of all. Rousseau rejected representative sovereignty, not all government.

quiz.why: It is the first line of Book I of The Social Contract.

quiz.why: Rousseau distinguished it from the sum of private wills.

quiz.why: J.L. Talmon traced totalitarian democracy to Rousseau.

questions.why: Virtù is the capacity to master fortune and act effectively.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Bentham, J.S. Mill, Hegel and Marx
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Western Political Thought core)
courses.summary: Bentham's utilitarianism and felicific calculus; Mill's revision of utilitarianism, liberty, representative government and women's rights; Hegel's dialectic and state; Marx's historical materialism, class struggle, surplus value and revolution.
outcomes: Apply Bentham's felicific calculus and explain his legal and political reforms
Explain Mill's qualitative utilitarianism, liberty and representative government
Explain Hegel's dialectic and theory of the state
Explain Marx's historical materialism, surplus value, alienation and the state

scenes.text: Bentham's preserved skeleton, dressed in his clothes, sits in a cabinet at University College London.
He wanted every law judged by one test: does it increase happiness?
That test reshaped British law reform.

steps.title: Principle of utility
steps.body: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789): 'Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.' An action is right if it tends to produce the greatest happiness of the greatest number. Pleasures differ only in quantity: 'quantity of pleasure being equal, push-pin is as good as poetry.'

steps.title: Felicific (hedonic) calculus
steps.body: Seven dimensions to measure pleasure/pain: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity (nearness), fecundity (chance of being followed by more pleasure), purity (chance of not being followed by pain), extent (number of persons affected). Four sanctions: physical, political (legal), moral (popular), religious.

steps.title: Worked example: a policy choice
steps.body: Policy A (new hospital): 10,000 people × +6 happiness units = +60,000; cost borne by 50,000 taxpayers × −0.5 = −25,000; net +35,000. Policy B (luxury stadium): 2,000 × +10 = +20,000; taxpayers −25,000; net −5,000. Bentham's calculus favours A. (Units are illustrative — Bentham's critics doubt such measurement.)

steps.title: Political and legal reforms
steps.body: State's purpose: promote happiness; law as a 'necessary evil' that restricts liberty. Rejected natural rights ('nonsense upon stilts') and social contract as fictions. Supported universal male suffrage, secret ballot, annual parliaments, abolition of the House of Lords and monarchy (later), codification of law, prison reform (Panopticon).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bentham's utilitarianism is quantitative; Mill's is qualitative. 'Greatest happiness of the greatest number' can justify sacrificing minorities — a core criticism.

activity.prompt: Match the felicific dimension to its meaning
pairs: Chance of being followed by more pleasure
Chance of not being followed by pain
Likelihood that the pleasure will occur

quiz.q: Policy gives 4,000 people +5 each and costs 20,000 people −1 each. Net utility
'Push-pin is as good as poetry' shows Bentham's
quiz.why: For him only quantity of pleasure matters.

quiz.q: Bentham's prison design is the
quiz.why: The Panopticon let a single watchman observe all inmates.

scenes.text: James Mill taught his son Greek at three and Latin at eight.
At twenty the young Mill suffered a 'mental crisis', finding pure calculation joyless.
Poetry and feeling led him to reshape utilitarianism.

steps.title: Revision of utilitarianism
steps.body: Utilitarianism (1861): pleasures differ in quality — higher (intellectual, moral) vs lower (bodily). 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' Competent judges who have experienced both decide which is higher.

steps.title: Liberty
steps.body: On Liberty (1859): harm principle; liberty of thought and discussion, of tastes and pursuits, of association; individuality as an element of well-being; warning against 'tyranny of the majority' and social conformity.

steps.title: Representative government and women
steps.body: Considerations on Representative Government (1861): representative democracy is the ideal form; proportional representation (Thomas Hare's scheme) to protect minorities; plural votes for the educated; open (not secret) ballot; literacy test; participation educates citizens. The Subjection of Women (1869): legal subordination of women is wrong; he moved a women's suffrage amendment in Parliament (1867).

steps.title: Worked example: Mill as 'reluctant democrat'
steps.body: Democratic: universal suffrage including women, participation, PR. Elitist: plural voting for the educated, literacy qualification, fear of mediocrity of the masses. Conclusion: Mill sought democracy with safeguards for competence and minorities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mill favoured open voting, not the secret ballot (unlike Bentham). The Subjection of Women was co-influenced by Harriet Taylor Mill.

items.text: Socrates dissatisfied over a fool satisfied

quiz.q: Mill supported which electoral scheme?
quiz.why: He backed Thomas Hare's PR to protect minorities.

quiz.q: The Subjection of Women was published in
quiz.why: It appeared in 1869.

quiz.q: Mill's 'higher pleasures' are judged by
options: Competent judges who have experienced both
quiz.why: Only those acquainted with both kinds can rank them.

scenes.text: In 1806 Hegel saw Napoleon ride through Jena.
He wrote that he had seen the 'world-soul' on horseback.
History, for Hegel, is Spirit unfolding toward freedom.

steps.title: Dialectic and Spirit
steps.body: Hegel (1770–1831): reality is the self-unfolding of Geist (Spirit/Mind). Dialectic: a movement where a position generates its contradiction and both are overcome and preserved (Aufhebung) at a higher level — often summarised as thesis–antithesis–synthesis (terms Hegel himself rarely used). 'The history of the world is none other than the progress of the consciousness of freedom.' 'What is rational is actual and what is actual is rational.'

steps.title: Family, civil society, state
steps.body: Philosophy of Right (1820): ethical life (Sittlichkeit) has three moments — family (unity based on love; thesis), civil society (sphere of particular needs and market competition, 'system of needs'; antithesis), state (synthesis — universal ethical community reconciling individual and universal). The state is 'the march of God in the world' (a much-debated translation) and the actuality of concrete freedom. Constitutional monarchy, estates, a universal class (bureaucracy).

steps.title: Worked example: dialectic of master and slave
steps.body: Phenomenology of Spirit (1807): two self-consciousnesses struggle for recognition; one becomes master, the other slave. The slave, through labour, transforms the world and gains self-consciousness, while the master becomes dependent. Marx and Kojève later built on this.

steps.title: Interpretations
steps.body: Right Hegelians (conservative, Prussian state) vs Left/Young Hegelians (Feuerbach, Marx — critical, radical). Popper and Hobhouse saw Hegel as a forerunner of authoritarian statism; others (Avineri, Charles Taylor) read him as a theorist of rational freedom in modern institutions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hegel's dialectic is idealist (Spirit drives history); Marx's is materialist (production drives history). Marx said he found Hegel's dialectic 'standing on its head' and turned it right side up.

activity.prompt: Order Hegel's moments of ethical life
items: Civil society — sphere of particular interests

quiz.q: Philosophy of Right was published in
quiz.why: Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right appeared in 1820 (dated 1821).

quiz.q: Hegel's dialectic is
quiz.why: For Hegel, Spirit or Idea is the driving force of history.

quiz.q: Master–slave dialectic appears in
quiz.why: It is a famous section of the 1807 Phenomenology.

scenes.text: In February 1848 a slim pamphlet appeared in London.
Within weeks revolutions swept Europe.
The Communist Manifesto ended: 'Workers of all countries, unite!'

steps.title: Historical materialism
steps.body: Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859): relations of production correspond to a stage of the forces of production; together they form the economic base on which rises a legal and political superstructure and forms of social consciousness. 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but their social being that determines their consciousness.' Modes of production: primitive communism → slavery → feudalism → capitalism → socialism → communism.

steps.title: Class struggle and revolution
steps.body: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (Manifesto, 1848). Capitalism splits into bourgeoisie and proletariat; crises and pauperisation sharpen conflict; proletarian revolution → dictatorship of the proletariat → withering away of the state → communism: 'from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs' (Critique of the Gotha Programme, 1875).

steps.title: Worked example: surplus value
steps.body: Capital (vol. I, 1867): a worker's labour power is bought at its value (wages). Working day 10 hours; necessary labour (to produce value equal to wages) 4 hours; surplus labour 6 hours. Rate of surplus value s/v = 6/4 = 150%. If the capitalist lengthens the day to 12 hours with the same wage — absolute surplus value — s/v = 8/4 = 200%. If productivity cuts necessary labour to 2 hours in a 10-hour day — relative surplus value — s/v = 8/2 = 400%.

steps.title: Alienation
steps.body: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts (1844): under capitalism workers are alienated from the product, the process of labour, their species-being, and other humans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Dictatorship of the proletariat' is transitional, not the final stage. 'From each according to ability, to each according to needs' describes higher-phase communism, not socialism.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Indian Thought: Kautilya to the Renaissance
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Political Thought core)
courses.summary: Kautilya's Arthashastra (saptanga, mandala, statecraft); Rammohun Roy and liberal reform; Jyotirao Phule and Pandita Ramabai on caste and gender; Vivekananda, Tilak and Aurobindo on nationalism.
outcomes: Explain Kautilya's saptanga theory, mandala theory and four upayas
Explain Rammohun Roy's liberalism and social reform
Analyse Phule's anti-caste thought and Pandita Ramabai's critique of patriarchy
Compare the nationalism of Vivekananda, Tilak and Aurobindo

scenes.text: In 1905 R. Shamasastry identified a palm-leaf manuscript of the Arthashastra in Mysore.
It was a manual for kings on war, diplomacy, economy and spies.
Its author, Kautilya (Chanakya), is linked to the Mauryan court of Chandragupta.

steps.title: Nature of the text
steps.body: The Arthashastra has 15 books (adhikaranas). 'Artha' — wealth and the earth inhabited by people; the science of acquiring and protecting territory. Dating is debated; many scholars (e.g. Thomas Trautmann, Patrick Olivelle) see the text compiled over time, roughly between the 2nd century BCE and 3rd century CE, while tradition ties it to Chandragupta Maurya's minister.

steps.title: Saptanga (seven limbs of the state)
steps.body: Swami (king), Amatya (ministers), Janapada (territory and people), Durga (fortified capital), Kosha (treasury), Danda (army/coercive power), Mitra (ally). They are organically linked; the king is foremost. Comparable to the organic theory of the state.

steps.title: Mandala theory and foreign policy
steps.body: The vijigishu (would-be conqueror) is at the centre of circles of states: the immediate neighbour is the natural enemy (ari), the neighbour's neighbour a natural friend (mitra), plus madhyama (middle king) and udasina (neutral). Six measures (shadgunya): sandhi (peace treaty), vigraha (war), asana (staying quiet), yana (marching), samshraya (seeking shelter/alliance), dvaidhibhava (double policy — peace with one, war with another). Four upayas: sama (conciliation), dana (gifts), bheda (dissension), danda (force).

steps.title: King's duties and welfare
steps.body: 'In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness; in their welfare his welfare.' Detailed administration: superintendents (adhyakshas), taxation, spies, justice. Matsyanyaya (law of the fish — the big eat the small) as the condition without danda.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Kautilya is often called 'India's Machiavelli', but the Arthashastra also stresses dharma and welfare; the comparison is partial. The text was rediscovered in 1905, not continuously studied in modern times.

quiz.q: In Mandala theory, the neighbour's neighbour is a
quiz.why: An enemy's enemy is likely to be an ally.

quiz.q: Saptanga has how many elements?
quiz.why: The seven limbs make up the state.

quiz.q: Matsyanyaya means
options: Big fish eat small fish in absence of authority
quiz.why: It describes anarchy without the king's coercive power.

scenes.text: Rammohun Roy witnessed his sister-in-law's death by sati.
He campaigned with scripture and reason against the practice.
Lord William Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 1829 banned sati in Bengal.

steps.title: The 'father of the Indian Renaissance'
steps.body: Rammohun Roy (1772–1833): founded Atmiya Sabha (1815) and Brahmo Sabha (1828, later Brahmo Samaj); monotheism based on the Upanishads; rationalism; drew on Western liberalism and Indian texts.

steps.title: Political ideas
steps.body: Civil liberties: protested the Press Ordinance of 1823 (memorial to the Supreme Court and King in Council) — freedom of press; trial by jury; separation of executive and judiciary; codification of law; Indianisation of services; protection of ryots from zamindars. Supported English education (letter to Lord Amherst, 1823). Rights of women: abolition of sati, property rights, against polygamy.

steps.title: Worked example: liberal or not?
steps.body: Liberal: individual rights, press freedom, rule of law, reason. Limitations: accepted British rule as providential, mostly upper-caste urban focus, gradualist. Conclusion: an early constitutional liberal seeking reform within colonial framework.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sati was banned in 1829 by Bentinck; Rammohun did not legislate it but campaigned. Brahmo Samaj, not Arya Samaj (Dayanand Saraswati, 1875).

statements.s: Rammohun Roy founded the Arya Samaj.
statements.why: Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875; Rammohun founded the Brahmo Sabha.

statements.s: He protested the 1823 Press Ordinance.
statements.why: He petitioned against restrictions on the press.

statements.s: Sati was banned by Regulation XVII of 1829.
statements.why: Bentinck's regulation outlawed it in the Bengal Presidency.

statements.s: Rammohun opposed English education.
statements.why: He urged the government to promote Western scientific education.

quiz.why: Rammohun Roy founded it in 1828.

quiz.why: He argued for modern Western education over Sanskrit schooling.

quiz.q: Rammohun Roy is often called
quiz.why: He pioneered rational reform and liberal ideas in 19th-century India.

story.title: A school for girls in Pune

scenes.text: In 1848 Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune.
Savitribai was pelted with mud on her way to teach.
Education became a weapon against caste and patriarchy.

steps.title: Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890)
steps.body: Gulamgiri (Slavery, 1873), dedicated to African-American anti-slavery campaigners: compared caste to slavery and Brahminical dominance to colonial domination of shudras and ati-shudras. Founded Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) — truth-seekers' society, rejecting priestly mediation. Shetkaryacha Asud (Cultivator's Whipcord, 1883): exploitation of peasants by priests, moneylenders and officials. Education of women and lower castes; widow remarriage; home for widows' children.

steps.title: Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922)
steps.body: Sanskrit scholar given the titles 'Pandita' and 'Saraswati' in Calcutta. The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887): critique of child marriage, enforced widowhood and patriarchy within Brahminical society. Founded Arya Mahila Samaj (1882), Sharada Sadan (1889) for widows, and Mukti Mission (Kedgaon). Testified before the Hunter Commission (1882) for women's education and women doctors.

steps.title: Worked example: linking caste and gender
steps.body: Phule saw women of all castes as oppressed by Brahminical patriarchy; Ramabai showed even upper-caste women were subordinated. Together they anticipate the intersectional idea that caste and gender hierarchies reinforce each other — later central to Ambedkar's analysis of endogamy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Gulamgiri (1873) is Phule's; The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887) is Ramabai's. Satyashodhak Samaj was founded in 1873, the same year as Gulamgiri.

quiz.why: Phule likened shudras' condition to slavery in the Americas.

scenes.text: In Chicago in 1893 a young monk began, 'Sisters and brothers of America'.
The Parliament of Religions applauded for minutes.
His confidence in India's spiritual heritage inspired a generation of nationalists.

steps.title: Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902)
steps.body: Practical Vedanta: service to humanity as worship of God ('Daridra Narayan'). Founded Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Cultural nationalism: national regeneration through spiritual strength, education and uplift of the masses; criticised untouchability and priestcraft. Not a party politician, but inspired Tilak, Aurobindo, Subhas Bose.

steps.title: Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1856–1920)
steps.body: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it.' Extremist leader (Lal-Bal-Pal); used Ganapati (1893) and Shivaji (1895) festivals for mass mobilisation; newspapers Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English); four-fold programme: swaraj, swadeshi, boycott, national education. Gita Rahasya (written in Mandalay jail, 1908–14) — karmayoga, activism. Home Rule League (1916); Lucknow Pact (1916).

steps.title: Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950)
steps.body: Bande Mataram editor; theory of passive resistance (1907); nationalism as religion — the nation as Mother; Alipore Bomb Case (1908, acquitted); later withdrew to Pondicherry (1910) for spiritual work. The Human Cycle and The Ideal of Human Unity — world union beyond nations.

steps.title: Worked example: moderates vs extremists
steps.body: Moderates (Naoroji, Gokhale, Ranade): constitutional methods, petitions, faith in British justice, economic critique (drain theory). Extremists (Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Pal, Aurobindo): self-reliance, mass mobilisation, swadeshi and boycott, swaraj as a right. The Surat split (1907) divided the Congress.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Tilak's Home Rule League (April 1916) was separate from Annie Besant's (September 1916). Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission, not the Brahmo Samaj.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Modern Indian Thought: Gandhi, Ambedkar, Nehru and Others
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Political Thought core)
courses.summary: Gandhi on swaraj, satyagraha, ahimsa and trusteeship; Ambedkar on caste, social democracy and constitutionalism; Nehru on secularism, socialism and non-alignment; Savarkar, Iqbal and Lohia on nation, community and socialism.
outcomes: Explain Gandhi's Hind Swaraj, satyagraha and trusteeship
Explain Ambedkar's critique of caste and his idea of social democracy
Explain Nehru's democratic socialism and secularism
Compare Savarkar's Hindutva, Iqbal's thought and Lohia's socialism

scenes.text: In June 1893 a young lawyer was thrown off a first-class train compartment in South Africa.
Shivering in the waiting room, he resolved to resist injustice.
From that night grew satyagraha.

steps.title: Hind Swaraj (1909)
steps.body: Written in Gujarati aboard the ship Kildonan Castle (London to South Africa). Critique of modern Western civilisation — railways, lawyers, doctors, machinery — as materialist. Swaraj is not just political independence ('English rule without the Englishman') but self-rule — moral self-control of individuals and village self-government.

steps.title: Satyagraha and ahimsa
steps.body: Satyagraha — 'truth-force' or 'soul-force': non-violent resistance seeking to convert, not coerce, the opponent; willing self-suffering. Forms: non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting, hartal, picketing. Rules: truth, non-violence, no hatred, openness, readiness to suffer. Ahimsa is not cowardice — 'where there is only a choice between cowardice and violence, I would advise violence'. Ends and means are inseparable: 'means are to ends as seed is to tree'.

steps.title: State, economy and society
steps.body: State as 'violence in a concentrated and organised form'; ideal of enlightened anarchy; Ram Rajya; decentralised village republics (oceanic circles rather than a pyramid). Trusteeship: the rich hold wealth in trust for society. Swadeshi, khadi, bread labour, constructive programme; Sarvodaya (welfare of all, inspired by Ruskin's Unto This Last). Opposed untouchability (Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1932).

steps.title: Worked example: Salt Satyagraha
steps.body: 12 March–6 April 1930: Gandhi marched about 385 km (240 miles) with 78 satyagrahis from Sabarmati to Dandi in 24 days and broke the salt law. Average pace = 385 ÷ 24 ≈ 16 km per day. Elements: symbolic issue affecting all, open notice to the Viceroy, non-violence, mass participation leading to civil disobedience nationwide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Satyagraha differs from passive resistance: passive resistance can be a weapon of the weak and allow hatred; satyagraha is the weapon of the strong and excludes hatred (Gandhi's own distinction).

activity.prompt: Satyagraha or passive resistance (as Gandhi distinguished them)?

items.text: May harbour hatred for the opponent
Aims to convert the opponent through self-suffering
May use violence if it becomes expedient

quiz.why: Gandhi wrote it in 1909 aboard a ship.

quiz.why: Owners should use wealth for the common good.

quiz.why: Gandhi paraphrased Ruskin's book as Sarvodaya.

scenes.text: In March 1927 at Mahad, Ambedkar led thousands to drink from a public tank closed to Dalits.
That December, Manusmriti was publicly burned.
He later chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.

steps.title: Critique of caste
steps.body: Castes in India (1916): endogamy is the essence of caste; superimposition of endogamy on exogamy created castes; sati, enforced widowhood and child marriage arose to maintain endogamy — linking caste and gender. Annihilation of Caste (1936, undelivered speech to Jat-Pat Todak Mandal): caste is 'a division of labourers', not just of labour; reform needs destroying the religious sanction of shastras. Graded inequality.

steps.title: Political ideas
steps.body: Separate electorates for depressed classes at the Round Table Conferences; Communal Award (1932) → Gandhi's fast → Poona Pact (24 September 1932): reserved seats in joint electorates (148 seats in provincial legislatures instead of 71). Founded Independent Labour Party (1936), Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). States and Minorities (1947): state socialism.

steps.title: Social democracy and constitutionalism
steps.body: Speech of 25 November 1949: political democracy must be backed by social democracy — a way of life recognising liberty, equality and fraternity as a trinity; warned against 'grammar of anarchy' (unconstitutional methods) and 'hero-worship'; 'On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality.' Conversion to Buddhism at Nagpur (14 October 1956); The Buddha and His Dhamma.

steps.title: Worked example: Gandhi vs Ambedkar on caste
steps.body: Gandhi: reformed varna as division of labour without hierarchy; untouchability a sin to be removed by caste Hindus' change of heart. Ambedkar: varna and caste inseparable; untouchability rooted in shastras; needs legal rights, separate political representation, education, conversion. Points of convergence: Poona Pact, Article 17.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Annihilation of Caste was never delivered as a speech; Ambedkar published it himself after the Mandal cancelled the event. The Poona Pact increased reserved seats compared with the Communal Award.

activity.prompt: Order these events in Ambedkar's life

quiz.why: Castes in India identifies endogamy as its defining feature.

quiz.q: The Poona Pact gave depressed classes
quiz.why: Gandhi and Ambedkar agreed on reserved seats within joint electorates.

quiz.q: 'Grammar of anarchy' refers to
options: Unconstitutional methods once constitutional ones exist
quiz.why: Ambedkar urged abandoning civil disobedience after independence.

scenes.text: At Bhakra Nangal in 1954 Nehru called dams the 'temples of modern India'.
He championed science, planning and secular democracy.
Abroad he led non-alignment.

steps.title: Democracy and scientific temper
steps.body: Works: Glimpses of World History (1934), An Autobiography (1936), The Discovery of India (1946). Liberal democracy with parliamentary institutions and civil liberties; 'scientific temper' (later Article 51A(h)); composite culture — India as 'an ancient palimpsest'.

steps.title: Democratic socialism
steps.body: Influenced by Fabians and the Soviet experience but rejected violence and dictatorship. Planned economy (Planning Commission 1950; Five-Year Plans from 1951), mixed economy, public sector at the 'commanding heights', Industrial Policy Resolution (1956), Avadi session (1955) — 'socialistic pattern of society'.

steps.title: Secularism and nationalism
steps.body: Secularism as equal respect and state neutrality, opposed to communalism of all kinds ('majority communalism' as most dangerous because it can masquerade as nationalism). Internationalism: Panchsheel, NAM, anti-colonialism, disarmament.

steps.title: Worked example: Gandhi vs Nehru
steps.body: Industry: Gandhi — village industries, critique of machinery; Nehru — heavy industry, dams, planning. State: Gandhi — minimal, decentralised; Nehru — strong developmental state. Religion: Gandhi — religious ethics in politics; Nehru — secular, rationalist. Shared: non-violence in freedom struggle, anti-untouchability, anti-communalism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The 'socialistic pattern of society' resolution was adopted at Avadi in 1955, not at Karachi (Karachi 1931 was the Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy resolution).

quiz.why: Nehru wrote it in Ahmednagar Fort during 1942–46 imprisonment.

quiz.why: It was established in March 1950 by Cabinet resolution.

quiz.q: Nehru's socialism was
quiz.why: He combined planning with parliamentary democracy.

story.title: Three answers to 'Who is the nation?'

scenes.text: Savarkar answered with Hindutva — a cultural nation.
Iqbal imagined a Muslim homeland in the north-west.
Lohia answered with seven revolutions for equality.

steps.title: V.D. Savarkar (1883–1966)
steps.body: Hindutva: Who is a Hindu? (1923): a Hindu is one who regards Bharatvarsha as both pitribhu (fatherland) and punyabhu (holy land); elements — common nation (rashtra), race (jati), culture (sanskriti). Distinguished Hindutva (cultural-political identity) from Hinduism (religion). The Indian War of Independence of 1857 (1909). President of Hindu Mahasabha (1937–43). Supported social reform against untouchability (Patit Pavan temple, Ratnagiri).

steps.title: Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938)
steps.body: Poet-philosopher; 'Saare Jahan Se Achha' (1904). Later pan-Islamic: concept of khudi (selfhood); The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam (1930). Allahabad address (Muslim League, 1930): proposed a consolidated north-west Indian Muslim state within or outside the British Empire — often seen as an intellectual precursor of Pakistan.

steps.title: Ram Manohar Lohia (1910–1967)
steps.body: Socialist; Marx, Gandhi and Socialism (1963); critique of both capitalism and communism as products of Europe; 'equidistance'. Saptakranti (seven revolutions): against gender inequality, colour/race inequality, caste inequality, foreign domination, economic inequality (and for planned production), against invasion of privacy, and for non-violent means against weapons. Four-pillar state: village, district, province, centre. Backed preferential opportunities for backward castes and women ('Pichhda pave sau mein saath' — backward classes should get 60 out of 100).

steps.title: Worked example: comparing conceptions of nation
steps.body: Territorial-composite (Nehru, Gandhi): all who live in India regardless of religion. Cultural (Savarkar): shared holy land and culture. Religious-communitarian (later Iqbal): Muslims as a distinct nation. Exam answers should present each fairly before evaluation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Iqbal's 1930 address did not use the word 'Pakistan' (coined by Choudhry Rahmat Ali, 1933). Savarkar distinguished Hindutva from Hinduism.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, practicals & exam
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Western and Indian Political Thought core)
courses.summary: Thinker–book–idea sheets for Western and Indian thought, a comparative-thinkers lab, a quotation-identification lab, and previous-year-style questions with the final exam.
outcomes: Recall each thinker's key works, dates and concepts
Compare thinkers systematically on common themes
Identify and explain famous quotations
Write structured answers on political thought

scenes.text: Every thinker reduces to a book, a date and a big idea.
Learn them as triples.
Then build answers around them.

steps.title: Ancient and early modern Western
steps.body: Plato — Republic — justice as functional harmony · Aristotle — Politics — polity, revolution · Machiavelli — The Prince (1513) — virtù/fortuna · Hobbes — Leviathan (1651) — absolute sovereign · Locke — Two Treatises (1689) — natural rights, trust · Rousseau — Social Contract (1762) — general will.

steps.title: Modern Western
steps.body: Bentham — Introduction (1789) — felicific calculus · Mill — On Liberty (1859) — harm principle; Representative Government (1861); Subjection of Women (1869) · Hegel — Philosophy of Right (1820) — state as ethical whole · Marx — Manifesto (1848), Capital (1867) — class struggle, surplus value.

steps.title: Indian
steps.body: Kautilya — Arthashastra — saptanga, mandala · Rammohun Roy — Brahmo Sabha (1828) · Phule — Gulamgiri (1873) · Pandita Ramabai — High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887) · Vivekananda — practical Vedanta · Tilak — Gita Rahasya · Aurobindo — passive resistance (1907) · Gandhi — Hind Swaraj (1909) · Ambedkar — Annihilation of Caste (1936) · Nehru — Discovery of India (1946) · Savarkar — Hindutva (1923) · Iqbal — Allahabad address (1930) · Lohia — saptakranti.

steps.title: Memory chain
steps.body: Contract thinkers in date order: Hobbes 1651 → Locke 1689 → Rousseau 1762 — roughly one every half-century or more, each more democratic than the last.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Don't swap Gulamgiri (Phule) with Hind Swaraj (Gandhi), or Philosophy of Right (Hegel) with Phenomenology of Spirit (Hegel, 1807).

activity.prompt: Match the thinker to the work

quiz.q: Two Treatises of Government is by
quiz.why: Locke published it in 1689.

quiz.q: Saptanga is from
quiz.why: Kautilya lists the seven limbs of the state.

quiz.q: Felicific calculus belongs to
quiz.why: Bentham devised it to measure pleasure and pain.

lessons.title: Lab: Comparing thinkers on common themes

scenes.text: Examiners love 'compare and contrast'.
A grid of themes makes comparison effortless.
Fill it before writing.

steps.title: Theme 1: human nature
steps.body: Hobbes — selfish, fearful · Locke — rational, social · Rousseau — naturally good, corrupted by society · Machiavelli — ungrateful, fickle · Gandhi — capable of moral conversion · Marx — shaped by social relations.

steps.title: Theme 2: the state
steps.body: Plato — rule of wisdom · Aristotle — natural, for the good life · Hobbes — absolute protector · Locke — limited trust · Hegel — ethical whole · Marx — class instrument, will wither · Gandhi — organised violence; minimal · Kautilya — saptanga with king foremost · Nehru — developmental and secular.

steps.title: Theme 3: equality and caste
steps.body: Plato — functional hierarchy · Aristotle — proportional equality, natural slavery · Rousseau — inequality from property · Phule — caste as slavery · Gandhi — reformed varna, end untouchability · Ambedkar — annihilate caste; social democracy · Lohia — preferential opportunity for backward classes and women.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Write a 12-line comparison: 'Hobbes and Locke on the state of nature and the social contract.' Use the grid.

quiz.q: Who saw the state as the 'actuality of the ethical Idea'?
quiz.why: Hegel's Philosophy of Right defines the state this way.

quiz.q: Who believed inequality began with private property?
quiz.why: Rousseau's Second Discourse traces inequality to property.

quiz.q: Proportional equality and natural slavery are views of
quiz.why: Aristotle held justice as proportional and defended natural slavery.

scenes.text: A quotation in the answer lifts it.
But only if attributed correctly.
Test yourself.

steps.title: Western quotations
steps.body: 'Man is by nature a political animal' — Aristotle. 'Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' — Hobbes. 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' — Rousseau. 'Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied' — Mill. 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' — Marx and Engels.

steps.title: Indian quotations
steps.body: 'In the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness' — Kautilya. 'Swaraj is my birthright' — Tilak. 'Means are to ends as seed is to tree' — Gandhi. 'Political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy' — Ambedkar. 'Temples of modern India' — Nehru.

steps.title: How to use a quotation
steps.body: Quote once, attribute precisely (author and work), then explain in your own words what it shows — a quotation alone earns little.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Workers of the world, unite' and 'class struggles' are from the Manifesto (Marx and Engels), not Capital. 'Forced to be free' is Rousseau, not Hegel.

uni-ba-pol-public-administration.title: Public Administration
uni-ba-pol-public-administration.description: Nature and evolution of public administration, organisation theories, principles of organisation, personnel and financial administration, Indian administrative system, accountability and good governance. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Political Science and Public Administration programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature, Scope and Evolution of Public Administration
courses.summary: Meaning, nature and scope of public administration; public vs private administration; Wilson's politics–administration dichotomy and the stages of the discipline; New Public Administration, New Public Management, New Public Service and good governance.
outcomes: Define public administration and explain POSDCORB and other scope views
Distinguish public from private administration
Trace the evolution of the discipline from Wilson to the present
Compare NPA, NPM, NPS and good governance

story.title: From policy to the ration shop

scenes.text: Parliament passes the National Food Security Act, 2013.
Officials identify households, procure grain and move it to fair-price shops.
A widow in a village receives her grain — that delivery is public administration.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Woodrow Wilson: 'detailed and systematic execution of public law'. L.D. White: 'all those operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy'. Luther Gulick: 'that part of the science of administration which has to do with government, and thus concerns itself primarily with the executive branch'. Dwight Waldo: 'the art and science of management as applied to the affairs of state'.

steps.title: Nature: integral vs managerial
steps.body: Integral view (L.D. White, Marshall Dimock): includes all activities — manual, clerical, technical, managerial. Managerial view (Simon, Gulick, Luther): only managerial activities that plan, organise and direct. Is it a science or an art? Robert Dahl (1947) argued it is not yet a science because of values, human behaviour and cultural context.

steps.title: Scope: POSDCORB
steps.body: Luther Gulick (Papers on the Science of Administration, 1937, with Lyndall Urwick): Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting. Critique: technique-focused, ignores substance (policy content) — 'POSDCORB view' vs 'subject-matter view'. Modern scope includes policy analysis, development administration, comparative administration, public finance, e-governance.

steps.title: Worked example: apply POSDCORB to a vaccination drive
steps.body: Planning — targets and cold-chain map; Organising — district task force; Staffing — vaccinators and ASHA workers; Directing — daily orders; Co-ordinating — health, police, panchayats; Reporting — CoWIN dashboard; Budgeting — vaccine and logistics funds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: POSDCORB was coined by Gulick (not Fayol), though it built on Fayol's functions (planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling).

quiz.q: POSDCORB was coined by
quiz.why: Gulick introduced it in 1937 in Papers on the Science of Administration.

quiz.q: The integral view of administration includes
options: All activities from manual to managerial
quiz.why: It treats every activity in pursuit of a purpose as administration.

quiz.q: Dahl's 1947 essay questioned whether public administration is
quiz.why: He argued values, behaviour and culture limit a universal science.

story.title: The bank and the post office

scenes.text: A private bank can choose its customers and close unprofitable branches.
India Post must serve remote villages even at a loss.
Public and private administration differ in purpose and constraints.

steps.title: Differences (Appleby, Simon)
steps.body: Paul Appleby: 'Government is different' — breadth of scope and impact, public accountability, political character. Other differences: profit vs public interest motive; rule of law and uniformity of treatment; legislative and financial control; monopoly character of many services; public scrutiny (RTI, audit); difficulty measuring outputs.

steps.title: Similarities (Fayol, Urwick)
steps.body: Henri Fayol: administration is a universal activity — the same principles apply to all organisations. Shared techniques: accounting, HR management, IT systems. NPM brought private methods into government.

steps.title: Worked example: classify
steps.body: A municipal hospital must treat every patient regardless of ability to pay — public (uniformity, service motive). A pharma company prices drugs to maximise return — private (profit). A public sector bank lending to priority sectors at regulated rates — public obligations within commercial form.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Public enterprises can earn profits; the distinction is about primary purpose and accountability, not whether money is made.

items.text: Uniformity of treatment for all citizens

quiz.why: Paul Appleby stressed the political and public character of government.

scenes.text: A young professor named Woodrow Wilson published 'The Study of Administration' in 1887.
He argued administration should be run like a business, apart from politics.
Thus began a discipline.

steps.title: Stage I (1887–1926): politics–administration dichotomy
steps.body: Wilson's 'The Study of Administration' (1887): 'it is getting to be harder to run a constitution than to frame one'; administration is a field of business removed from politics. Frank Goodnow (Politics and Administration, 1900): politics expresses the will of the state; administration executes it. L.D. White's Introduction to the Study of Public Administration (1926) — the first textbook.

steps.title: Stage II (1927–37): principles
steps.body: W.F. Willoughby's Principles of Public Administration (1927); Mooney and Reiley (Onward Industry, 1931); Gulick and Urwick (1937) — universal principles (POSDCORB).

steps.title: Stage III–V (1938–1970)
steps.body: Challenge (1938–47): Chester Barnard (Functions of the Executive, 1938), Herbert Simon (Administrative Behaviour, 1947; 'proverbs of administration'), Dahl. Identity crisis (1948–70): drift to political science and management; comparative and development administration (Fred Riggs). Stage V: New Public Administration (Minnowbrook I, 1968).

steps.title: Later phases
steps.body: Public policy and public choice (1970s), NPM (1980s–90s), governance and New Public Service (2000s), digital governance. Minnowbrook II (1988) and III (2008) conferences revisited the field.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Simon's 'proverbs' critique was of the principles approach — he showed principles contradict each other (e.g. span of control vs short hierarchy).

quiz.q: The politics–administration dichotomy was proposed by
quiz.why: Wilson's 1887 essay separated administration from politics.

quiz.q: Simon called traditional principles
quiz.why: His 1946 article 'The Proverbs of Administration' showed they contradict one another.

quiz.q: The first textbook of public administration (1926) was by
quiz.why: White's Introduction to the Study of Public Administration was the first.

lessons.title: NPA, NPM, NPS and good governance

scenes.text: In the 1970s a citizen queued for hours for a form.
By the 2010s she applied online and tracked progress.
Reform ideas changed how government saw its citizens.

steps.title: New Public Administration (NPA)
steps.body: Minnowbrook Conference (1968), organised by Dwight Waldo; Frank Marini's Toward a New Public Administration (1971). Themes: relevance, values, social equity, change, client-focus, participation. H. George Frederickson: social equity as the 'third pillar' alongside efficiency and economy.

steps.title: New Public Management (NPM)
steps.body: 1980s–90s (Thatcher's UK, New Zealand, Reagan's USA). Christopher Hood (1991) listed doctrines: hands-on professional management, explicit performance standards, output controls, disaggregation into units, competition, private-sector management styles, discipline and parsimony in resources. Osborne and Gaebler (Reinventing Government, 1992): 'steering rather than rowing', ten principles — catalytic, community-owned, competitive, mission-driven, results-oriented, customer-driven, enterprising, anticipatory, decentralised, market-oriented.

steps.title: New Public Service and good governance
steps.body: Denhardt and Denhardt (2000): 'serving rather than steering' — citizens, not customers; public interest as shared values. World Bank (1989, 1992) on good governance; UNDP features: participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus orientation, equity and inclusiveness, effectiveness and efficiency, accountability. India: 'Minimum government, maximum governance'; Second ARC Report on Ethics in Governance (2007).

steps.title: Worked example: classify reforms
steps.body: Corporatising Indian Railways' catering (IRCTC) — NPM (agencification). Social audit of MGNREGA in gram sabhas — NPA/NPS (participation, equity). Performance-linked incentives for officers — NPM. Citizens' charters with grievance redress — good governance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Steering rather than rowing' is Osborne and Gaebler (NPM); 'serving rather than steering' is Denhardt and Denhardt (NPS).
