courses.title: Unit 2 · Theories of Organisation
courses.summary: Classical theory (Fayol, Gulick, Urwick) and scientific management (Taylor); Weber's bureaucracy; human relations (Mayo) and behavioural theory (Barnard, Simon); motivation theories; ecological approach (Riggs).
outcomes: Explain Taylor's scientific management and Fayol's 14 principles
Explain Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy and its critiques
Explain the Hawthorne studies and Simon's bounded rationality
Apply Maslow, Herzberg and McGregor, and explain Riggs's prismatic model

scenes.text: At Bethlehem Steel, workers loaded about 12.5 tons of pig iron a day.
F.W. Taylor timed every motion and redesigned the work with rest breaks.
A worker he called 'Schmidt' loaded 47.5 tons a day.

steps.title: Taylor's scientific management
steps.body: The Principles of Scientific Management (1911). Principles: (1) develop a science for each element of work, replacing rule of thumb (time and motion study); (2) scientific selection and training of workers; (3) cooperation between management and workers; (4) equal division of work and responsibility between management and workers. Techniques: functional foremanship (eight foremen), differential piece-rate, standardisation of tools. 'Mental revolution' on both sides.

steps.title: Worked example: productivity and piece-rate
steps.body: Output rose from 12.5 to 47.5 tons/day: increase = (47.5 − 12.5)/12.5 = 35/12.5 = 2.8 = 280%. Under a differential piece-rate, a worker meeting standard earns a higher rate per unit: e.g. ₹10/unit below 40 units and ₹12/unit at or above 40. 38 units → ₹380; 42 units → ₹504.

steps.title: Fayol's classical theory
steps.body: Henri Fayol (General and Industrial Management, 1916): five functions — planning, organising, commanding, coordinating, controlling. 14 principles: division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain (with 'gang plank' for horizontal communication), order, equity, stability of tenure, initiative, esprit de corps. Gulick and Urwick extended the principles.

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body: Machine model — treats workers as appendages; ignores social and psychological factors; opposed by trade unions; Simon's 'proverbs'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Functional foremanship (Taylor) violates Fayol's unity of command — a common exam comparison point.

quiz.why: General and Industrial Management lists 14 principles.

scenes.text: An application moves from desk to desk, each officer bound by written rules.
Weber saw this as the most rational, efficient form of administration.
Yet he also feared an 'iron cage'.

steps.title: Ideal type
steps.body: Based on legal-rational authority (Economy and Society, published 1922). Features: fixed jurisdictional areas governed by rules; hierarchy of offices; management based on written documents (files); expert training; full-time officials; impersonal rules applied uniformly; appointment on merit and qualifications; salary and pension; career with promotion by seniority or merit; separation of office from personal property.

steps.title: Strengths and Weber's fear
steps.body: Precision, speed, unambiguity, continuity, discretion, unity, reduction of friction — 'technically superior to any other form'. But rationalisation risks an 'iron cage' (stahlhartes Gehäuse) in which individuals are trapped by rules; bureaucrats might dominate elected politicians.

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body: Robert Merton: 'bureaucratic personality' and 'trained incapacity' — rules become ends (goal displacement). Philip Selznick: sub-goal formation. Alvin Gouldner: punishment-centred vs representative bureaucracy. Peter Blau: informal relations. Warren Bennis predicted the end of bureaucracy. Fred Riggs: Weberian model ill-suited to developing societies. Marxists: bureaucracy serves the ruling class.

steps.title: Worked example: red tape
steps.body: A pensioner's file is returned because a form lacks a signature on page 3, although all information is correct. This illustrates Merton's goal displacement: compliance with the rule overrides the purpose (timely pension). Remedies: self-attestation (India, 2014), single-window systems, time-bound delivery laws.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Weber's 'ideal type' is an analytical model, not a moral ideal or description of any real organisation.

statements.s: Weber's bureaucracy rests on traditional authority.
statements.why: It rests on legal-rational authority.

statements.s: Merton described goal displacement in bureaucracies.
statements.why: Rules can become ends in themselves, displacing goals.

statements.s: In Weber's model, officials own the means of administration.
statements.why: Office and personal property are separated.

statements.s: An ideal type is a model built by accentuating features.
statements.why: Weber constructed ideal types as analytical tools.

quiz.why: Documentation and impersonality ensure uniform application.

quiz.why: He worried that rules would confine human freedom.

scenes.text: At Western Electric's Hawthorne Works, researchers raised and lowered lighting.
Output rose in both test and control groups.
Being observed and valued mattered more than lighting — a new view of workers.

steps.title: Hawthorne studies (1924–32)
steps.body: Elton Mayo, Roethlisberger and Dickson. Phases: illumination experiments (1924–27), relay assembly test room (1927–32), mass interviewing programme (1928–30), bank wiring observation room (1931–32). Findings: social and psychological factors affect productivity; informal groups set their own output norms (bank wiring room); attention and participation raise morale. Critiques: neglect of unions and conflict ('cow sociology'), manipulative, methodological flaws.

steps.title: Barnard and Simon
steps.body: Chester Barnard: organisation as a cooperative system; authority accepted from below — 'zone of indifference'; executive functions: communication, securing efforts, formulating purpose. Herbert Simon (Administrative Behaviour, 1947): decision-making is the heart of administration; fact–value distinction; bounded rationality — administrators 'satisfice' (seek satisfactory solutions) rather than maximise; three phases — intelligence, design, choice. Nobel Prize in Economics, 1978.

steps.title: Worked example: satisficing
steps.body: A district officer must choose a site for a new school among 40 possible plots. Full rationality would compare all 40 on every criterion. Simon's satisficing: set minimum criteria (≥1 acre, within 2 km of the village, government land) and pick the first plot that meets them — saving time under limited information and capacity.

steps.title: Mary Parker Follett
steps.body: Constructive conflict and integration (vs domination or compromise); 'power with' rather than 'power over'; 'law of the situation' — orders should arise from the situation, depersonalising authority.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The 'zone of indifference' is Barnard (Simon later called it 'zone of acceptance'). Hawthorne effect refers to behaviour change from being observed.

lessons.title: Motivation theories and Riggs's ecological approach

story.title: Why did the clerk stay late?

scenes.text: Not for overtime pay — the clerk stayed to finish a project she cared about.
Her boss praised her work publicly.
Motivation theories explain what really drives people.

steps.title: Maslow and Herzberg
steps.body: Abraham Maslow (1943): hierarchy of needs — physiological, safety, social (belonging), esteem, self-actualisation; lower needs must be largely met before higher ones motivate. Frederick Herzberg (1959): two-factor theory — hygiene factors (salary, policy, working conditions, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction; motivators (achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, advancement) create satisfaction.

steps.title: McGregor and others
steps.body: Douglas McGregor (The Human Side of Enterprise, 1960): Theory X (people dislike work, need control) vs Theory Y (people seek responsibility, self-direction). Chris Argyris: immaturity–maturity. Rensis Likert: four systems — exploitative-authoritative, benevolent-authoritative, consultative, participative.

steps.title: Riggs's ecological approach
steps.body: Fred Riggs (Administration in Developing Countries, 1964): administration shaped by its environment (economy, social structure, communication, ideology, politics). Fused (agrarian, traditional) → prismatic (transitional — like light passing through a prism) → diffracted (industrial, specialised). Prismatic 'sala' model features: heterogeneity, formalism (gap between formal rules and actual practice), overlapping (formal structures overlap with traditional ones), 'bazaar-canteen' economy, poly-communalism, 'clects'.

steps.title: Worked example: formalism in India
steps.body: A rule requires tenders to be open and online, but in practice contracts go to local favourites through pre-arranged bids. The formal rule exists; actual behaviour differs — Riggs's formalism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: In Herzberg, salary is a hygiene factor, not a motivator. Riggs's prismatic society is transitional, not traditional.

quiz.why: Self-actualisation is realising one's full potential.

quiz.why: McGregor's Theory Y sees people as self-directed when committed.

quiz.q: Riggs's 'formalism' means
options: Gap between formal rules and actual practice
quiz.why: In prismatic societies, prescribed norms are often not followed.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Principles of Organisation, Personnel and Financial Administration
courses.summary: Hierarchy, span of control, unity of command, delegation, centralisation; line, staff and auxiliary agencies; recruitment, training and civil services in India; budget types and the budgetary process, CAG and parliamentary financial control.
outcomes: Apply principles of hierarchy, span of control and delegation
Distinguish line, staff and auxiliary agencies
Explain recruitment, training and the UPSC

lessons.title: Lab: Hierarchy, span of control and delegation

scenes.text: A collector has 40 officers reporting directly to her.
Files pile up; decisions slow.
Reorganising spans and delegating authority fixes the bottleneck.

steps.title: Hierarchy and unity of command
steps.body: Hierarchy (scalar principle): graded levels of authority and responsibility, forming a pyramid; communication flows 'through proper channel'. Unity of command: each employee receives orders from one superior. Advantages: clear authority, coordination, accountability. Drawbacks: delay, rigidity, distorted communication.

steps.title: Span of control
steps.body: The number of subordinates a superior can effectively supervise. V.A. Graicunas (1933) showed relationships grow far faster than subordinates. Formula for total relationships: R = n(2ⁿ⁻¹ + n − 1). Urwick suggested an ideal span of 5–6 at higher levels where work interlocks. Factors: nature of work, competence, time, communication technology, geography.

steps.title: Worked example: Graicunas's formula
steps.body: n = 4: R = 4 × (2³ + 4 − 1) = 4 × (8 + 3) = 4 × 11 = 44. n = 5: R = 5 × (2⁴ + 5 − 1) = 5 × (16 + 4) = 5 × 20 = 100. n = 6: R = 6 × (2⁵ + 6 − 1) = 6 × 37 = 222. Adding one subordinate (5 → 6) more than doubles possible relationships.

steps.title: Worked example: levels needed
steps.body: An organisation of 625 front-line workers with a uniform span of 5: level 1 supervisors = 625/5 = 125; level 2 = 125/5 = 25; level 3 = 25/5 = 5; level 4 = 5/5 = 1 head. So 4 supervisory levels above workers. With a span of 25: 625/25 = 25, then 25/25 = 1 → only 2 levels (flatter, but each manager supervises 25).

steps.title: Delegation and centralisation
steps.body: Delegation: conferring authority on a subordinate while the delegator retains ultimate responsibility; authority can be delegated, responsibility cannot be abdicated. Centralisation vs decentralisation (functional and territorial); deconcentration (field offices) vs devolution (to elected local bodies).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Narrow spans create tall hierarchies; wide spans create flat ones. Deconcentration is not devolution — field officers remain agents of the centre.

statements.s: By Graicunas's formula, 3 subordinates give 18 relationships.
Responsibility can be fully delegated to subordinates.
statements.why: The delegator remains ultimately responsible.

statements.s: Wider spans of control produce flatter organisations.
statements.why: Fewer levels are needed when each manager oversees more people.

statements.s: Devolution transfers power to field offices of the same ministry.
statements.why: That is deconcentration; devolution goes to autonomous elected bodies.

quiz.q: Graicunas: relationships for n = 2

quiz.why: 729 → 81 → 9 → 1, i.e. three supervisory levels.

scenes.text: In an army, the infantry fights while staff officers plan.
In government, ministries deliver while advisory bodies plan.
Auxiliary units like printing and purchase serve both.

steps.title: Line agencies
steps.body: Directly carry out primary objectives and exercise command: ministries and departments (e.g. Ministry of Railways), public corporations, independent regulatory commissions. Types in India: departments, public sector undertakings, boards.

steps.title: Staff agencies
steps.body: Advise, plan and research without command authority: general staff (PMO, Cabinet Secretariat), technical staff (NITI Aayog, earlier Planning Commission), auxiliary staff. Characteristics: advisory, no direct command, 'thinking' rather than 'doing'.

steps.title: Auxiliary (housekeeping) agencies
steps.body: Provide common services to line agencies: recruitment (UPSC), purchase (Government e-Marketplace — GeM, 2016), printing, accounts (Controller General of Accounts), audit (CAG).

steps.title: Worked example: classify
steps.body: Ministry of Health running hospitals — line. NITI Aayog drafting a health strategy — staff. UPSC recruiting medical officers — auxiliary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Staff agencies lack command authority; if they start issuing orders, line–staff conflict arises.

quiz.why: It advises and plans; it has no command over ministries.

scenes.text: Each year around ten lakh candidates apply for the Civil Services Examination.
Only about a thousand are recommended.
Merit-based recruitment is the backbone of a neutral civil service.

steps.title: Recruitment
steps.body: Merit system vs spoils system (USA's Pendleton Act 1883 introduced merit). Methods: direct recruitment (competitive exams), promotion, deputation. India: UPSC (Art. 315–323) conducts the Civil Services Examination in three stages — preliminary (objective), main (written), personality test (interview). State PSCs. Staff Selection Commission for Group B/C. All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) under Art. 312, recruited by the Centre and serving states.

steps.title: Training and conduct
steps.body: LBSNAA (Mussoorie) for IAS; SVPNPA (Hyderabad) for IPS; Mission Karmayogi (2020) — competency-based capacity building. Conduct rules, neutrality, anonymity; Article 311 protection — no dismissal by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority and only after inquiry.

steps.title: Reform commissions
steps.body: Kothari Committee (1976) on recruitment; Satish Chandra (1989); Alagh (2001); Hota (2004); Second ARC Report on Refurbishing Personnel Administration (2008). Debates: lateral entry (from 2018), generalist vs specialist, civil service neutrality vs commitment.

steps.title: Worked example: selection ratio
steps.body: If 10,00,000 apply, 5,00,000 sit the prelims, 13,000 qualify for mains, 2,800 are called for interview and 1,000 are recommended: selection ratio = 1,000/5,00,000 = 0.2% of those who appeared; interview-to-selection ratio = 1,000/2,800 ≈ 36%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The UPSC recommends; the government appoints. Article 311 protects civil servants but has exceptions (e.g. conviction, security of the state).

scenes.text: On 1 February the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget.
Behind it lie months of estimates and negotiations.
Afterwards, the CAG and Parliament check how the money was spent.

steps.title: Budget types
steps.body: Line-item (traditional) budget: allocations by object of expenditure (salaries, travel) — control-oriented. Performance budget (Hoover Commission, USA 1949; India from 1969 on ARC advice): links money to activities and outputs. PPBS (Planning-Programming-Budgeting System, US Defense 1961). Zero-based budgeting (Peter Pyhrr, Texas Instruments 1970; Jimmy Carter in Georgia; India attempted from 1986–87): every item justified afresh each year. Outcome budget (India from 2005–06): links outlays to outcomes. Gender budgeting (India from 2005–06).

steps.title: Worked example: incremental vs zero-based
steps.body: Last year's school-meal budget in a state: ₹500 crore. Incremental budgeting adds 8% → ₹540 crore. Zero-based: estimate need from scratch — 12 lakh children × 200 school days × ₹22 per meal = 12,00,000 × 200 × 22 = ₹5,28,00,00,000 = ₹528 crore. ZBB shows ₹528 crore is needed, ₹12 crore less than the incremental figure.

steps.title: Worked example: fiscal deficit
steps.body: Total expenditure ₹50 lakh crore; revenue receipts ₹34 lakh crore; non-debt capital receipts ₹1 lakh crore. Fiscal deficit = 50 − (34 + 1) = ₹15 lakh crore. If GDP is ₹330 lakh crore, fiscal deficit/GDP = 15/330 ≈ 4.5%.

steps.title: Accountability
steps.body: Budget process: preparation (Finance Ministry, budget circular), enactment (Parliament — Arts 112–117), execution, audit. CAG (Art. 148; reports under Art. 151 to President/Governor, laid before legislature; examined by PAC). FRBM Act 2003 set fiscal targets. Since 2017: budget on 1 February, Railway Budget merged, plan/non-plan distinction removed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The CAG audits after expenditure (post-audit); it does not approve spending in advance. Outcome budgeting measures results, not just activities. Remember 1 crore = 100 lakh = 10⁷.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Indian Administration, Accountability and Governance
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Public Administration core; Indian Administration)
courses.summary: Central administration (Cabinet Secretariat, PMO, ministries), district administration and the Collector; legislative, executive and judicial control; RTI, Lokpal, CVC, citizens' charters and e-governance.
outcomes: Describe the Cabinet Secretariat, PMO and structure of ministries
Explain the role of the District Collector and district administration
Explain legislative, executive and judicial control over administration
Explain RTI, Lokpal, CVC, citizens' charters and e-governance reforms

scenes.text: A ministry drafts a Cabinet note proposing a new scheme.
It circulates to Finance, Law and other ministries for comments.
The Cabinet Secretariat places it before the Cabinet; the decision is minuted and monitored.

steps.title: Ministries and departments
steps.body: Ministry headed by a minister; department is the administrative unit headed by a Secretary (the administrative head). Structure: Secretary → Additional/Joint Secretary (wing) → Director/Deputy Secretary (division) → Under Secretary (branch) → Section Officer (section). Business is governed by the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules and (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, made under Article 77(3).

steps.title: Cabinet Secretariat
steps.body: Under the PM; headed by the Cabinet Secretary (senior-most civil servant, since 1950). Functions: secretarial assistance to Cabinet and its committees, inter-ministerial coordination, monitoring decisions, chairing Committee of Secretaries, crisis management. Cabinet committees include Appointments, Security, Economic Affairs, Political Affairs, Parliamentary Affairs.

steps.title: Prime Minister's Office (PMO)
steps.body: Originally the PM's Secretariat (1947), renamed PMO in 1977. Headed by the Principal Secretary. Functions: assist the PM, coordinate policy, handle public grievances addressed to the PM, liaison with ministries and states. Debate: the PMO as a 'super-cabinet' centralising power vs efficient coordination.

steps.title: Worked example: file hierarchy
steps.body: A proposal starts in a section (Section Officer notes), goes to Under Secretary, Deputy Secretary/Director, Joint Secretary, Additional Secretary and Secretary — up to 6 levels before the minister. Reforms like 'desk officer system' and e-Office aim to cut levels and time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The minister is the political head; the Secretary is the administrative head. PMO is not mentioned in the Constitution; the Cabinet Secretariat operates under the Business Rules.

activity.prompt: Order the levels from top to bottom in a department

quiz.q: The administrative head of a department is the
quiz.why: The Secretary heads the department administratively.

quiz.why: The renaming happened in 1977.

quiz.why: Article 77(3) empowers the President to make rules for transaction of business.

scenes.text: A river breaches its embankment at midnight.
The District Collector convenes police, health, revenue and NDRF teams.
By dawn, relief camps are running — the district is where the state meets the citizen.

steps.title: The district
steps.body: Basic territorial unit of administration; India has about 780 districts (the number keeps changing). Subdivisions under SDOs/SDMs; tehsils/talukas under Tehsildars; blocks under Block Development Officers for development.

steps.title: The Collector / District Magistrate / Deputy Commissioner
steps.body: Origin: Warren Hastings created the post of Collector in 1772 for revenue collection. Roles: (1) revenue — land records, collection, land acquisition; (2) magisterial — law and order (with SP), executive magistrate powers under the BNSS 2023, licences; (3) development — chair of the District Rural Development Agency (now merged into Zila Parishad in many states), coordination of schemes; (4) disaster management — chairperson of the District Disaster Management Authority (Disaster Management Act, 2005); (5) elections — District Election Officer; (6) census, protocol, crisis management.

steps.title: Changing role
steps.body: From colonial 'mai-baap' controller to development manager and coordinator; tension with elected Zila Parishad leadership after the 73rd Amendment; work overload; proposals to separate regulatory and developmental roles (ARC).

steps.title: Worked example: identify the role
steps.body: Issuing Section 163 BNSS prohibitory orders (formerly Section 144 CrPC) — magisterial. Updating land mutation records — revenue. Reviewing PM Awas Yojana progress — development. Chairing the DDMA during floods — disaster management.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The SP heads district police; the DM coordinates law and order but does not command police in commissionerate cities. Use BNSS 2023 for the new procedural code.

quiz.q: The post of Collector was created by
quiz.why: Hastings created it in 1772.

quiz.q: The DDMA is chaired by the
quiz.why: The Disaster Management Act 2005 makes the Collector its chairperson.

quiz.q: Prohibitory orders formerly under Section 144 CrPC are now under
quiz.why: The BNSS 2023 renumbered the power as Section 163.

scenes.text: An MP asks a starred question about a delayed highway.
A citizen files a writ against an arbitrary order.
Multiple controls keep administration accountable.

steps.title: Legislative control
steps.body: Question Hour (starred — oral answers with supplementaries; unstarred — written), Zero Hour, calling attention, adjournment motions, no-confidence motion, budget debate and cut motions, financial committees (PAC, Estimates, COPU), DRSCs, Committee on Subordinate Legislation (delegated legislation), Committee on Government Assurances.

steps.title: Executive control
steps.body: Political direction by ministers, budget control by Finance Ministry, civil service rules, appointments and transfers, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG), CPGRAMS grievance portal, performance appraisal (APAR).

steps.title: Judicial control
steps.body: Writs (Arts 32, 226), judicial review of administrative action on grounds of illegality, irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness) and procedural impropriety (Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister, UK 1984 — 'GCHQ case'), principles of natural justice — audi alteram partem (hear the other side), nemo judex in causa sua (no one judge in own cause); proportionality; administrative tribunals (Art. 323A; Central Administrative Tribunal, 1985).

steps.title: Worked example: natural justice
steps.body: A teacher is dismissed without being told the charges or allowed to respond. A court will quash the order for violating audi alteram partem, and may direct a fresh inquiry where the teacher is heard.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Unstarred questions get written answers with no supplementaries. Courts review the decision-making process mostly, not the merits of policy.

quiz.q: 'Audi alteram partem' means
options: No one should judge own cause
quiz.why: It requires giving the affected person a fair hearing.

quiz.q: The Central Administrative Tribunal was set up in
quiz.why: It was established under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.

quiz.q: Starred questions receive
quiz.why: They are answered orally on the floor.

scenes.text: A farmer files an RTI application with a ₹10 fee asking why his compensation is delayed.
Within 30 days the department replies — and releases the payment.
Transparency changed the balance of power.

steps.title: Right to Information Act, 2005
steps.body: Every citizen may seek information from public authorities; PIOs must reply within 30 days (48 hours where life or liberty is involved); first appeal to the appellate officer; second appeal to the Central/State Information Commission. Exemptions in Section 8 (sovereignty, security, cabinet papers until decision, personal information). Penalty up to ₹25,000 (₹250 per day) on PIOs. 2019 amendment let the Centre fix information commissioners' terms and salaries.

steps.title: Anti-corruption institutions
steps.body: Central Vigilance Commission (1964 on Santhanam Committee advice; statutory by CVC Act 2003); CBI (under DSPE Act 1946); Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 (amended 2018 — bribe-giving also an offence); Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 (Lokpal: chairperson + up to 8 members, half judicial; first Lokpal appointed 2019); Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014.

steps.title: Citizens' charters and e-governance
steps.body: Citizens' charters introduced in India in 1997 (inspired by UK's 1991 Citizen's Charter); Sevottam model (DARPG). E-governance: National e-Governance Plan (2006), Digital India (2015), Aadhaar-based Direct Benefit Transfer, CPGRAMS, e-Office, UMANG app, GeM, DigiLocker. Right to Services Acts in states (Madhya Pradesh first, 2010).

steps.title: Worked example: RTI penalty
steps.body: A PIO delays a reply by 60 days without reasonable cause. Penalty = ₹250 × 60 = ₹15,000 (within the ₹25,000 cap). At 120 days, ₹250 × 120 = ₹30,000, but the penalty is capped at ₹25,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: RTI replies are due in 30 days, not 15. The CVC is an advisory/supervisory body, not a prosecuting agency.

scenes.text: Elderly pensioners in a district wait months for their old-age pension.
Files move through five desks; signatures are missing; funds arrive late.
You are the new Collector. Diagnose and fix it.

steps.title: Diagnosis using theory
steps.body: Weber/Merton: goal displacement — rule compliance over timely payment. Simon: bounded rationality — officers satisfice with incomplete data. Riggs: formalism — rules exist but practice differs. Span of control: one tehsildar supervising 40 verification clerks. Accountability gap: no time-bound delivery.

steps.title: Interventions
steps.body: Process re-engineering — cut desks from 5 to 2; self-attestation; Aadhaar-linked DBT to bank accounts; public display of beneficiary lists (social audit); Right to Services timelines with penalties; CPGRAMS/state grievance portal; monthly review meeting chaired by the Collector; performance dashboard.

steps.title: Measuring success
steps.body: Baseline: 1,200 pending cases; average delay 90 days. After 3 months: 300 pending; average delay 25 days. Reduction in pendency = (1,200 − 300)/1,200 = 75%. Reduction in delay = (90 − 25)/90 ≈ 72%.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Write a one-page note to the Chief Secretary using NPM (targets, DBT) and NPS/good governance (social audit, grievance redress) ideas.

uni-ba-psy-psychology.title: B.A. Psychology
uni-ba-psy-psychology.description: General, developmental, social and abnormal psychology, statistics for psychology, and classic laboratory experiments with revision. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Psychology programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · General psychology: sensation, perception, learning, memory
courses.summary: Psychology as a science, schools of thought, sensation and perception, learning (classical, operant, observational) and memory (models, forgetting).
outcomes: Describe major schools of psychology
Explain thresholds, Weber's law and Gestalt principles
Distinguish classical, operant and observational learning
Describe the multi-store and working memory models

lessons.title: Psychology as a science and its schools

scenes.text: Ananya knew the answers but froze in her viva.
A behaviourist, a psychoanalyst and a cognitive psychologist would each explain it differently.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Psychology is the **scientific study of behaviour and mental processes**. Goals: describe, explain, predict and change behaviour.

steps.title: Schools of thought
steps.body:
- **Structuralism** (Wundt, Titchener): elements of consciousness via introspection. Wundt's lab: Leipzig, 1879.
- **Functionalism** (William James): purpose of consciousness in adaptation.
- **Behaviourism** (Watson 1913, Skinner): observable behaviour only.
- **Gestalt** (Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka): 'the whole is different from the sum of its parts'.
- **Psychoanalysis** (Freud): unconscious motives.
- **Humanistic** (Maslow, Rogers): growth, free will.
- **Cognitive** (Neisser, 1967 *Cognitive Psychology*): information processing.
- **Biological, evolutionary, sociocultural** perspectives.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Ananya's freezing:
- Behaviourist: past punishment conditioned fear to examiners.
- Psychoanalytic: unconscious conflict about authority.
- Cognitive: catastrophic thoughts ('I'll fail') overload working memory.
- Biological: stress hormones (cortisol, adrenaline) disrupt retrieval.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling Freud the founder of experimental psychology — that is Wundt.

activity.prompt: Which school does each statement fit?

items.text: Break consciousness into sensations via introspection
Only observable behaviour should be studied
We see a melody, not separate notes

quiz.why: Watson's 1913 paper 'Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It' launched behaviourism.

quiz.q: Introspection was the main method of:
quiz.why: Wundt and Titchener trained observers to report the elements of their conscious experience.

quiz.q: Gestalt psychology emphasises:
quiz.why: Gestaltists argued that perception is organised into wholes that differ from the sum of parts.

scenes.text: One extra spoon in a sweet cup of tea is hardly noticed; in unsweetened tea, it is obvious.
Weber's law describes this.

steps.title: Thresholds
steps.body:
- **Absolute threshold:** minimum stimulus detected 50% of the time.
- **Difference threshold (JND):** smallest detectable change, 50% of the time.
- **Weber's law:** ΔI / I = k (constant). The JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus.
- **Signal detection theory:** detection depends on sensitivity and response bias (hits, misses, false alarms, correct rejections).
- **Sensory adaptation:** reduced sensitivity to constant stimuli.

steps.title: Worked example: Weber's law
steps.body:
For lifted weights, k ≈ 0.02 (illustrative).
Standard 500 g: JND = 0.02 × 500 = 10 g.
Standard 2,000 g: JND = 0.02 × 2000 = 40 g.
So a heavier standard needs a bigger change to be noticed.

steps.title: Perceptual organisation
steps.body:
Gestalt laws: **figure–ground**, **proximity**, **similarity**, **closure**, **continuity**, **Prägnanz** (simplicity).
Depth cues: **binocular** (retinal disparity, convergence) and **monocular** (linear perspective, interposition, relative size, texture gradient, motion parallax).
**Perceptual constancy:** size, shape, brightness, colour. Illusions (Müller-Lyer) show perception is constructive.

steps.title: Bottom-up and top-down
steps.body: Bottom-up processing starts from sensory data; top-down uses expectations and knowledge (perceptual set). Reading misspelt words easily is top-down.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating sensation and perception as the same: sensation is detection by receptors; perception is organisation and interpretation.

quiz.q: If k = 0.05 and the standard is 200 g, the JND is:
Seeing an incomplete circle as complete is the law of:
quiz.why: Closure is the tendency to fill gaps to perceive complete figures.

quiz.q: Saying 'yes' when no signal was present is a:
quiz.why: In signal detection theory, responding yes to a noise-only trial is a false alarm.

scenes.text: Rahul feels a thrill every time his phone buzzes, even before he looks.
The buzz has become a conditioned stimulus.

steps.title: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
steps.body:
UCS (food) → UCR (salivation). Neutral stimulus (bell) paired with UCS becomes CS → CR (salivation).
Processes: acquisition, **extinction** (CS without UCS), **spontaneous recovery**, **generalisation**, **discrimination**. Watson & Rayner's 'Little Albert' (1920) conditioned fear.

steps.title: Operant conditioning (Thorndike, Skinner)
steps.body:
Thorndike's **law of effect**. Skinner box.
- **Positive reinforcement:** add pleasant → behaviour ↑.
- **Negative reinforcement:** remove unpleasant → behaviour ↑.
- **Positive punishment:** add unpleasant → ↓.
- **Negative punishment:** remove pleasant → ↓.
Schedules: fixed ratio, variable ratio (most resistant to extinction — gambling), fixed interval (scalloped pattern), variable interval. **Shaping** by successive approximations.

steps.title: Observational and cognitive learning
steps.body: **Bandura's Bobo doll** studies (1961): children imitated aggressive models. Steps: **attention, retention, reproduction, motivation**. **Köhler's** chimpanzees (insight learning); **Tolman's** rats (latent learning, cognitive maps).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A seatbelt beep stops when you buckle up, so you buckle faster next time. The unpleasant beep is removed → behaviour increases → **negative reinforcement** (not punishment).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equating negative reinforcement with punishment. Reinforcement always increases behaviour.

items.text: Bonus for meeting a sales target
Taking a painkiller removes headache, so you take it again
Fine for jumping a red light
Phone taken away for coming home late

quiz.q: Slot machines use which schedule?
quiz.why: Payouts come after an unpredictable number of plays, a variable-ratio schedule that strongly resists extinction.

quiz.q: In Pavlov's experiment, the bell after conditioning is the:
quiz.why: The once-neutral bell becomes the conditioned stimulus after pairing with food.

quiz.q: Bandura's four processes include all EXCEPT:
quiz.why: Bandura listed attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; extinction is a conditioning process.

scenes.text: You read a 6-digit OTP and type it before it fades.
That's short-term memory at work.

steps.title: Multi-store model (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968)
steps.body:
- **Sensory memory:** iconic (~0.25–0.5 s, Sperling 1960), echoic (2–4 s).
- **Short-term memory:** about 18–30 s without rehearsal; capacity **7 ± 2** items (Miller, 1956); chunking increases capacity.
- **Long-term memory:** unlimited, long-lasting.
Rehearsal transfers STM → LTM.

steps.title: Working memory (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974)
steps.body: Central executive + phonological loop + visuospatial sketchpad (+ episodic buffer, added 2000). LTM types: **explicit** (episodic, semantic) and **implicit** (procedural, priming). **Levels of processing** (Craik & Lockhart, 1972): deeper semantic processing → better recall.

steps.title: Forgetting
steps.body:
- **Ebbinghaus forgetting curve** (1885): rapid early loss, then levelling; used nonsense syllables and savings method.
- **Decay**, **interference** (proactive: old blocks new; retroactive: new blocks old), **retrieval failure** (tip-of-the-tongue, cue-dependent), **motivated forgetting** (repression).
- Serial position effect: primacy and recency.

steps.title: Worked example: savings score
steps.body:
First learning of a list took 20 trials; relearning a week later took 8.
Savings = (20 − 8)/20 × 100 = 60%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Swapping proactive and retroactive interference. **Pro** = forward (old affects new); **retro** = backward (new affects old).

items.text: Writing last year's date in January
After learning French, you forget Spanish words learned earlier
Old phone number blocks recall of the new one
New password makes you forget the old one

quiz.q: Miller's magical number for STM is:
quiz.why: Miller (1956) proposed that STM holds about seven plus or minus two chunks.

quiz.q: Original learning 25 trials; relearning 10. Savings?
The phonological loop is part of:
quiz.why: Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model includes the phonological loop for verbal material.

questions.q: Wundt founded the first psychology lab in:
questions.why: Wundt opened his Leipzig laboratory in 1879.

questions.q: k = 0.1 and the standard is 60 units. JND?
questions.why: JND = 0.1 × 60 = 6 units.

questions.q: Railway tracks appearing to meet is:
questions.why: Parallel lines converging with distance is the monocular cue of linear perspective.

questions.q: Extinction in classical conditioning occurs when:
options: CS is presented without UCS repeatedly
questions.why: Repeated CS presentation without the UCS weakens the CR.

questions.q: Removing a pleasant stimulus to reduce behaviour is:
questions.why: Taking away something pleasant to decrease behaviour is negative punishment.

questions.q: Latent learning was demonstrated by:
questions.why: Tolman's rats learned maze layouts without reward, showing it once reward appeared.

questions.q: Iconic memory lasts about:
questions.why: Sperling's studies showed visual sensory memory fades within about a quarter to half a second.

questions.q: Deeper semantic processing improves recall — this is:
questions.why: Craik and Lockhart's levels-of-processing framework links depth to durability.

questions.q: Ebbinghaus used:
questions.why: He used nonsense syllables to minimise the effect of prior meaning.

questions.q: Relearning took 6 trials after original 24. Savings?
Which schedule produces a scalloped response pattern?
questions.why: Under fixed interval, responding rises near the time reinforcement is due, creating scallops.

questions.q: Remembering first and last items best is the:
questions.why: Better recall at both ends of a list is the serial position effect (primacy and recency).

questions.q: Insight learning was shown with chimpanzees by:
questions.why: Köhler's chimpanzee Sultan suddenly solved stick and box problems.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Developmental psychology
courses.summary: Principles and methods of lifespan development, Piaget and Vygotsky on cognition, Erikson and Freud on personality, Kohlberg on morality, attachment, adolescence and ageing.
outcomes: Describe principles of development and research designs
Explain Piaget's stages and Vygotsky's ZPD
Explain Erikson's psychosocial stages and Kohlberg's moral levels
Describe attachment research and styles
Discuss adolescence and adulthood issues

scenes.text: A baby controls her head before she can sit, and sits before she walks.
Development follows predictable directions.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body:
- **Cephalocaudal:** head to tail.
- **Proximodistal:** centre to periphery (trunk before fingers).
- General to specific; continuous and lifelong; individual differences; **critical/sensitive periods**.
- **Nature vs nurture**, **continuity vs discontinuity** (stages), **stability vs change**.

steps.title: Research designs
steps.body:
- **Cross-sectional:** different age groups at one time — fast, but **cohort effects**.
- **Longitudinal:** same people over years — shows change, but costly and **attrition**.
- **Sequential (cross-sequential):** several cohorts followed over time — combines both.
Methods: observation, interviews, case studies, twin and adoption studies.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A 2025 study finds 70-year-olds score lower on a computer test than 20-year-olds. Is it ageing? Not necessarily — the older cohort grew up without computers (cohort effect). A longitudinal or sequential design would separate age from cohort.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing cephalocaudal and proximodistal. Cephalo = head; proximo = near the centre.

items.text: Following 300 children from birth to age 18
Following three birth cohorts for ten years each
Comparing different age groups at one time point
A study that suffers most from attrition

quiz.q: Gaining control of arms before fingers illustrates:
quiz.why: Proximodistal development moves from the body's centre outward to the extremities.

quiz.q: Cohort effects are a major problem in:
quiz.why: Cross-sectional studies compare people born in different eras, so generational differences confound age differences.

quiz.q: Attrition means:
quiz.why: In longitudinal research, participants are lost over time, which can bias results.

scenes.text: Juice is poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin one. Four-year-old Riya says there's more now.
Her seven-year-old brother laughs: 'It's the same juice!'

steps.title: Piaget's stages
steps.body:
Key processes: **schema**, **assimilation**, **accommodation**, **equilibration**.
1. **Sensorimotor (0–2):** object permanence (~8 months onwards), deferred imitation.
2. **Preoperational (2–7):** symbolic play, **egocentrism** (three mountains task), **centration**, animism, no conservation.
3. **Concrete operational (7–11):** conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation.
4. **Formal operational (11+):** abstract and hypothetico-deductive reasoning.

steps.title: Vygotsky
steps.body:
Learning is social and cultural.
- **Zone of proximal development (ZPD):** gap between what a child can do alone and with guidance.
- **Scaffolding** (term from Wood, Bruner & Ross, 1976): temporary support withdrawn as competence grows.
- **Private speech** guides thought; language is a key cultural tool.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A 9-year-old solves 2-digit addition alone but needs hints for word problems with two steps. The word problems lie in her ZPD; the teacher scaffolds by underlining key numbers, then removes the support.

steps.title: Critiques of Piaget
steps.body: He underestimated infants (e.g. violation-of-expectation studies), and stages are less uniform across tasks and cultures than he claimed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying object permanence appears in the preoperational stage. It develops during the sensorimotor stage.

items.text: Searches for a toy hidden under a cloth
Understands that clay rolled long is still the same amount
Cannot see the mountains from the doll's view
Arranges sticks in order of length

quiz.q: Failing conservation tasks is typical of:
quiz.why: Preoperational children centre on one dimension, such as height, and fail conservation.

quiz.q: Changing an existing schema to fit new information is:
quiz.why: Accommodation modifies schemas when new information doesn't fit them.

quiz.q: ZPD is a concept of:
quiz.why: Vygotsky defined the zone of proximal development as what a learner can achieve with guidance.

scenes.text: Heinz's wife is dying; the chemist demands ₹10 lakh for a drug. Should Heinz steal it?
Kohlberg cared less about the answer than the reasoning behind it.

steps.title: Erikson's eight stages
steps.body:
1. Trust vs mistrust (0–1)
2. Autonomy vs shame and doubt (1–3)
3. Initiative vs guilt (3–6)
4. Industry vs inferiority (6–12)
5. **Identity vs role confusion** (adolescence)
6. Intimacy vs isolation (young adulthood)
7. Generativity vs stagnation (middle adulthood)
8. Integrity vs despair (late adulthood)

steps.title: Freud's psychosexual stages
steps.body: Oral (0–1), anal (1–3), phallic (3–6; Oedipus complex), latency (6–puberty), genital (puberty+). **Fixation** at a stage is said to shape adult personality. Criticised as hard to test.

steps.title: Kohlberg's moral levels
steps.body:
- **Pre-conventional:** (1) obedience and punishment; (2) self-interest/instrumental exchange.
- **Conventional:** (3) good boy/good girl (interpersonal accord); (4) law and order.
- **Post-conventional:** (5) social contract; (6) universal ethical principles.
**Carol Gilligan** (*In a Different Voice*, 1982) criticised male bias and proposed an **ethics of care**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Classifying a stage by the decision ('steal' or 'not steal'). Stages depend on the reasoning.

activity.prompt: Kohlberg level of each reasoning about Heinz?

items.text: He shouldn't steal; he'll go to jail
He should steal; his family will think he's a good husband
Stealing breaks the law, and laws keep society working
Life is a universal right above property law
He should steal because he'll get his wife back to cook for him

quiz.q: Erikson's crisis of adolescence is:
quiz.why: Erikson saw adolescence as the time to form a coherent identity or face role confusion.

quiz.q: Gilligan criticised Kohlberg for:
options: Male bias and neglecting care ethics
quiz.why: Gilligan argued that Kohlberg's all-male sample undervalued a morality of care and relationships.

quiz.q: Generativity vs stagnation occurs in:
quiz.why: Middle adults seek to contribute to the next generation through work, parenting or mentoring.

scenes.text: A mother leaves her toddler with a stranger for three minutes, then returns.
How the child greets her reveals attachment style.

steps.title: Attachment research
steps.body:
- **Harlow's monkeys** (1958): infants preferred a cloth mother over a wire mother with milk — contact comfort.
- **Bowlby:** attachment is innate and adaptive; internal working models; maternal deprivation.
- **Ainsworth's Strange Situation** (1970s): styles — **secure (B)**, **insecure-avoidant (A)**, **insecure-resistant/ambivalent (C)**; Main & Solomon added **disorganised (D)**.
- Lorenz: **imprinting** in goslings (critical period).

steps.title: Adolescence
steps.body: Puberty, growth spurt, brain development (prefrontal cortex matures into the mid-20s). **Marcia's identity statuses:** diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium, achievement. Elkind's adolescent egocentrism: **imaginary audience** and **personal fable**.

steps.title: Adulthood and ageing
steps.body: Fluid intelligence tends to decline with age while crystallised intelligence is maintained or grows (Cattell, Horn). Theories: disengagement vs activity theory. Kübler-Ross's grief stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance (not strictly sequential).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking securely attached infants show no distress when the mother leaves; they may be distressed but are easily comforted when she returns.

items.text: Upset at separation, quickly comforted on reunion
Clings yet pushes mother away angrily on return
Uses mother as a safe base to explore
Treats stranger and mother much the same

quiz.q: Harlow's research showed the importance of:
quiz.why: Infant monkeys clung to the soft cloth mother even when the wire mother provided milk.

quiz.q: A teen who adopts parents' career choice without exploring is in:
quiz.why: Marcia's foreclosure means commitment without exploration.

quiz.q: 'Everyone is looking at my pimple' illustrates:
quiz.why: Elkind's imaginary audience is the adolescent belief that others are constantly watching.

questions.q: Development from head downward is:
questions.why: Cephalocaudal development proceeds from head to feet.

questions.q: Best design to separate age and cohort effects:
questions.why: Sequential designs follow several cohorts over time, separating age from cohort.

questions.q: Object permanence develops in:
questions.why: Infants come to understand that objects exist when unseen during the sensorimotor stage.

questions.q: The three mountains task tests:
questions.why: Piaget used it to show preoperational children assume others see what they see.

questions.q: Scaffolding refers to:
questions.why: Scaffolding is guidance that is reduced as the learner becomes competent.

questions.q: Erikson's stage for ages 6–12:
questions.why: School-age children develop competence or feelings of inferiority.

questions.q: Law-and-order orientation is Kohlberg's stage:
questions.why: Stage 4 focuses on maintaining social order and obeying laws.

questions.q: The Oedipus complex occurs in Freud's:
questions.why: Freud placed the Oedipus complex in the phallic stage (about 3–6 years).

questions.q: The Strange Situation was devised by:
questions.why: Mary Ainsworth developed the Strange Situation procedure.

questions.q: Imprinting in goslings was studied by:
questions.why: Konrad Lorenz showed goslings follow the first moving object they see in a critical period.

questions.q: Exploring options without commitment is Marcia's:
questions.why: Moratorium is active exploration before commitment.

questions.q: Which intelligence tends to be maintained in old age?
questions.why: Crystallised knowledge and vocabulary tend to be maintained or increase while fluid reasoning declines.

questions.q: 'Nothing bad can happen to me' reflects:
questions.why: The personal fable is the adolescent belief in being unique and invulnerable.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Social psychology
courses.summary: Social cognition and attribution, attitudes and persuasion, conformity, obedience and group processes, prejudice, aggression and prosocial behaviour.
outcomes: Apply Kelley's covariation model and identify attribution biases
Explain cognitive dissonance and the elaboration likelihood model
Describe Asch, Milgram and group phenomena
Explain causes and reduction of prejudice
Explain bystander effect and theories of aggression

scenes.text: Your colleague arrives late. 'Lazy,' you think.
When you are late, you blame the traffic.

steps.title: Attribution
steps.body:
Heider (1958): people explain behaviour by **internal (dispositional)** or **external (situational)** causes.
**Kelley's covariation model:** consensus, distinctiveness, consistency.
- Low consensus + low distinctiveness + high consistency → **internal**.
- High consensus + high distinctiveness + high consistency → **external**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Ravi laughs at a comedian. Others also laugh (high consensus), Ravi rarely laughs at other comedians (high distinctiveness), Ravi always laughs at this comedian (high consistency) → the cause is the comedian (external).

steps.title: Attribution biases
steps.body:
- **Fundamental attribution error** (Ross, 1977): overemphasising dispositions for others.
- **Actor–observer bias:** situational for self, dispositional for others.
- **Self-serving bias:** success internal, failure external.
- **Just-world belief** (Lerner): victims 'deserve' their fate.

steps.title: Schemas and heuristics
steps.body: Schemas and stereotypes speed processing. Tversky & Kahneman: **availability** and **representativeness** heuristics; anchoring. Primacy effect in impression formation (Asch, 1946: warm–cold central traits).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing self-serving bias (about success vs failure) with actor–observer bias (self vs others).

items.text: A waiter is rude, so he must be a rude person
I topped because I'm smart; I failed because the paper was unfair
Accident victims must have done something to deserve it
Fearing flights after news of one crash

quiz.q: Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency suggests:
quiz.why: Kelley's model predicts a dispositional cause when only this person behaves this way in many situations, consistently.

quiz.q: The 'warm–cold' study on impression formation is by:
quiz.why: Asch (1946) showed that switching warm and cold changed impressions of an otherwise identical list of traits.

quiz.q: The actor–observer bias means:
options: Situational for self, dispositional for others
quiz.why: Actors see the situation around them while observers focus on the actor.

scenes.text: Students paid $1 to say a dull task was fun later rated it more enjoyable than those paid $20.
Festinger & Carlsmith (1959) explained it with cognitive dissonance.

steps.title: Attitudes
steps.body: ABC model: **Affective**, **Behavioural**, **Cognitive** components. LaPiere (1934) found a gap between stated attitudes and behaviour. Ajzen's **theory of planned behaviour**: attitude + subjective norms + perceived behavioural control → intention → behaviour.

steps.title: Cognitive dissonance
steps.body: Festinger (1957): inconsistency between cognitions creates discomfort. Reduce it by changing behaviour, changing a belief, adding consonant cognitions or trivialising. **Insufficient justification** (small reward) → more attitude change. Bem's **self-perception theory** offers an alternative.

steps.title: Persuasion
steps.body:
Yale approach: **source** (credibility, attractiveness), **message** (one-sided vs two-sided, fear appeals), **audience**.
**Elaboration likelihood model** (Petty & Cacioppo): **central route** (strong arguments; high motivation and ability; lasting change) vs **peripheral route** (cues like celebrity; short-lived).
Techniques: foot-in-the-door, door-in-the-face, low-ball. **Sleeper effect:** low-credibility message gains influence over time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking the $20 group changed attitudes more — they had sufficient justification, so less dissonance.

items.text: Comparing mileage and safety data before buying a car
Buying a drink because a film star endorses it
Reading clinical trial results of a vaccine
Liking an ad because of catchy music
Being swayed by the sheer number of arguments, not their quality

quiz.q: In Festinger and Carlsmith's study, more attitude change occurred with:
quiz.why: The $1 group lacked justification for lying, so they reduced dissonance by liking the task more.

quiz.q: Asking a small favour first, then a big one, is:
quiz.why: Foot-in-the-door uses agreement to a small request to increase compliance with a larger one.

quiz.q: The ELM was proposed by:
quiz.why: Petty and Cacioppo described central and peripheral routes to persuasion.

scenes.text: Six confederates confidently give the wrong answer about line length.
The real participant hesitates, then agrees with them.

steps.title: Conformity
steps.body:
- **Sherif (1935):** autokinetic effect — group norms in ambiguous situations (informational influence).
- **Asch (1951):** line judgement; about **37%** of critical responses conformed, ~75% conformed at least once. Conformity fell sharply with one dissenter.
- **Normative influence** (to be liked) vs **informational** (to be right).
- Kelman: compliance, identification, internalisation.

steps.title: Obedience: Milgram (1963)
steps.body: Participants as 'teachers' gave apparent shocks to a 'learner'. **65%** went to the maximum 450 V. Obedience fell when the learner was in the same room, when the experimenter gave orders by phone, or when peers refused. Raises ethical issues: deception, distress, right to withdraw.

steps.title: Group processes
steps.body:
- **Social facilitation** (Triplett 1898; Zajonc): presence of others improves simple, well-learned tasks and impairs complex ones.
- **Social loafing** (Ringelmann; Latané): less effort in groups.
- **Groupthink** (Janis, 1972): e.g. Bay of Pigs.
- **Group polarisation**, **deindividuation**.
- Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Citing Asch's 75% as the overall conformity rate — 75% conformed at least once; the overall rate on critical trials was about a third.

items.text: A sprinter runs faster with a crowd watching
One member does nothing in a group project
A board ignores warnings to keep harmony
Tug-of-war effort per person drops as team grows

quiz.q: In Milgram's original study, what share went to 450 V?
quiz.why: Twenty-six of 40 participants, 65%, obeyed to the maximum shock level.

quiz.q: Conforming to be accepted by others is:
quiz.why: Normative influence comes from wanting approval and avoiding rejection.

quiz.q: Groupthink was described by:
quiz.why: Irving Janis analysed policy fiascos to describe groupthink.

scenes.text: A man collapses on a busy footpath. Dozens walk past.
Each assumes someone else will call.

steps.title: Prejudice
steps.body:
Prejudice (attitude), stereotype (belief), discrimination (behaviour).
- **Sherif's Robbers Cave** (1954): competition created hostility; **superordinate goals** reduced it.
- **Tajfel's social identity theory:** minimal groups; in-group favouritism.
- **Allport's contact hypothesis** (1954): equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support.
- Aronson's **jigsaw classroom**.

steps.title: Aggression
steps.body:
- Instinct (Freud, Lorenz).
- **Frustration–aggression hypothesis** (Dollard et al., 1939), revised by Berkowitz (weapons effect).
- **Social learning** (Bandura).
- Hostile vs instrumental aggression.

steps.title: Prosocial behaviour
steps.body: Kitty Genovese case (1964) spurred research. **Latané & Darley:** bystander effect via **diffusion of responsibility** and pluralistic ignorance. Five steps: notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → know how to help → decide to help. Batson's **empathy–altruism** hypothesis; kin selection; reciprocity norm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying more bystanders means more help. Research shows the likelihood of any one person helping falls as group size grows.

items.text: Rival hostel groups unite to repair the water tank
No one helps because many people are present
After losing his job, a man snaps at his family
Favouring your own college team members

quiz.q: Hostility in Robbers Cave was reduced by:
quiz.why: Goals that needed both groups' cooperation reduced intergroup conflict.

quiz.q: The bystander effect is mainly explained by:
quiz.why: With others present, each person feels less personal responsibility to act.

quiz.q: The contact hypothesis was proposed by:
quiz.why: Gordon Allport's The Nature of Prejudice (1954) set out conditions for contact to reduce prejudice.

questions.q: Heider is known for:
questions.why: Fritz Heider founded attribution theory with internal versus external causes.

questions.q: High consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency suggests:
questions.why: When everyone reacts this way only to this stimulus, consistently, the stimulus is the cause.

questions.q: Overestimating personality and underestimating situation in others is:
questions.why: Ross named this the fundamental attribution error.

questions.q: Theory of planned behaviour adds which factor to attitudes and norms?
questions.why: Ajzen added perceived behavioural control to the theory of reasoned action.

questions.q: A large request refused, followed by a smaller one, is:
questions.why: Door-in-the-face uses a rejected large request to make a smaller one seem reasonable.

questions.q: Sherif's autokinetic study showed:
questions.why: Estimates of light movement converged into a group norm.

questions.q: Conformity in Asch's study dropped most when:
questions.why: A single ally who broke unanimity sharply reduced conformity.

questions.q: Presence of others impairs performance on:
questions.why: Zajonc's drive theory says arousal strengthens dominant responses, which are errors on new complex tasks.

questions.q: Tuckman's second stage is:
questions.why: Groups go through forming, then storming, then norming and performing.

questions.q: Minimal group experiments are linked to:
questions.why: Tajfel showed in-group favouritism even in trivially formed groups.

questions.q: The jigsaw classroom was developed by:
questions.why: Elliot Aronson designed jigsaw classrooms to reduce prejudice through cooperation.

questions.q: Frustration–aggression hypothesis was proposed in 1939 by:
questions.why: Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer and Sears proposed it in 1939.

questions.q: Pluralistic ignorance means:
options: Everyone wrongly assumes others see no emergency
questions.why: Each bystander reads others' calm as a sign nothing is wrong.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Abnormal psychology
courses.summary: Defining abnormality, classification (DSM-5-TR, ICD-11), models of psychopathology, anxiety and related disorders, mood disorders, schizophrenia, and therapies, with India's Mental Healthcare Act 2017.
outcomes: Apply criteria of abnormality and describe DSM/ICD classification
Explain biological, psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive and diathesis–stress models
Describe key features of anxiety, OCD, PTSD and mood disorders
Describe positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia
Compare major therapies

scenes.text: Sunil checks the lock once before leaving. His neighbour checks it 40 times and is late daily.
Frequency, distress and impairment make the difference.

steps.title: Criteria (the 4 Ds)
steps.body:
- **Deviance** from norms (statistical or social).
- **Distress** to the person.
- **Dysfunction** — impaired daily functioning.
- **Danger** to self or others.
No single criterion is sufficient; culture shapes what is seen as deviant.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **DSM-5** (APA, 2013); text revision **DSM-5-TR** (2022).
- **ICD-11** (WHO, in effect from 1 January 2022), chapter 6 for mental, behavioural or neurodevelopmental disorders.
Benefits: communication, research, treatment. Risks: labelling and stigma (Rosenhan's 'On Being Sane in Insane Places', 1973).

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- **Biological:** genes, neurotransmitters, brain structure.
- **Psychodynamic:** unconscious conflict, defence mechanisms.
- **Behavioural:** learned maladaptive responses.
- **Cognitive:** distorted thinking (Beck, Ellis).
- **Humanistic:** blocked growth.
- **Sociocultural** and **diathesis–stress** (vulnerability + stressor) → **biopsychosocial** integration.

steps.title: India
steps.body: The **Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** gives a right to access mental healthcare, allows advance directives and **decriminalised attempted suicide** in effect by presuming severe stress (Section 115). Tele-MANAS helpline (14416) launched in 2022.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using 'statistically rare' alone — high IQ is rare but not a disorder.

items.text: Low serotonin activity contributes to depression
Fear of dogs learned after a bite
'I always fail' thoughts maintain low mood
Genetic vulnerability plus job loss triggers an episode

quiz.q: ICD-11 is published by:
quiz.why: The World Health Organization publishes the International Classification of Diseases.

quiz.q: Rosenhan's study highlighted:
quiz.why: Pseudo-patients were admitted and their normal behaviour was interpreted through the label.

quiz.q: Diathesis–stress model says disorder results from:
quiz.why: A predisposition becomes a disorder when triggered by sufficient stress.

story.title: The racing heart in the metro

scenes.text: Without warning, Pooja's heart pounds and she feels she is dying.
Afterwards she avoids the metro — fear of the next attack.

steps.title: Anxiety disorders (DSM-5)
steps.body:
- **Generalised anxiety disorder:** excessive worry most days for **at least 6 months**, hard to control; restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep problems.
- **Panic disorder:** recurrent unexpected panic attacks + ≥1 month of worry or behaviour change.
- **Specific phobia**, **social anxiety disorder**, **agoraphobia**.
Learning account: Mowrer's **two-factor theory** — classical conditioning creates fear, operant avoidance maintains it (negative reinforcement).

steps.title: OCD
steps.body:
In DSM-5, OCD is in a separate chapter ('Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders').
- **Obsessions:** intrusive unwanted thoughts (contamination, harm).
- **Compulsions:** repetitive acts to reduce anxiety (washing, checking).
Treatment: **exposure and response prevention (ERP)**; SSRIs.

steps.title: PTSD
steps.body: After exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence. Four clusters: **intrusion**, **avoidance**, **negative changes in cognition and mood**, **arousal and reactivity**; duration **more than 1 month**. Acute stress disorder: 3 days to 1 month.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Classifying OCD and PTSD as anxiety disorders under DSM-5. They now have their own chapters (they were anxiety disorders in DSM-IV).

items.text: Worries about everything for a year, can't stop
Sudden attacks of terror, fears the next one
Washes hands 60 times a day to stop contamination thoughts
Flashbacks and nightmares two months after a flood

quiz.q: GAD requires symptoms for at least:
quiz.why: DSM-5 requires excessive worry occurring more days than not for at least six months.

quiz.q: Mowrer's two-factor theory says avoidance is maintained by:
quiz.why: Avoiding the feared situation removes anxiety, which negatively reinforces avoidance.

quiz.q: The treatment of choice for OCD is:
quiz.why: ERP exposes the person to triggers while preventing the compulsion, so anxiety habituates.

scenes.text: For three weeks Arif has lost interest in everything, sleeps badly and feels worthless.
His doctor checks DSM criteria for a major depressive episode.

steps.title: Major depressive disorder
steps.body:
At least **5 of 9 symptoms** for **2 weeks**, including depressed mood or loss of interest (anhedonia). Others: weight/appetite change, sleep change, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness/guilt, poor concentration, thoughts of death.
Theories: monoamine hypothesis; **Beck's cognitive triad** (negative views of self, world, future); **Seligman's learned helplessness**; hopelessness theory.

steps.title: Bipolar disorders
steps.body:
- **Bipolar I:** at least one manic episode (≥1 week; elevated mood, grandiosity, less need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas).
- **Bipolar II:** hypomania (≥4 days) + major depression.
- **Cyclothymic disorder:** 2 years of fluctuating sub-threshold symptoms.
Lithium is a classic mood stabiliser.

steps.title: Schizophrenia
steps.body:
Two or more symptoms for a significant part of 1 month, with signs for **6 months**; at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech.
- **Positive:** delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech/behaviour.
- **Negative:** flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality.
The **dopamine hypothesis**; genetic risk (Gottesman: ~48% concordance in identical twins vs ~17% in fraternal); diathesis–stress; expressed emotion in families.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Equating schizophrenia with 'split personality'. That is dissociative identity disorder, a different condition.

activity.prompt: Positive or negative symptom of schizophrenia?

items.text: Belief that TV sends personal messages

quiz.q: A major depressive episode needs symptoms for at least:
quiz.why: DSM-5 requires five or more symptoms nearly every day for at least two weeks.

quiz.q: Bipolar II differs from Bipolar I by having:
quiz.why: Bipolar II involves hypomanic episodes with major depression but never a full manic episode.

quiz.q: Learned helplessness was studied by:
quiz.why: Martin Seligman showed that uncontrollable shocks led dogs to stop trying to escape.

scenes.text: One client lies on a couch talking about childhood; another fills in a thought record; a third practises facing a fear step by step.
Each reflects a different model of the problem.

steps.title: Psychodynamic and humanistic
steps.body:
- **Psychoanalysis** (Freud): free association, dream analysis, interpretation of **resistance** and **transference**.
- **Client-centred therapy** (Rogers): **unconditional positive regard, empathy, genuineness (congruence)**; non-directive.

steps.title: Behaviour therapy
steps.body:
- **Systematic desensitisation** (Wolpe): relaxation + graded anxiety hierarchy.
- **Flooding**, **exposure**, **aversion therapy**.
- **Token economy** (operant) in institutions.
- **Modelling** (Bandura).

steps.title: Cognitive therapies
steps.body:
- **REBT** (Albert Ellis): **ABC** — Activating event, Belief, Consequence; dispute irrational beliefs (D) for effective new beliefs (E).
- **Beck's cognitive therapy:** identify automatic thoughts and distortions (all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, catastrophising).
- **CBT** combines cognitive and behavioural methods; also third-wave therapies (mindfulness, ACT, DBT).

steps.title: Biomedical
steps.body: Antidepressants (SSRIs), antipsychotics, anxiolytics (benzodiazepines), lithium; **ECT** for severe depression (modified, under anaesthesia). Indian approaches: yoga-based interventions are studied as adjuncts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assigning 'unconditional positive regard' to Freud. It is Carl Rogers's core condition.

quiz.q: Systematic desensitisation was developed by:
quiz.why: Joseph Wolpe paired relaxation with a graded hierarchy of feared situations.

quiz.q: In REBT's ABC, 'B' stands for:
quiz.why: Ellis argued that beliefs about activating events, not the events themselves, cause emotional consequences.

quiz.q: Transference refers to:
options: Client redirecting feelings about others onto the therapist
quiz.why: In psychoanalysis, clients project feelings from earlier relationships onto the analyst.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the 4 Ds?
questions.why: The 4 Ds are deviance, distress, dysfunction and danger.

questions.q: DSM is published by:
questions.why: The American Psychiatric Association publishes the DSM.

questions.q: Panic disorder requires at least how long of worry after an attack?
questions.why: DSM-5 requires at least one month of persistent concern or behaviour change.

questions.q: PTSD symptoms must last more than:
questions.why: PTSD is diagnosed when symptoms last over one month; shorter periods fit acute stress disorder.

questions.q: Beck's cognitive triad concerns negative views of:
questions.why: Beck described negative views of the self, the world and the future.

questions.q: A manic episode lasts at least:
questions.why: DSM-5 requires one week (or any duration if hospitalised).

questions.q: Avolition is a:
questions.why: Avolition, a lack of motivation, is a negative symptom of schizophrenia.

questions.q: Dopamine hypothesis is linked mainly to:
questions.why: Excess dopamine activity in certain pathways is linked to positive symptoms of schizophrenia.

questions.q: Gottesman's identical twin concordance for schizophrenia is about:
questions.why: Gottesman's review gave about 48% for identical twins, showing genes matter but are not everything.

questions.q: ERP is used mainly for:
questions.why: Exposure and response prevention is the leading psychological treatment for OCD.

questions.q: Core conditions of client-centred therapy include:
questions.why: Rogers held these three conditions to be necessary for change.

questions.q: Mental Healthcare Act in India was passed in:
questions.why: The Mental Healthcare Act was passed in 2017, replacing the Mental Health Act 1987.

questions.q: Catastrophising is a:
questions.why: Beck listed catastrophising — expecting the worst — among cognitive distortions.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Statistics in psychology
courses.summary: Scales of measurement, central tendency and variability, the normal curve and z-scores, correlation (Pearson and Spearman), and hypothesis testing with t and chi-square.
outcomes: Identify scales of measurement and choose suitable statistics
Compute mean, median, mode, variance and SD
Compute z-scores and use normal-curve areas
Compute Pearson r and Spearman rho
Explain hypothesis testing, errors and compute a chi-square

scenes.text: Class A scores: 48, 50, 52. Class B: 20, 50, 80. Both average 50.
Only a measure of spread shows how different they are.

steps.title: Scales (S.S. Stevens, 1946)
steps.body:
- **Nominal:** categories (gender, religion) → mode, chi-square.
- **Ordinal:** ranks → median, Spearman rho.
- **Interval:** equal units, no true zero (IQ, °C) → mean, SD, Pearson r.
- **Ratio:** true zero (reaction time, weight).

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Mean x̄ = Σx/N. Median = middle ordered value. Mode = most frequent.
Range = highest − lowest.
Variance (sample) s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (N − 1); SD = √s².
In a **positively skewed** distribution: mean > median > mode.

steps.title: Worked example 2: two classes
steps.body:
Class A 48, 50, 52: deviations −2, 0, 2 → Σd² = 8 → sample SD = √(8/2) = 2.
Class B 20, 50, 80: deviations −30, 0, 30 → Σd² = 1800 → SD = √900 = 30.
Same mean, very different spread.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing by N for a sample SD when the question asks for an estimate of the population (use N − 1). Always state which you used.

quiz.why: The sum is 35 and 35 ÷ 5 = 7.

quiz.q: Sample SD of 2, 4, 6 is:
quiz.why: Mean 4, squared deviations 4 + 0 + 4 = 8, 8 ÷ (3 − 1) = 4, √4 = 2.

quiz.q: In a positively skewed distribution:
quiz.why: The long right tail pulls the mean above the median, which lies above the mode.

scenes.text: Meera scored 70 in a test with mean 60 and SD 5.
Her z-score of +2 puts her near the top 2–3%.

steps.title: Normal probability curve
steps.body:
Symmetrical, bell-shaped, mean = median = mode, asymptotic tails.
Empirical rule: about **68.26%** within ±1 SD, **95.44%** within ±2 SD, **99.74%** within ±3 SD.
Skewness and **kurtosis** (leptokurtic = peaked, platykurtic = flat, mesokurtic = normal).

steps.title: z-score
steps.body: z = (X − μ) / σ. It tells how many SDs a score is from the mean. T-score = 50 + 10z.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
X = 70, μ = 60, σ = 5 → z = 10/5 = 2.
Area above z = 2 ≈ 2.28%, so Meera scored higher than about 97.7% of the group.
T-score = 50 + 10 × 2 = 70.

steps.title: Worked example 2: comparing tests
steps.body:
Maths: 65, μ 55, σ 10 → z = 1.0. English: 72, μ 66, σ 4 → z = 1.5.
Relative to classmates, English (z = 1.5) is the better performance even though the maths mark looks closer to the top.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the sign: a score below the mean has a negative z.

quiz.q: About what % of scores fall within ±1 SD?
quiz.why: In a normal curve about 68.26% of cases lie between −1 and +1 SD.

quiz.q: z = 1.5 corresponds to T-score:

scenes.text: Five students report study hours and test marks.
How strongly do the two move together?

steps.title: Correlation coefficient
steps.body:
Ranges from −1 to +1. Sign = direction; size = strength. Correlation ≠ causation.
**Pearson r** = Σ(dx·dy) / √(Σdx² · Σdy²) for interval/ratio data.
**Spearman ρ** = 1 − 6Σd² / [N(N² − 1)] for ranks.

steps.title: Coefficient of determination
steps.body: r² gives the proportion of variance shared. With r = 0.77, r² ≈ 0.59, so about 59% of variation in marks is associated with study hours in this sample.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking r = −0.8 is weaker than r = +0.5. Strength depends on the absolute value.

items.text: Hours of practice and typing speed
Anxiety level and test performance on a hard exam (high range)
Shoe size and IQ in adults
Hours of sleep deprivation and attention accuracy

quiz.q: N = 6, Σd² = 14. Spearman ρ = ?
Which is the strongest correlation?
quiz.why: Strength is judged by absolute value, and |−0.85| is the largest.

quiz.q: r = 0.6, so r² = ?
quiz.why: 0.6 squared is 0.36, meaning 36% of variance is shared.

scenes.text: Group A studies with music, Group B in silence.
Is the difference in recall real or just chance?

steps.title: Logic of testing
steps.body:
H₀: no difference; H₁: a difference. Choose α (usually 0.05 or 0.01). If p < α, reject H₀.
- **Type I error (α):** rejecting a true H₀ (false positive).
- **Type II error (β):** failing to reject a false H₀ (false negative). Power = 1 − β.
One-tailed vs two-tailed tests; **degrees of freedom**.

steps.title: Choosing a test
steps.body:
- **t-test:** compare two means (independent or paired/related groups).
- **ANOVA (F):** three or more means.
- **Chi-square (χ²):** frequencies in categories (nominal).
- Non-parametric: Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis.

steps.title: Worked example: chi-square goodness of fit
steps.body:
60 students choose among 3 elective courses. Expected (equal) = 20 each. Observed: 30, 20, 10.
χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = (10²/20) + (0²/20) + (10²/20) = 5 + 0 + 5 = **10**.
df = k − 1 = 2. Critical χ² at 0.05 with df 2 = 5.99.
10 > 5.99 → reject H₀: preferences are not equal.

steps.title: Worked example: df for t
steps.body:
Independent groups of 12 and 10: df = 12 + 10 − 2 = 20.
Paired design with 15 participants: df = 15 − 1 = 14.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying 'we proved H₁'. We only reject or fail to reject H₀ at a given α.

items.text: Recall scores: music group vs silence group
Same participants' anxiety before and after therapy
Reaction time across three noise levels, different people
Number of men and women preferring tea vs coffee

Rejecting a true null hypothesis is:
quiz.why: A Type I error is a false positive, with probability α.

quiz.q: Independent groups of 8 and 8. df for t = ?

questions.why: Ratio scales such as reaction time have a true zero point.

questions.q: Median of 7, 2, 9, 4, 5 = ?
questions.why: Ordered: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9 so the median is 5.

questions.q: Population SD of 2, 4, 6, 8 (mean 5) is:
About what % of cases lie beyond +2 SD?
questions.why: About 47.72% lies between mean and +2 SD, leaving about 2.28% above it.

questions.q: A peaked distribution is:
questions.why: Leptokurtic curves are more peaked than the normal curve.

questions.q: N = 5, Σd² = 10. Spearman ρ = ?
Σdxdy = 12, Σdx² = 16, Σdy² = 25. Pearson r = ?
Correlation of −0.9 means:
questions.why: An absolute value near 1 with a minus sign shows a strong inverse relation.

questions.q: Power of a test equals:
questions.why: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null, 1 − β.

questions.q: Comparing four group means uses:
questions.why: ANOVA tests differences among three or more means without inflating Type I error.

questions.q: Chi-square with 4 categories: df = ?
questions.why: Goodness-of-fit df = k − 1 = 3.

questions.q: Observed 40, 20; expected 30, 30. χ² = ?
Non-parametric alternative to independent t-test:
questions.why: The Mann–Whitney U test compares two independent groups on ranks.
