courses.summary: Standard B.A. psychology laboratory experiments — Müller-Lyer illusion, bilateral transfer, serial position effect and Stroop interference — with procedures, worked observation tables, viva questions, and a full revision sheet.
outcomes: Conduct and report a psychophysics experiment using the method of average error
Calculate transfer of training percentages
Plot and interpret a serial position curve
Measure Stroop interference
Revise key concepts and answer exam-style questions

lessons.title: Lab: Müller-Lyer illusion (method of average error)

scenes.text: Two lines are equal, but the one with outward fins looks longer.
The participant adjusts a variable line until it 'looks equal' — and overshoots.

steps.title: Aim and design
steps.body:
**Aim:** to measure the extent of the Müller-Lyer illusion.
**Apparatus:** Müller-Lyer board with a fixed standard (arrow-heads, 10 cm) and an adjustable variable (fins outward).
**Method:** method of average error (adjustment). IV: direction of starting position (in/out), side (left/right). DV: point of subjective equality (PSE).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Seat the participant at arm's length; give instructions.
2. Trial starts with the variable clearly shorter (in) or longer (out).
3. Participant adjusts until both lines look equal; experimenter notes the reading from the back scale.
4. Alternate in/out and left/right (counterbalancing) for, say, 20 trials.
5. Compute the mean PSE and constant error.

steps.title: Worked observation table
steps.body:
Standard = 10 cm. Four sample settings of the variable: 11.2, 11.6, 10.8, 11.4 cm.
Mean = 45.0/4 = 11.25 cm.
**Constant error (illusion)** = 11.25 − 10 = 1.25 cm.
Percentage illusion = 1.25/10 × 100 = 12.5%.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- What is PSE? (The value judged equal to the standard.)
- Why counterbalance in/out trials? (To control movement and starting-point errors.)
- One explanation of the illusion? (Gregory's misapplied size constancy: depth cues of corners.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Letting the participant see the scale — readings must be hidden on the back.

activity.prompt: Classify each element of the experiment.

items.text: Starting position of the variable line (in/out)

quiz.q: Settings 10.9, 11.3, 11.1, 10.7 cm; standard 10 cm. Constant error?
The method of adjustment is also called:
quiz.why: Participants adjust the stimulus themselves and errors are averaged, hence method of average error.

quiz.q: Gregory explained the illusion through:
quiz.why: Gregory argued the fins act as depth cues so the brain wrongly scales the line's size.

story.title: Drawing a star in a mirror

scenes.text: Rohan traces a star seeing only its mirror image; it feels impossible.
After practice with his right hand, his left hand also improves.

steps.title: Aim and design
steps.body:
**Aim:** to study transfer of training from the practised hand to the unpractised hand.
**Apparatus:** mirror-drawing apparatus, star pattern, stopwatch.
**Design:** pre-test (unpractised hand, e.g. left) → practice trials (right hand) → post-test (left hand). DV: time and/or errors.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Explain the task; screen blocks direct view.
2. Pre-test: left hand, 2 trials, record time and errors.
3. Practice: right hand, 10 trials.
4. Post-test: left hand, 2 trials.
5. Compute transfer.

steps.title: Worked observation table
steps.body:
Left hand mean time: pre-test 140 s, post-test 105 s.
Amount of transfer = 140 − 105 = 35 s.
% transfer = (pre − post)/pre × 100 = 35/140 × 100 = **25%**.
Errors: pre 28, post 14 → (28 − 14)/28 × 100 = **50%** improvement.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Positive vs negative transfer? (Prior learning helps vs hinders new learning.)
- Why is a control group useful? (Improvement could be from repeated pre/post testing alone.)
- Theory: identical elements (Thorndike) vs generalisation of principles (Judd).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing by the post-test score instead of the pre-test score when computing % transfer.

items.text: Riding a bicycle makes learning a scooter easier
Driving on the left makes driving in the USA harder
Knowing Hindi helps learn Marathi script
QWERTY habit slows typing on a different layout

quiz.q: Pre-test 120 s, post-test 90 s. % transfer?
Identical elements theory of transfer was given by:
quiz.why: Thorndike held that transfer occurs to the extent tasks share identical elements.

quiz.q: Errors fall from 30 to 18. % reduction?

scenes.text: Participants hear 15 words and write all they recall.
Plotted by position, recall makes a U-shape.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body:
**Aim:** to study the effect of serial position on free recall.
1. Prepare lists of 15 unrelated concrete nouns.
2. Present one word every 2 seconds.
3. Immediate free recall for 1 minute.
4. Repeat for 5 lists (or use 10 participants).
5. For each position, compute % of trials recalled; plot position (x) vs % recall (y).

steps.title: Worked observation table
steps.body:
10 participants. Number recalling the word at positions 1, 2, 8, 14, 15: 8, 7, 3, 7, 9.
% recall: 80%, 70%, 30%, 70%, 90%.
High at the start (**primacy**: rehearsed into LTM) and end (**recency**: still in STM); low in the middle.

steps.title: Variations and interpretation
steps.body: Glanzer & Cunitz (1966): a 30-second distractor (counting backwards) before recall removes the recency effect but leaves primacy — supporting separate STM and LTM. Slower presentation improves primacy.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why unrelated words? (To prevent chunking by meaning.)
- What does a delay do to recency? (Eliminates it.)
- Which store underlies primacy? (Long-term memory.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Scoring order of recall instead of the word's original position in the list.

items.text: Last words still in short-term memory
Effect disappears after 30 s counting task

quiz.q: 6 of 12 participants recall the 10th word. % recall?
A delayed recall task mainly removes:
quiz.why: The distractor displaces items from STM, removing recency while primacy remains.

quiz.q: The serial position curve is typically:
quiz.why: Recall is high at both ends and low in the middle.

scenes.text: Name the ink colour: the word says RED but the ink is blue.
You slow down — reading is automatic, colour naming is not.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body:
**Aim:** to measure interference of word reading on colour naming (Stroop, 1935).
Conditions (within-subjects, counterbalanced):
- **Neutral/control:** colour patches or XXXX.
- **Incongruent:** colour words in conflicting ink.
Task: name ink colours of 20 items aloud as fast as possible; record time and errors.

steps.title: Worked observation table
steps.body:
Mean time — neutral 12 s, incongruent 20 s.
Interference = 20 − 12 = **8 s**.
% interference = 8/12 × 100 ≈ **66.7%**.
With a group, test the difference using a **paired t-test** (same participants in both conditions).

steps.title: Explanation
steps.body: **Automaticity:** practised readers process word meaning automatically; it competes with the controlled colour-naming response. Speed-of-processing and selective attention accounts also exist.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why counterbalance? (To control practice and fatigue order effects.)
- Why use a paired test? (Repeated-measures design.)
- Would young children who can't read show the effect? (Little or none.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Running all participants in the same order (neutral first) — practice effects then reduce the measured interference.

items.text: Time to name all ink colours

quiz.q: Neutral 15 s, incongruent 24 s. Interference?
quiz.why: Interference is 24 − 15 = 9 seconds.

quiz.q: The statistical test for Stroop data from one group in both conditions:
quiz.why: The same participants do both conditions, so scores are related and a paired t-test fits.

quiz.q: Stroop effect is explained mainly by:
quiz.why: Reading is automatic for skilled readers and interferes with naming the ink colour.

Practise writing structured answers.

steps.title: Key names
steps.body: Wundt (1879 lab); Watson (1913); Pavlov (classical); Skinner (operant); Bandura (Bobo doll); Atkinson–Shiffrin; Baddeley–Hitch; Ebbinghaus; Piaget; Vygotsky (ZPD); Erikson (8 stages); Kohlberg (3 levels, 6 stages); Ainsworth; Asch; Milgram (65%); Festinger; Latané & Darley; Beck; Ellis; Rogers; Wolpe.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Weber: ΔI/I = k. Savings = (OL − RL)/OL × 100.
SD (sample) = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(N − 1)]. z = (X − μ)/σ; T = 50 + 10z.
Pearson r = Σdxdy / √(Σdx²Σdy²). Spearman ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/[N(N² − 1)].
χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. % transfer = (pre − post)/pre × 100.

questions.q: z = 2.5 gives T-score:
Savings when OL = 30 trials, RL = 12 trials:
Observed 18, 12; expected 15, 15. χ² = ?
Bandura's Bobo doll study demonstrated:
questions.why: Children imitated an adult model's aggression without direct reinforcement.

questions.q: Kohlberg's post-conventional level includes:
questions.why: Stages 5 (social contract) and 6 (universal principles) form the post-conventional level.

questions.q: Anhedonia means:
questions.why: Anhedonia is loss of interest or pleasure, a core symptom of depression.

questions.q: Which design uses the same participants in all conditions?
questions.why: In repeated measures (within-subjects) every participant experiences each condition.

uni-ba-soc-sociology.title: B.A. Sociology
uni-ba-soc-sociology.description: Introductory sociology, classical and modern theory, Indian society, research methods, rural and urban sociology, with revision and fieldwork practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Sociology programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction to sociology and basic concepts
courses.summary: What sociology studies, how it emerged, and its core concepts: society, community, institution, group, status and role, norms, values, culture and socialisation.
outcomes: Define sociology and explain its emergence after the industrial and French revolutions
Distinguish society, community, association and institution
Classify groups (primary/secondary, in-group/out-group, reference group)
Explain status, role, role conflict and role set
Describe culture, norms, values and agencies of socialisation

lessons.title: Nature, scope and emergence of sociology

scenes.text: At Pune station, Ritu notices people queue at one counter but crowd at another.
Her professor says: no law forces either behaviour — shared expectations do. That is sociology's subject matter.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
**Sociology** is the systematic study of social relationships, groups, institutions and society. The term was coined by **Auguste Comte** (1838), the 'father of sociology', who imagined a positive science of society.
- Durkheim: the study of **social facts**.
- Weber: the interpretive understanding of **social action**.

steps.title: Why it emerged in 19th-century Europe
steps.body:
- **Industrial Revolution:** factories, migration to cities, new working class, poverty.
- **French Revolution (1789):** collapse of old feudal and church authority; ideas of liberty and equality.
- **Enlightenment and natural science:** belief that reason and observation could explain society too.
Thinkers asked: what holds a society together when tradition breaks down?

steps.title: Scope: two schools
steps.body:
- **Formal (specialistic) school** — Simmel, Tönnies, Weber: sociology studies the *forms* of social relations (competition, conflict, cooperation).
- **Synthetic school** — Durkheim, Hobhouse, Sorokin: sociology is a general science that links all social sciences.
Today sociology has many branches: rural, urban, industrial, gender, medical, environmental, political sociology.

steps.title: Sociology vs other social sciences
steps.body: Economics studies production and exchange; political science studies power and the state; psychology studies the individual mind. Sociology studies **patterns of relationships** that cut across all of these, e.g. how caste shapes both voting and occupation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Comte founded the first sociology department — Durkheim held early sociology teaching posts in France; Comte only named and outlined the discipline.
- Treating sociology as 'common sense': it tests beliefs against evidence and often finds them wrong.

activity.prompt: Which discipline mainly studies each question?

items.text: How does caste affect choice of marriage partner?
How does a rise in interest rates affect investment?
How does short-term memory capacity limit recall?
How are powers divided between Union and States?
Why do urban families become nuclear?
What determines the price of onions?

quiz.q: Who coined the term 'sociology'?
quiz.why: Auguste Comte coined the word sociology in 1838 while outlining a positive science of society.

quiz.q: The formal school of sociology is associated with:
quiz.why: Georg Simmel argued sociology should study the forms of interaction such as conflict and cooperation, which defines the formal school.

quiz.q: Which event is NOT usually cited as a cause of sociology's emergence?
quiz.why: The Green Revolution happened in the 1960s, long after sociology emerged in the 19th century.

scenes.text: Aman's college is a group of people organised for education — an association.
Its exam system, a set of established rules, is an institution.

steps.title: Society
steps.body: **Society** (MacIver & Page): 'a web of social relationships'. It is abstract — you cannot see relationships, only people. Features: likeness and difference, interdependence, cooperation and conflict, it is dynamic.

steps.title: Community
steps.body: A **community** is a group living in a definite locality with a **community sentiment** (we-feeling, role feeling, dependency feeling). It is concrete and fulfils most of life's needs — e.g. a village. Tönnies contrasted **Gemeinschaft** (community: close, traditional) with **Gesellschaft** (society/association: impersonal, contractual).

steps.title: Association and institution
steps.body:
- **Association:** a group organised to pursue specific interests — a trade union, a school, a club. Membership is voluntary and it can be dissolved.
- **Institution:** an established set of **norms and procedures** — marriage, the exam system, property. MacIver: 'we belong to associations, not to institutions.'
Example: the family (group) is an association; marriage is an institution.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Classify 'State Bank of India' and 'banking'.
Step 1: SBI is a concrete organised group of people → association.
Step 2: banking is a set of rules and procedures (loans, deposits, interest) → institution.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling a village 'an association'. A village is a community: people are born into it and it meets most needs, not one specific interest.

items.text: A trade union of mill workers
A fishing hamlet with strong we-feeling

quiz.q: 'We belong to associations, not to institutions' is a point made by:
quiz.why: MacIver and Page stressed that associations are groups of people while institutions are rules and procedures, so we can only be members of associations.

quiz.q: Gemeinschaft refers to:
quiz.why: Tönnies used Gemeinschaft for close, personal, traditional community bonds, in contrast to the impersonal Gesellschaft.

quiz.q: Which is an essential element of community?
quiz.why: A community needs a locality and community sentiment — a we-feeling — that binds members together.

scenes.text: Dr. Meera must stay at the hospital for an emergency on the evening of her mother's surgery.
Two of her statuses pull her in opposite directions — sociologists call this role conflict.

steps.title: Types of group
steps.body:
- **Primary group** (C.H. Cooley): small, face-to-face, intimate, lasting — family, play group. Cooley called them the 'nursery of human nature'.
- **Secondary group:** large, formal, goal-oriented — a company, a political party.
- **In-group / out-group** (W.G. Sumner): 'we' vs 'they'; leads to ethnocentrism.
- **Reference group** (Robert Merton, building on Hyman): a group whose standards a person uses to judge themselves, even if not a member.

steps.title: Status and role
steps.body:
- **Status:** a position in society. **Ascribed** (by birth: caste, sex, age) or **achieved** (by effort: doctor, IAS officer). Ralph Linton (1936) made the distinction.
- **Role:** the expected behaviour attached to a status — the dynamic aspect of status.
- **Role set** (Merton): the many roles linked to one status — a teacher relates to students, colleagues, principal, parents.
- **Role conflict:** incompatible demands, either between two statuses or within one role set.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A Dalit woman becomes a district collector.
Ascribed statuses: female, caste identity. Achieved status: collector. If upper-caste staff resist her orders, there is a clash between ascribed and achieved status — a key theme in Indian sociology.

steps.title: Anticipatory socialisation
steps.body: Merton noted that people adopt the values of a reference group they hope to join — e.g. a student copying the dress and speech of corporate employees before campus placement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying 'role conflict' for any personal dilemma. It must arise from the expectations of social positions.

items.text: Being born into a Brahmin family

quiz.q: Who introduced the concept of primary group?
quiz.why: Charles Horton Cooley described primary groups as intimate face-to-face groups that form the nursery of human nature.

quiz.q: The concept 'role set' was given by:
quiz.why: Robert Merton used role set for the cluster of role relationships attached to a single status.

quiz.q: Ethnocentrism is linked most closely to:
quiz.why: Sumner showed that strong in-group loyalty leads people to judge out-groups by their own group's standards, which is ethnocentrism.

scenes.text: A child in Chennai learns to touch elders' feet; her cousin in London learns to shake hands.
Neither is born knowing — both learnt through socialisation.

steps.title: Culture
steps.body:
**E.B. Tylor (1871):** culture is 'that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society.'
- **Material culture:** tools, buildings, phones.
- **Non-material culture:** beliefs, language, values.
- **Cultural lag** (W.F. Ogburn): non-material culture changes more slowly than material culture — e.g. mobile phones spread faster than norms about privacy.

steps.title: Norms and values
steps.body:
- **Values:** shared ideas of what is good (honesty, equality).
- **Norms:** rules for behaviour. Sumner: **folkways** (mild customs — eating with the right hand) and **mores** (strongly moral — not stealing). Breaking mores brings severe sanctions.
- **Laws:** formal norms enforced by the state.

steps.title: Socialisation
steps.body:
Socialisation is the lifelong process by which a person learns the culture of society.
- **Agencies:** family (primary), peer group, school, religion, mass media, workplace.
- **Cooley's looking-glass self:** we see ourselves as we imagine others see us.
- **G.H. Mead:** the self develops through play and game stages; the 'I' (spontaneous) and 'me' (social) and the **generalised other**.
- **Resocialisation:** learning new norms, e.g. army training; **anticipatory socialisation** prepares for future roles.

steps.title: Feral children
steps.body: Cases of children raised in extreme isolation (e.g. 'Genie' in the USA, 1970) show that language and social skills do not develop normally without socialisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing up folkways and mores: the difference is the moral weight and severity of sanction, not whether a law exists.

items.text: Removing shoes before entering a home
Wearing a helmet on a two-wheeler
Not insulting one's parents in public

quiz.q: 'Cultural lag' was proposed by:
quiz.why: William F. Ogburn argued that non-material culture lags behind changes in material culture, creating cultural lag.

quiz.q: The 'looking-glass self' is Cooley's idea that:
options: We see ourselves as we imagine others see us
quiz.why: Cooley said our self-image forms from how we imagine others perceive and judge us.

quiz.q: In Mead's theory, the 'generalised other' refers to:
options: The organised attitudes of the whole community
quiz.why: Mead's generalised other is the internalised set of expectations of society as a whole, formed in the game stage.

questions.q: Durkheim defined sociology as the study of:
questions.why: Durkheim held that sociology studies social facts — external, constraining ways of acting.

questions.q: Which is an institution?
questions.why: The education system is a set of rules and procedures; a school or club is an association.

questions.q: Primary groups are called the 'nursery of human nature' by:
questions.why: Cooley used this phrase because primary groups shape a person's earliest self and values.

questions.q: A student who adopts the values of IAS officers before selection shows:
questions.why: Adopting the values of a group one hopes to join is anticipatory socialisation, a concept from Merton.

questions.q: Ascribed and achieved status were distinguished by:
questions.why: Ralph Linton in The Study of Man (1936) distinguished status by birth from status by effort.

questions.q: Breaking which norm brings the strongest moral sanction?
questions.why: Mores carry moral weight, so their violation brings strong disapproval or punishment.

questions.q: Tylor's definition of culture stresses that culture is:
options: Acquired as a member of society
questions.why: Tylor described culture as capabilities and habits acquired by humans as members of society.

questions.q: Which school saw sociology as a general science linking all social sciences?
questions.why: The synthetic school of Durkheim, Hobhouse and Sorokin viewed sociology as a general, synthesising science.

questions.q: A teacher dealing with students, parents and principal illustrates:
questions.why: The many role relationships attached to the single status of teacher form a role set.

questions.q: Gesellschaft relationships are typically:
questions.why: Tönnies used Gesellschaft for impersonal, interest-based relations typical of modern urban society.

questions.q: Mead's 'I' represents:
questions.why: For Mead the 'I' is the spontaneous, creative response, while the 'me' is the internalised social attitudes.

questions.q: Privacy norms lagging behind smartphone use is an example of:
questions.why: When non-material norms change more slowly than technology, Ogburn called it cultural lag.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: W.G. Sumner wrote Folkways (1906) and classified norms into folkways and mores.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Classical sociological thinkers
courses.summary: Comte, Spencer, Marx, Durkheim and Weber: positivism, evolution, historical materialism, social facts, solidarity, suicide, social action, ideal types, authority and the Protestant ethic.
outcomes: Explain Comte's law of three stages and Spencer's organic analogy
Outline Marx's historical materialism, class struggle and alienation
Explain Durkheim's social facts, solidarity and types of suicide
Explain Weber's social action, ideal type, authority and Protestant ethic
Compare positivist and interpretive approaches

lessons.title: Comte and Spencer: positivism and evolution

scenes.text: Grandmother prays to Indra for rain; the farmer's son checks the IMD forecast app.
Comte would call this a shift from the theological to the positive stage of thought.

steps.title: Comte's law of three stages
steps.body:
Human thought passes through:
1. **Theological** — events explained by gods and spirits (fetishism → polytheism → monotheism).
2. **Metaphysical** — explained by abstract forces ('nature', 'essence').
3. **Positive (scientific)** — explained by observation, experiment and laws.
Comte also divided sociology into **social statics** (order) and **social dynamics** (progress), and proposed a hierarchy of sciences with sociology at the top.

steps.title: Spencer: organic analogy and evolution
steps.body:
Herbert Spencer compared society to a living organism: both grow, become more complex, and have differentiated, interdependent parts.
Social evolution moves from **simple to compound** societies and from **militant** (coercion, central control) to **industrial** (voluntary cooperation) societies. He coined 'survival of the fittest' (1864).

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Mention Spencer's key difference too: an organism has one centre of consciousness, but in society consciousness is spread among individuals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Survival of the fittest' was coined by Spencer, not Darwin.
- Comte's positivism is not the same as logical positivism of the 20th century.

activity.prompt: Which of Comte's stages does each explanation belong to?

items.text: An epidemic is punishment by a goddess
Disease arises from an imbalance in 'vital nature'
Cholera spreads via contaminated water, shown by data
A comet signals a king's death
Crop yields rise with irrigation, measured over trials

quiz.q: In Comte's scheme, the stage that explains events by abstract forces is:
quiz.why: The metaphysical stage replaces gods with abstract forces or essences before scientific explanation arrives.

quiz.q: Spencer's 'militant society' is based on:
quiz.why: Spencer described militant societies as centralised and coercive, unlike industrial societies based on voluntary cooperation.

quiz.q: Social statics in Comte refers to:
quiz.why: Comte used social statics for the study of order and social dynamics for the study of progress.

lessons.title: Karl Marx: materialism, class and alienation

scenes.text: Imran delivers food for a platform; he controls neither the app, the prices nor the profit.
Marx would ask: who owns the means of production, and what does that do to the worker?

steps.title: Historical materialism
steps.body:
The **economic base** (forces of production + relations of production) shapes the **superstructure** (law, politics, religion, ideology).
History moves through modes of production: primitive communism → ancient (slave) → feudal → capitalist → (predicted) socialist/communist. Change occurs when forces of production outgrow relations of production.

steps.title: Class and class struggle
steps.body:
'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (*Communist Manifesto*, 1848, with Engels).
In capitalism: **bourgeoisie** (own the means of production) vs **proletariat** (sell labour power).
- **Class in itself:** shared objective position.
- **Class for itself:** class conscious and organised.
**Surplus value:** the value workers produce beyond their wage, appropriated as profit.

steps.title: Alienation
steps.body:
In the *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts* (1844), Marx said the worker is alienated from:
1. the **product** of labour,
2. the **process** of labour,
3. their **species-being** (human creative nature),
4. **other people**.

steps.title: Worked example: surplus value
steps.body:
A worker paid ₹600 per 8-hour day produces goods worth ₹1,500 (after materials).
Surplus value = 1,500 − 600 = ₹900.
Rate of surplus value = s/v = 900/600 = 1.5 = 150%.
In hours: the worker 'earns' the wage in 600/1500 × 8 = 3.2 hours; the remaining 4.8 hours are surplus labour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Marx thought the base mechanically determines everything; he (and Engels later) allowed for interaction, but the base is determining 'in the last instance'.

quiz.q: A worker paid ₹500 produces value of ₹1,250. Rate of surplus value?
quiz.why: Surplus value is 1,250 − 500 = 750, and 750 ÷ 500 = 1.5, so the rate is 150%.

quiz.q: 'Class for itself' means a class that is:
options: Conscious of its interests and organised
quiz.why: Marx distinguished a class merely sharing a position from one that has become conscious and organised to act.

quiz.q: Marx's theory of alienation appears mainly in:
quiz.why: The 1844 Manuscripts set out the four dimensions of alienation under capitalism.

lessons.title: Émile Durkheim: social facts, solidarity, suicide

scenes.text: News reports discuss student suicides in coaching hubs.
Durkheim argued that suicide rates, not single cases, reveal social causes such as weak integration or regulation.

steps.title: Social facts (Rules of Sociological Method, 1895)
steps.body: Social facts are ways of acting, thinking and feeling that are **external** to the individual and exert **constraint** on them — language, law, currency, religious beliefs. Rule: 'treat social facts as things' and explain a social fact by another social fact.

steps.title: Division of Labour in Society (1893)
steps.body:
- **Mechanical solidarity:** simple societies; similarity; strong collective conscience; **repressive law** (punishment).
- **Organic solidarity:** modern societies; specialisation and interdependence; **restitutive law** (restore the situation — contract, civil law).
Abnormal forms: anomic and forced division of labour.

steps.title: Suicide (1897): four types
steps.body:
Two dimensions — **integration** and **regulation**:
- **Egoistic:** too little integration (Protestants had higher rates than Catholics; unmarried higher than married).
- **Altruistic:** too much integration (soldier sacrifice).
- **Anomic:** too little regulation (sudden economic boom or crash).
- **Fatalistic:** too much regulation (slaves; mentioned in a footnote).

steps.title: Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912)
steps.body: Religion is a unified system of beliefs and practices relative to **sacred** things, uniting followers into a moral community (church). Based on Australian **totemism**; when people worship the totem they are really worshipping society.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing up mechanical (traditional) and organic (modern). Remember: organic = organs that differ but depend on each other.

items.text: Isolated elderly man with no family ties
Soldier sacrificing himself for his unit
Trader after a sudden market crash
Lottery winner losing all sense of limits

quiz.q: Restitutive law is typical of:
quiz.why: In organic solidarity law aims to restore relations, e.g. contract law, rather than to punish.

quiz.q: Anomic suicide results from:
quiz.why: Anomic suicide occurs when norms break down and desires are no longer regulated, as in sudden economic change.

quiz.q: Durkheim's Elementary Forms is based mainly on:
quiz.why: Durkheim studied Australian Aboriginal totemism as the simplest religion to find its basic elements.

lessons.title: Max Weber: action, ideal type, authority, Protestant ethic

scenes.text: In a district office, clerks follow written rules no matter who the collector is.
Weber called this legal-rational authority and its machinery, bureaucracy.

steps.title: Social action and Verstehen
steps.body:
Sociology is the interpretive understanding (**Verstehen**) of social action — action that takes others into account. Four types:
1. **Zweckrational** (instrumentally rational): means–ends calculation.
2. **Wertrational** (value-rational): acting for a value regardless of cost.
3. **Affectual:** driven by emotion.
4. **Traditional:** by habit and custom.

steps.title: Ideal type
steps.body: An analytical construct made by exaggerating key features of a phenomenon. It is not 'ideal' in the moral sense and not an average; it is a yardstick to compare real cases (e.g. ideal type of bureaucracy).

steps.title: Authority and bureaucracy
steps.body:
Authority = legitimate power. Types:
- **Traditional** (kings, elders),
- **Charismatic** (extraordinary personal qualities — Gandhi), later **routinised**,
- **Legal-rational** (rules, office).
Bureaucracy: hierarchy, written rules, specialisation, impersonality, appointment by merit, salaried careers. Weber feared the 'iron cage' of rationality.

steps.title: Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905)
steps.body: Calvinist doctrine of **predestination** created anxiety; worldly success in a **calling** became a sign of grace. Disciplined work plus ascetic saving encouraged reinvestment — an 'elective affinity' with the spirit of capitalism. Weber argued ideas can shape economic life, a counterpoint to Marx.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing that Weber said Protestantism *caused* capitalism alone; he claimed it was one significant contributory factor.

items.text: A revered spiritual leader with mass following
A municipal commissioner acting under rules
A tribal chief obeyed by custom
An elected Prime Minister acting under the Constitution

quiz.q: Acting to uphold honour regardless of cost is:
quiz.why: Value-rational action is guided by belief in a value for its own sake, whatever the consequences.

quiz.q: An ideal type is:
options: An analytical construct accentuating key features
quiz.why: Weber's ideal type exaggerates essential features to serve as a measuring rod for real cases.

quiz.q: Weber's 'iron cage' refers to:
quiz.why: Weber feared that rationalisation and bureaucracy would trap modern people in an impersonal iron cage.

questions.q: Comte's three stages in order are:
questions.why: Thought moves from theological to metaphysical to positive explanation according to Comte.

questions.q: 'Survival of the fittest' was coined by:
questions.why: Herbert Spencer coined the phrase in 1864 in his Principles of Biology.

questions.q: For Marx, religion and law belong to the:
questions.why: Marx placed law, politics, religion and ideology in the superstructure built on the economic base.

questions.q: A worker is paid ₹400 and produces ₹1,000 of value in 8 hours. Necessary labour time is:
questions.why: The wage is 400/1000 = 0.4 of the value, and 0.4 × 8 = 3.2 hours of necessary labour.

questions.q: Repressive law indicates:
questions.why: Durkheim saw punitive law as the index of mechanical solidarity based on a strong collective conscience.

questions.q: Durkheim found suicide higher among Protestants than Catholics, explained as:
questions.why: Protestantism integrates believers less tightly, so higher rates were explained as egoistic suicide.

questions.q: 'Treat social facts as things' is a rule from:
questions.why: The rule appears in The Rules of Sociological Method (1895).

questions.q: Verstehen means:
questions.why: Weber's Verstehen is understanding action through the meanings actors attach to it.

questions.q: Routinisation of charisma happens when:
options: A leader's authority is converted into stable rules or tradition
questions.why: After a charismatic leader, followers convert personal authority into traditional or legal forms to make it last.

questions.q: Weber linked capitalism's spirit to which doctrine?
questions.why: Calvinist predestination drove believers to seek signs of grace through disciplined work in a calling.

questions.q: Which pairing is WRONG?
questions.why: Verstehen belongs to Weber; Spencer is linked with social evolution and the organic analogy.

questions.q: Fatalistic suicide is due to:
questions.why: Durkheim described fatalistic suicide as arising from oppressive over-regulation.

questions.q: Calculating cheapest route to work is which action type?
questions.why: Choosing efficient means to a given end is Weber's instrumentally rational (zweckrational) action.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Indian society: caste, kinship, religion and change
courses.summary: Perspectives on Indian society, varna and jati, theories of caste, dominant caste and Sanskritisation, family and kinship, tribes, and processes of change such as Westernisation and modernisation.
outcomes: Distinguish varna and jati and list features of caste (Ghurye)
Explain Sanskritisation, Westernisation and dominant caste (M.N. Srinivas)
Describe joint family, kinship terms and marriage rules
Describe scheduled tribes and constitutional safeguards
Discuss perspectives: Indological, structural-functional, Marxian, subaltern

scenes.text: One scholar studies caste through the Manusmriti; another lives in a Karnataka village for a year.
Their pictures of caste differ — this is the 'book view' versus the 'field view'.

steps.title: Indological / textual
steps.body: Uses classical texts (Vedas, Dharmashastras) to understand Indian institutions. **G.S. Ghurye** (*Caste and Race in India*, 1932) and **Louis Dumont** (*Homo Hierarchicus*, 1966 — caste is based on the opposition of **purity and pollution**).

steps.title: Structural-functional / field view
steps.body: **M.N. Srinivas** (*Religion and Society among the Coorgs*, 1952; Rampura village study, *The Remembered Village*, 1976) and **S.C. Dube** (*Indian Village*, 1955). Stress fieldwork and how institutions function in daily life. Srinivas contrasted 'book view' with 'field view'.

steps.title: Marxian and subaltern
steps.body:
- **Marxian:** **D.P. Mukerji** (dialectics of tradition), **A.R. Desai** (*Social Background of Indian Nationalism*, 1948) — class and economy.
- **Subaltern / Dalit perspective:** **B.R. Ambedkar** (*Annihilation of Caste*, 1936; caste as 'graded inequality'), later Subaltern Studies historians (Ranajit Guha).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Putting Ghurye in the Marxian camp. He combined Indology with ethnography, while A.R. Desai is the classic Marxian.

activity.prompt: Match each scholar to the perspective.

quiz.q: Homo Hierarchicus was written by:
quiz.why: Louis Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus (1966) explains caste through the opposition of purity and pollution.

quiz.q: The 'field view' of Indian society is associated with:
quiz.why: Srinivas used the field view for knowledge gained through intensive fieldwork rather than from sacred texts.

quiz.q: Ambedkar described caste as:
quiz.why: Ambedkar called caste a system of graded inequality in which each caste looks down on those below.

lessons.title: Caste: varna, jati, dominant caste, Sanskritisation

scenes.text: In a village, a middle-ranking caste gives up meat, adopts the sacred thread, and claims higher status.
Srinivas named this Sanskritisation — positional change, not structural change.

steps.title: Varna and jati
steps.body:
- **Varna:** the four-fold textual scheme — Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra (with 'untouchables' outside it). All-India, ideological.
- **Jati:** thousands of local, endogamous, hereditary groups with occupations — the real unit of caste in practice.

steps.title: Ghurye's six features of caste
steps.body:
1. Segmental division of society
2. Hierarchy
3. Restrictions on feeding and social intercourse
4. Civil and religious disabilities and privileges
5. Lack of unrestricted choice of occupation
6. Restrictions on marriage (**endogamy**)

steps.title: Dominant caste (Srinivas)
steps.body: A caste is dominant when it: is numerically strong, owns much of the land, has economic and political power, and has a relatively high ritual status (Western education and jobs add to it). Example in his studies: the Okkaligas of Rampura (Mysore).

steps.title: Sanskritisation and Westernisation
steps.body:
- **Sanskritisation:** a 'low' caste or tribe changes its customs, rituals and way of life in the direction of a high (often twice-born) caste to claim higher status. It gives **positional change** without changing the structure.
- **Westernisation:** changes due to over 150 years of British rule — technology, institutions, ideology, values (education, law, dress).
- **De-Sanskritisation** and caste associations show caste adapting to democracy.

steps.title: Constitution
steps.body: Article 15 prohibits discrimination; **Article 17 abolishes untouchability**; reservations for SCs/STs (Articles 330, 332, 15(4), 16(4)). The Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying Sanskritisation abolishes caste. It only moves a group within the hierarchy; the hierarchy remains.

items.text: A caste adopts vegetarianism and a sacred thread
Families start sending girls to English-medium schools

Adopting courts and written legal procedures

quiz.why: M.N. Srinivas introduced Sanskritisation in his study of the Coorgs (1952).

quiz.why: Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.

lessons.title: Family, kinship and marriage in India

scenes.text: In Varanasi, grandparents, two married sons and their children share one hearth and property.
One grandson moves to Bengaluru and sets up a nuclear household but still sends money home.

steps.title: Joint family
steps.body:
**Irawati Karve:** a joint family is a group of people who generally live under one roof, eat food cooked at one hearth, hold property in common, participate in common worship and are related as kindred.
I.P. Desai measured jointness by function, not just residence. Studies (e.g. A.M. Shah) show nuclear households often keep strong functional ties.

steps.title: Kinship
steps.body:
- **Consanguineal** (blood) and **affinal** (marriage) kin.
- **Descent:** patrilineal (most of India), matrilineal (Nairs of Kerala, Khasi and Garo of Meghalaya).
- **Residence:** patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal.
- Karve's *Kinship Organisation in India* (1953) compared north and south zones: the north forbids marriage among close kin; the south allows cross-cousin and uncle–niece marriage.

steps.title: Marriage rules
steps.body:
- **Endogamy:** marry within caste/sub-caste.
- **Exogamy:** marry outside gotra / sapinda / village (north).
- **Hypergamy (anuloma):** woman marries into a higher group; **hypogamy (pratiloma)** the reverse.
- Forms: monogamy, polygyny, polyandry (fraternal polyandry historically among Todas, some Khasa groups).
Law: Hindu Marriage Act 1955; Special Marriage Act 1954; Dowry Prohibition Act 1961.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming joint families were universal before industrialisation; historical census data show many households were small even then.

activity.prompt: Classify the marriage rule or kin type.

items.text: Not marrying within the same gotra

quiz.q: Matrilineal descent is traditionally found among the:
quiz.why: The Khasi of Meghalaya trace descent through the mother and property passes through the youngest daughter.

quiz.q: Hypergamy means a woman marries:
quiz.why: Hypergamy, or anuloma, is marriage of a woman into a higher-status caste or group.

quiz.q: Kinship Organisation in India was written by:
quiz.why: Irawati Karve's 1953 book compared kinship zones of India.

lessons.title: Tribes and processes of social change

story.title: A dam and a forest village

scenes.text: A Gond village in central India faces displacement by a reservoir.
Debates on isolation, assimilation and integration shape what happens next.

steps.title: Tribes in India
steps.body:
Scheduled Tribes are notified under **Article 342**. Census 2011: about **8.6%** of India's population. Examples: Bhil, Gond, Santhal, Munda, Oraon, Naga groups.
Common features: distinct dialect, territory, kinship-based organisation, low hierarchy compared to caste, close ties with forest.

steps.title: Approaches to tribal policy
steps.body:
- **Isolation** (Verrier Elwin's early 'national park' idea).
- **Assimilation** (G.S. Ghurye: tribes are 'backward Hindus').
- **Integration** — Nehru's **Panchsheel** for tribes (1958 foreword to Elwin): development without imposing, respect for land and forest rights, work through their own institutions.
Laws: Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA 1996, Forest Rights Act 2006.

steps.title: Modernisation of Indian tradition
steps.body: **Yogendra Singh** (*Modernization of Indian Tradition*, 1973) analysed change at cultural and structural levels, from orthogenetic (internal) and heterogenetic (external) sources. Other processes: secularisation, industrialisation, urbanisation, globalisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating 'tribe' and 'caste' as totally separate in practice; many groups lie on a tribe–caste continuum (F.G. Bailey).

activity.prompt: Which approach to tribal policy is this?

items.text: Keep tribal areas closed to outsiders to protect them
Tribes should merge into Hindu society
Develop along their own genius with land rights protected
Gram sabha consent before land acquisition (PESA)

quiz.q: Scheduled Tribes are specified under Article:
quiz.why: Article 342 empowers the President to specify Scheduled Tribes for each state or union territory.

quiz.q: Nehru's tribal Panchsheel favours:
quiz.why: Panchsheel asked for development along tribal people's own lines with respect for their rights — integration.

quiz.q: Orthogenetic sources of change are:
quiz.why: Yogendra Singh used orthogenetic for change arising from within the tradition and heterogenetic for change from contact with other cultures.

questions.q: Purity and pollution as the basis of caste is the view of:
questions.why: Dumont argued that the opposition of pure and impure underlies caste hierarchy.

questions.q: The real unit of the caste system in practice is:
questions.why: Jatis are the local endogamous hereditary groups through which caste actually operates.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of Ghurye's features of caste?
questions.why: Adult franchise is a democratic institution; Ghurye's features include hierarchy, segmental division and marriage restrictions.

questions.q: A dominant caste typically has:
questions.why: Srinivas stressed numbers, land, economic and political power, plus reasonable ritual status.

questions.q: The Remembered Village is about:
questions.why: Srinivas wrote The Remembered Village (1976) about his fieldwork in Rampura near Mysore.

questions.q: S.C. Dube's Indian Village (1955) studied:
questions.why: Dube studied Shamirpet village near Hyderabad.

questions.why: Gotra exogamy requires marriage outside one's own gotra.

questions.why: Karve listed common residence, common hearth, common property and common worship.

questions.why: Census 2011 recorded about 8.6% of the population as Scheduled Tribes (SCs were about 16.6%).

questions.why: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act was passed in 2006.

questions.why: Srinivas defined Westernisation as changes brought by over 150 years of British rule.

questions.why: Ghurye argued tribes were backward Hindus and favoured assimilation.

questions.q: Modernization of Indian Tradition is by:
questions.why: Yogendra Singh published this analysis of cultural and structural change in 1973.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Social research methods
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Research Methods in Sociology)
courses.summary: Research design, hypotheses, variables, sampling, survey, interview, observation and case study, and basic statistics: mean, median, mode, standard deviation and percentages.
outcomes: Distinguish qualitative and quantitative research and research designs
Formulate a hypothesis and identify variables
Choose probability or non-probability sampling and compute sample sizes for strata
Choose suitable data collection tools
Compute mean, median, mode and standard deviation

scenes.text: Kavya wants to study whether SHG membership increases women's say in household decisions.
Her guide asks: what is your hypothesis, and how will you measure 'say'?

steps.title: Steps of research
steps.body: 1. Select problem → 2. Review literature → 3. Formulate hypothesis → 4. Research design → 5. Sampling → 6. Data collection → 7. Analysis → 8. Interpretation and report.

steps.title: Research designs
steps.body:
- **Exploratory:** little known; flexible; generates hypotheses.
- **Descriptive:** describes characteristics accurately (e.g. census-type survey).
- **Explanatory/causal:** tests cause–effect.
- **Experimental:** controlled comparison of experimental and control groups.
Also **cross-sectional** (one point in time) vs **longitudinal** (same units over time).

steps.title: Hypothesis and variables
steps.body:
A **hypothesis** is a testable statement about the relationship between variables. **Null hypothesis (H₀):** no relationship.
- **Independent variable:** presumed cause (SHG membership).
- **Dependent variable:** effect (decision-making score).
- **Operationalisation:** defining how to measure a concept (e.g. 'say' = number of 10 listed decisions where woman's view is decisive).

steps.title: Positivism vs interpretivism
steps.body: Quantitative research (positivist, Durkheim): measurement, statistics, generalisation. Qualitative research (interpretive, Weber): meanings, depth, small samples. Mixed methods combine both. Reliability = consistency; validity = measuring what you intend.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing a hypothesis that cannot be tested, e.g. 'SHGs are good'. State variables and a direction.

activity.prompt: Identify the variable in: 'Higher education of mothers reduces child marriage of daughters.'

quiz.q: A study following the same 500 households every year for 10 years is:
quiz.why: Repeated measurement of the same units over time defines a longitudinal design.

quiz.q: Reliability refers to:
quiz.why: A reliable tool gives consistent results on repetition; validity is about measuring the right thing.

quiz.q: The null hypothesis states that:
options: There is no relationship or difference
quiz.why: H₀ assumes no relationship, and the research tests whether evidence lets us reject it.

scenes.text: A college has 1,200 students; Arjun can interview only 120.
How he chooses those 120 decides whether he can generalise.

steps.title: Probability sampling
steps.body:
Every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection.
- **Simple random:** lottery or random numbers.
- **Systematic:** every k-th unit, k = N/n, random start.
- **Stratified:** divide into strata, sample from each (proportionate or not).
- **Cluster / multistage:** select groups (villages), then units within them (NSSO surveys use multistage).

steps.title: Non-probability sampling
steps.body:
- **Purposive/judgement:** chosen for relevance.
- **Quota:** fill fixed numbers per category non-randomly.
- **Snowball:** respondents refer others — useful for hidden populations (e.g. bonded labourers, sex workers).
- **Convenience/accidental:** whoever is available.

steps.title: Worked example 1: systematic sampling
steps.body:
N = 1,200, n = 120.
k = 1200 / 120 = 10.
Pick a random start between 1 and 10, say 7 → select 7, 17, 27, … 1197.

steps.title: Worked example 2: proportionate stratified
steps.body:
Strata: Arts 600, Science 400, Commerce 200 (total 1,200); n = 120.
Sampling fraction = 120/1200 = 0.1.
Arts 600 × 0.1 = 60; Science 400 × 0.1 = 40; Commerce 200 × 0.1 = 20. Check 60+40+20 = 120 ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling quota sampling 'stratified'. Quota fills categories by convenience, so it is non-probability; stratified selects randomly within strata.

items.text: Every 20th name on the voters' list after a random start
Asking migrant workers to refer others
Lottery from a list of all households
Interviewing whoever passes a bus stop
Random villages, then random households in them

quiz.q: Population 2,000, sample 80. Systematic sampling interval k = ?
quiz.why: k = N ÷ n = 2000 ÷ 80 = 25, so every 25th unit is chosen after a random start.

quiz.q: Strata of 300, 500, 200 and n = 50 (proportionate). Sample from the 500 stratum?
quiz.why: Sampling fraction is 50/1000 = 0.05 and 500 × 0.05 = 25.

quiz.q: Snowball sampling is best for:
quiz.why: When no list exists for a hard-to-reach group, respondents referring others is the practical method.

lessons.title: Tools: survey, interview, observation, case study

story.title: Living in a slum for six months

scenes.text: A researcher rents a room in a Mumbai basti to observe daily life.
Her field notes reveal things no questionnaire captured.

steps.title: Questionnaire and schedule
steps.body:
- **Questionnaire:** filled in by respondents themselves (needs literacy; often mailed/online; low response rate).
- **Schedule:** the researcher asks questions and records answers face to face (works with non-literate respondents).
Questions: closed (fixed options) vs open; avoid leading, double-barrelled and ambiguous questions. **Pilot study** tests the tool.

steps.title: Interviews
steps.body: Structured (fixed questions), semi-structured (guide with probes), unstructured/in-depth. **Focus group discussion (FGD):** 6–10 participants with a moderator. Rapport and neutral probing matter.

steps.title: Observation and case study
steps.body:
- **Participant observation:** researcher joins the group (Malinowski in Trobriand Islands; W.F. Whyte's *Street Corner Society*, 1943). Risk: 'going native'.
- **Non-participant observation:** watching without joining.
- **Case study:** intensive study of one unit (person, village, institution) using multiple sources; strong depth, weak generalisation.
- **Secondary data:** Census, NSSO/NSS, NFHS reports.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality/anonymity, no harm, honest reporting. Extra care with minors and vulnerable groups.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Double-barrelled question: 'Are roads and schools good in your village?' — split into two questions.

items.text: Survey of 2,000 college students by email
Household survey in a village with low literacy
Understanding street gang culture from inside
In-depth history of one cooperative dairy
Life of a single bonded labourer family over years

quiz.q: A schedule differs from a questionnaire because:
quiz.why: In a schedule the investigator asks questions and records answers, so it works with non-literate respondents.

quiz.q: Street Corner Society is a classic of:
quiz.why: W.F. Whyte lived among Italian-American youth in Boston and used participant observation.

quiz.q: 'Do you agree that the corrupt government should resign?' is a flaw of:
quiz.why: The wording pushes the respondent towards one answer, so it is a leading question.

scenes.text: Incomes (₹ thousand): 8, 10, 12, 10, 20.
Mean, median and mode tell different stories when one household earns much more.

steps.title: Measures of central tendency
steps.body:
- **Mean** = Σx / n.
- **Median** = middle value of ordered data (for even n, average of two middle values).
- **Mode** = most frequent value.
Median is preferred for skewed data like income.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
Data: 8, 10, 12, 10, 20.
Σx = 60, n = 5 → mean = 12.
Ordered: 8, 10, 10, 12, 20 → median = 10.
Mode = 10.
The mean (12) is pulled up by the outlier 20.

steps.title: Worked example 2: standard deviation
steps.body:
Same data, mean 12. Deviations: −4, −2, 0, −2, 8.
Squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 64 → sum = 88.
Population variance = 88/5 = 17.6; SD = √17.6 ≈ 4.20.
(Sample SD uses n−1: 88/4 = 22, √22 ≈ 4.69.)

steps.title: Worked example 3: percentages
steps.body:
Of 240 respondents, 66 favour inter-caste marriage.
Percentage = 66/240 × 100 = 27.5%.

steps.title: Levels of measurement
steps.body: Nominal (caste, religion), ordinal (rank, Likert scale), interval (temperature °C), ratio (income, age). Use mode for nominal, median for ordinal, mean for interval/ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting to order the data before finding the median.

quiz.why: The sum is 40 and 40 ÷ 5 = 8.

quiz.q: Median of 3, 9, 5, 7?
quiz.why: Ordered data are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the median is (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = 6.

quiz.q: For skewed income data the best average is usually:
quiz.why: The median is not pulled by extreme values, so it represents a typical income better.

quiz.q: 45 of 180 respondents agree. Percentage?

questions.q: A design used when little is known about a topic is:
questions.why: Exploratory research is flexible and aims to generate insights and hypotheses.

questions.q: In 'Urban residence increases nuclear families', the dependent variable is:
questions.why: Family type is the outcome expected to change with residence.

questions.q: Strata 400 and 600, n = 80 proportionate. Sample from 600 stratum?
Quota sampling is:
questions.why: Units within quotas are chosen non-randomly, so it is non-probability sampling.

questions.q: Which tool suits non-literate respondents?
questions.why: The investigator reads questions and records answers in a schedule.

questions.q: 'Going native' is a risk in:
questions.why: A participant observer may over-identify with the group and lose detachment.

questions.q: Population SD of 2, 4, 6 is about:
questions.why: Mean 4; squared deviations 4, 0, 4 sum to 8; 8/3 ≈ 2.667; √2.667 ≈ 1.63.

questions.q: A Likert scale gives which level of data?
questions.why: Likert responses are ordered categories without equal-interval guarantees, so they are ordinal.

questions.q: Asking 'Are wages and working hours fair?' is:
questions.why: It asks two things at once, so an answer cannot be interpreted clearly.

questions.q: Validity means:
questions.why: A valid tool measures the concept it claims to measure.
8 appears three times, more than any other value.

questions.q: NFHS is an example of:
questions.why: For a student researcher, published National Family Health Survey data are secondary data.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Rural and urban sociology
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Rural Sociology; Urban Sociology)
courses.summary: Rural–urban continuum, the Indian village and jajmani system, agrarian structure and land reforms, Panchayati Raj, urbanisation, Chicago school theories, slums and urban problems.
outcomes: Contrast rural and urban communities and explain the rural–urban continuum
Describe the jajmani system, agrarian classes and land reforms
Explain the 73rd and 74th Amendments
Explain Wirth's urbanism and Burgess's concentric zones
Analyse urbanisation, migration and slums in India

lessons.title: The Indian village and jajmani system

scenes.text: After harvest, a landowning family gives sacks of grain to the barber, potter and carpenter who served them all year.
W.H. Wiser called this the jajmani system (1936).

steps.title: Village as a unit
steps.body: Charles Metcalfe (1830s) called Indian villages 'little republics' — self-sufficient and unchanging. Srinivas, Dube and others showed villages were never fully isolated: they were linked by markets, marriage, pilgrimage and the state. **Robert Redfield's** 'little community' and **great and little traditions** (used by McKim Marriott in Kishan Garhi: universalisation and parochialisation).

steps.title: Jajmani system
steps.body: A hereditary patron–client relationship: **jajman** (patron, usually landowning caste) and **kamin/purjan** (service castes). Payment in kind at harvest plus customary rights. Seen by Wiser as reciprocal; critics (e.g. Beidelman) saw it as exploitative and feudal. It declined with cash economy, mechanisation and migration.

steps.title: Rural–urban contrast and continuum
steps.body: Sorokin & Zimmerman listed differences: occupation, environment, size, density, homogeneity, mobility, social interaction. In reality there is a **rural–urban continuum** — peri-urban villages and small towns share features of both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Describing the village as 'self-sufficient republic' without critique — examiners expect the later fieldwork correction.

items.text: Close link with nature and seasons

quiz.q: The jajmani system was first described in detail by:
quiz.why: William H. Wiser's The Hindu Jajmani System (1936) gave the classic description from Karimpur.

quiz.q: 'Little republics' for Indian villages was used by:
quiz.why: Charles Metcalfe described Indian villages as little republics, a view later questioned by fieldworkers.

quiz.q: Universalisation and parochialisation were concepts of:
quiz.why: Marriott used these terms in his Kishan Garhi study to show flows between little and great traditions.

lessons.title: Agrarian structure, land reforms and Panchayati Raj

scenes.text: In a Bihar village, a few families own most land while many work as sharecroppers.
A woman from a landless Dalit family is elected sarpanch in a reserved seat.

steps.title: Agrarian classes
steps.body: Daniel Thorner's classification: **maliks** (landlords and rich proprietors), **kisans** (working peasants), **mazdoors** (labourers, sharecroppers). Marxian scholars debated 'mode of production' in Indian agriculture. Colonial land tenure: **zamindari** (Permanent Settlement 1793, Bengal), **ryotwari** (Madras, Bombay), **mahalwari** (North-West Provinces/Punjab).

steps.title: Land reforms after 1947
steps.body:
1. Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari abolition) — most successful.
2. Tenancy reform — security, rent regulation.
3. Land ceiling and redistribution — weakly implemented.
4. Consolidation of holdings.
Success stories: West Bengal's **Operation Barga** (1978), Kerala's tenancy reforms. **Green Revolution** (mid-1960s) raised output but widened regional and class inequality (Punjab, Haryana, western UP).

steps.title: Panchayati Raj
steps.body: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended three tiers. **73rd Amendment (1992)**: Part IX, three-tier system (village, intermediate, district), gram sabha, 5-year terms, reservation for SC/ST and **not less than one-third seats for women**, State Election Commission, State Finance Commission, Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects). Many states have raised women's reservation to 50%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying 73rd Amendment covers municipalities — that is the 74th Amendment (Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule).

quiz.q: The 73rd Amendment added which Schedule?
quiz.why: The 73rd Amendment added the Eleventh Schedule listing 29 subjects for panchayats.

quiz.q: Operation Barga was a tenancy reform in:
quiz.why: West Bengal launched Operation Barga in 1978 to record sharecroppers and secure their rights.

quiz.q: Thorner's 'mazdoor' class refers to:
quiz.why: Thorner used mazdoors for those who earn mainly by working on others' land.

scenes.text: Hundreds of people stand inches apart in a Delhi Metro coach without speaking.
Louis Wirth described this as urbanism as a way of life.

steps.title: Louis Wirth (1938)
steps.body: 'Urbanism as a Way of Life': cities are defined by **size, density and heterogeneity**. These produce secondary, segmental, impersonal and superficial relations, weakened kinship, formal control and a blasé attitude. Georg Simmel ('The Metropolis and Mental Life', 1903) described the **blasé attitude**.

steps.title: Chicago school ecological models
steps.body:
- **Burgess's concentric zone model (1925):** 1 Central Business District, 2 Zone in transition (slums, immigrants), 3 Working-class homes, 4 Residential zone, 5 Commuter zone.
- **Hoyt's sector model (1939):** wedges along transport routes.
- **Harris & Ullman's multiple nuclei (1945):** several centres.
Concepts: invasion and succession (Park).

steps.title: Other views
steps.body:
- **Pre-industrial city** (Gideon Sjoberg).
- **Political economy:** David Harvey and Manuel Castells — cities shaped by capital and collective consumption.
- **Global cities** (Saskia Sassen).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Putting slums in Burgess's outer zone — in his model the zone in transition (zone 2) next to the CBD has the slums.

quiz.q: Wirth's three determinants of urbanism are:
quiz.why: Wirth argued that large size, high density and heterogeneity create the urban way of life.

quiz.q: In Burgess's model, zone 2 is the:
quiz.why: The zone in transition lies next to the CBD and houses slums, immigrants and decaying housing.

quiz.q: The 'blasé attitude' was described by:
quiz.why: Simmel argued that metropolitan overstimulation leads to a blasé, indifferent attitude.

lessons.title: Urbanisation, migration and slums in India

scenes.text: Rakesh leaves his village to work in a Surat textile unit and lives in a crowded room with six others.
He sends money home every month — circular migration ties city and village.

steps.title: Urbanisation in India
steps.body: Census 2011: urban population **31.2%** (377 million). **Census town** criteria: population ≥ 5,000, density ≥ 400 per km², and ≥ 75% of male main workers in non-agricultural work. Census 2011 counted 53 million-plus urban agglomerations.

steps.title: Worked example: growth rate
steps.body:
A town's population rises from 80,000 to 1,00,000 in 10 years.
Decadal growth = (100000 − 80000)/80000 × 100 = 25%.

steps.title: Migration
steps.body: Streams: rural→urban, rural→rural (largest, mainly women for marriage), urban→urban, urban→rural. **Push factors:** poverty, landlessness, drought. **Pull factors:** jobs, wages, education. Lee's push–pull theory (1966) adds intervening obstacles.

steps.title: Slums and urban problems
steps.body: Census 2011 recorded about 65 million slum dwellers. Problems: housing shortage, sanitation, water, informal work, pollution, crime and traffic. Policies: JNNURM (2005), PMAY-Urban (2015), Smart Cities Mission (2015), AMRUT (2015). **Over-urbanisation** means urban growth faster than jobs and services.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming most internal migration is rural→urban male labour. In census data the biggest stream is rural→rural, mostly women migrating on marriage.

activity.prompt: Push or pull factor for migration?

Census 2011 urban share of India's population was about:
quiz.why: Census 2011 counted about 31.2% of the population as urban.

quiz.q: The largest migration stream in India by census is:
quiz.why: Rural-to-rural migration, largely women moving after marriage, is the largest stream.

questions.why: The jajman receives services and pays the kamin in kind.

questions.q: Kishan Garhi was studied by:
questions.why: McKim Marriott studied Kishan Garhi in Uttar Pradesh.

questions.why: Louis Wirth published this essay in 1938.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Modern theories, revision, fieldwork practicals & exam
courses.summary: Functionalism (Parsons, Merton), conflict theory (Dahrendorf, Coser), symbolic interactionism (Blumer, Goffman), then hands-on fieldwork practicals and a full revision sheet with exam-style questions.
outcomes: Explain Parsons's AGIL and pattern variables and Merton's manifest/latent functions and anomie typology
Compare conflict theory and symbolic interactionism
Plan and order the steps of a small field survey
Tabulate and interpret field data with percentages
Answer exam-style questions across the whole syllabus

scenes.text: The Hopi rain dance may not bring rain.
Merton said its latent function is to bring the group together.

steps.title: Talcott Parsons
steps.body:
*The Social System* (1951). Every system must meet four functional prerequisites — **AGIL**: **A**daptation (economy), **G**oal attainment (polity), **I**ntegration (law, norms), **L**atency/pattern maintenance (family, education).
**Pattern variables:** affectivity vs affective neutrality; diffuseness vs specificity; particularism vs universalism; ascription vs achievement; collectivity vs self orientation.

steps.title: Robert K. Merton
steps.body:
*Social Theory and Social Structure* (1949). Theories of the **middle range**.
- **Manifest functions** (intended, recognised) vs **latent functions** (unintended, unrecognised); **dysfunctions**.
- **Anomie / strain theory:** gap between cultural goals and institutional means → five adaptations: **conformity** (+ +), **innovation** (+ −), **ritualism** (− +), **retreatism** (− −), **rebellion** (± ±).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A clerk who no longer cares about promotion but follows every rule rigidly: rejects goal (−), accepts means (+) → **ritualism**.
A student who wants top marks and cheats: accepts goal (+), rejects means (−) → **innovation**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing retreatism (drops both goals and means, e.g. vagrants) with rebellion (replaces both with new ones, e.g. revolutionaries).

Goffman would say she is managing impressions on the 'front stage'.

steps.title: Modern conflict theory
steps.body:
- **Ralf Dahrendorf** (*Class and Class Conflict in Industrial Society*, 1959): conflict arises from unequal **authority** in 'imperatively coordinated associations', not only ownership.
- **Lewis Coser** (*The Functions of Social Conflict*, 1956): conflict can strengthen group cohesion and act as a 'safety valve'.
- **C. Wright Mills:** *The Power Elite* (1956), *The Sociological Imagination* (1959) — linking personal troubles to public issues.

steps.title: Symbolic interactionism
steps.body:
**Herbert Blumer** coined the term (1937). Three premises: (1) people act towards things on the basis of meanings; (2) meanings arise from social interaction; (3) meanings are modified through interpretation.
**Erving Goffman** (*The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life*, 1959): **dramaturgy** — front stage, back stage, impression management. **Labelling theory** (Howard Becker, *Outsiders*, 1963): deviance is behaviour people so label.

steps.title: Other strands
steps.body: Phenomenology (Alfred Schutz), ethnomethodology (Harold Garfinkel — breaching experiments), structuration (Anthony Giddens), habitus and cultural capital (Pierre Bourdieu).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Attributing 'symbolic interactionism' as a term to Mead — Mead laid foundations; Blumer named it.

quiz.why: Goffman analysed social life as a performance with front and back stages.

quiz.why: Coser showed that conflict with outsiders and safety-valve institutions can increase cohesion.

quiz.why: C. Wright Mills introduced the distinction in The Sociological Imagination (1959).

lessons.title: Lab: Planning a mini field survey

scenes.text: Your practical asks for a 30-household survey on the use of a public distribution shop.
You must submit a plan, tool, data table and short report.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Choose a topic and write objectives.
2. Review 3–5 sources (Census tables, NFHS factsheet, one article).
3. Write a hypothesis and define variables.
4. Select the area and sampling method (e.g. systematic from a household list).
5. Draft a schedule of 15–20 questions; pilot with 3 households.
6. Take informed consent; collect data.
7. Code, tabulate, compute percentages.
8. Write the report: introduction, method, findings, conclusion, limitations.

steps.title: Worked example: sample
steps.body: The ward has 300 households and you need 30. k = 300/30 = 10. Random start 4 → households 4, 14, 24, … 294.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why did you choose a schedule over a questionnaire?
- What is your independent variable?
- How did you ensure confidentiality?
- What are the limitations of a 30-household sample?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Skipping the pilot. Unclear questions found only after data collection cannot be fixed.

activity.prompt: Which stage of research does each task belong to?

quiz.q: 300 households, sample 30: interval k = ?
The purpose of a pilot study is to:
quiz.why: Piloting reveals unclear or sensitive questions before full data collection.

quiz.q: Which belongs in the 'limitations' section?
quiz.why: Limitations explain what restricts generalisation, such as a small single-ward sample.

lessons.title: Lab: Tabulating and interpreting field data

scenes.text: Your 30 schedules are done. Now: what do they show?
A simple cross-table can reveal a pattern.

steps.title: Worked example 1: frequency table
steps.body:
Ration shop use (n = 30): Regular 18, Occasional 8, Never 4.
Percentages: 18/30 = 60%, 8/30 ≈ 26.7%, 4/30 ≈ 13.3%. Total 100%.

steps.title: Worked example 2: cross-tabulation
steps.body:
Regular users by card type:
- Antyodaya (AAY) cards: 10 households, 9 regular → 90%.
- Priority household cards: 20 households, 9 regular → 45%.
Interpretation: regular use is much higher among AAY holders, suggesting greater dependence of the poorest households (needs a larger sample to confirm).

steps.title: Writing findings
steps.body: Report numbers and percentages together ('18 of 30, i.e. 60%'). Compare categories by percentage within the independent variable. Avoid causal claims from a small descriptive survey.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Percentaging in the wrong direction: compute percentages within each category of the independent variable (card type), not within the dependent variable.

scenes.text: You have one page to revise the whole syllabus.
Thinkers, books, concepts — linked together.

steps.title: Thinkers and key works
steps.body:
- Comte: three stages; positivism.
- Spencer: organic analogy; militant → industrial.
- Marx: *Communist Manifesto* (1848), *Capital* (1867); alienation, surplus value.
- Durkheim: *Division of Labour* (1893), *Rules* (1895), *Suicide* (1897), *Elementary Forms* (1912).
- Weber: *Protestant Ethic* (1905); *Economy and Society* (posthumous); authority, ideal type.
- Parsons: AGIL; Merton: manifest/latent, anomie.
- Srinivas: Sanskritisation, dominant caste; Dumont: purity–pollution; Ghurye: features of caste; Karve: kinship.

steps.title: Indian society and rural–urban facts
steps.body: Art. 17 untouchability; Art. 342 STs; 73rd/74th Amendments (1992); Census 2011: urban 31.2%, ST 8.6%, SC 16.6%; Wirth: size, density, heterogeneity; Burgess: 5 concentric zones.

steps.title: Long-answer practice (original, exam-style)
steps.body:
1. 'Caste in India is changing but not disappearing.' Discuss with reference to Sanskritisation and dominant caste. (15 marks)
2. Compare Durkheim and Weber on the method of sociology. (15 marks)
3. Explain types of sampling with suitable examples from Indian research. (10 marks)
4. Critically assess Wirth's theory in the context of Indian cities. (10 marks)

steps.title: Answer-writing tip
steps.body: Structure: definition → thinker and work → 3–5 points with Indian examples → critique → conclusion. Underline key terms.
